P0139.d: The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor (about 0.1–0.9 V) used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. P0139 means the sensor reacts too slowly to mixture changes. Subaru measures it around fuel cut-off: rich to lean from 500 to 300 mV must take no more than 0.51 s, lean to rich from 300 to 500 mV no more than 2 s; two drive cycles set the MIL. CARB requires such a test because a sluggish downstream sensor could let a worn converter pass. Since about 2009–2011 GM and Ford report this as direction-specific codes P013A–P013F instead; P0139 remains in use on older, Asian and Jaguar Land Rover systems. When it fails, the control module stops the downstream trim and cannot evaluate the converter; there is no limp mode.

P013A.d: The downstream oxygen sensor (sensor 2, after the catalytic converter) is used for fine mixture trim and to monitor the converter. 'Slow response' means the signal transition itself is too sluggish – it takes too long to pass between two voltage levels. This code covers the rich-to-lean direction, usually tested during deceleration fuel cut-off. GM forces the test itself and measures how quickly the signal passes from 450 to 150 mV relative to air flow; a filtered value above its limit sets the code after one trip (fallback: target not reached before about 60 g of air). Ford measures the slew rate during fuel cut-off, normalised to the converter's stored oxygen. Lexus traced one case to a leaking manifold gasket ahead of the sensor; on Ram diesels it is soot-related. CARB requires separate detection of slow and delayed faults in each direction (phased in from 2009 for downstream and 2011 for upstream sensors).

No manufacturer document describing P015E itself, or its threshold, was found; the description rests on CARB and the sister code. P0163 means the signal stays close to 0 V – typically the signal wire is shorted to ground; on some modules an open circuit is also reported this way, and an exhaust leak ahead of the sensor can make it read lean. For the bank 2 sensor 2 counterpart GM uses below 50 mV within 50 s, Ford a pull-up resistance check (short below 10 Ω, open above 1 MΩ). Jaguar Land Rover assigns the code to that sensor and names software (fixed by reconfiguring the engine module) and water-induced thermal shock as causes; no thresholds are published for sensor 3, so the logic follows the sensor 2 checks. When it fails, the downstream evaluation of that converter is suspended; there is no limp mode.
s: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Catalyst readiness incomplete
Usually no noticeable change in driving

c: Signal wire shorted to voltage or to the heater wire
P0164.d: Sensor 3 on bank 2 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick. It is rare – documented for Jaguar Land Rover's supercharged V6 and V8 (2013–2016), where it is the 'post-cat' sensor of the second bank, and for Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. P0164 means the signal is above about 1.05–1.15 V. A switching sensor can produce at most about 1 V, so anything higher is electrical: a short to voltage or to the heater wire, or – on GM's bias logic – an open ground. Ford's over-voltage test (above 1.1 V for 10 s) explicitly covers downstream sensors 2 and 3. Jaguar Land Rover assigns the code to that sensor and names software (fixed by reconfiguring the engine module) and water-induced thermal shock as causes; no thresholds are published for sensor 3, so the logic follows the sensor 2 checks. When it fails, the downstream evaluation of that converter is suspended; there is no limp mode.
s: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Catalyst readiness incomplete
Usually no noticeable change in driving

c: Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor
P0165.d: Sensor 3 on bank 2 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick. It is rare – documented for Jaguar Land Rover's supercharged V6 and V8 (2013–2016), where it is the 'post-cat' sensor of the second bank, and for Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. P0165 means sensor 3 reacts too slowly to mixture changes, typically measured around fuel cut-off as for the downstream sensor 2 (Subaru limits for P0139: 0.51 s rich to lean, 2 s lean to rich). No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found – the Jaguar Land Rover bulletins list only P0162–P0164 and P0167 for this sensor. The description rests on CARB's response requirement for downstream sensors and the sensor 2 logic. When it fails, the downstream evaluation of that converter is suspended; there is no limp mode.
s: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Catalyst readiness incomplete
Usually no noticeable change in driving

c: Signal or ground wire open, connector corroded
P0166.d: Sensor 3 on bank 2 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick. It is rare – documented for Jaguar Land Rover's supercharged V6 and V8 (2013–2016), where it is the 'post-cat' sensor of the second bank, and for Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. P0166 means sensor 3 shows no voltage change or stays in the control module's bias band – an open or high-resistance circuit, or a cold or dead sensor. For downstream sensor 2 GM sets the equivalent code when the voltage does not change after heater warm-up (within 15 s) or sits at 401–548 mV. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; Jaguar Land Rover does not list it and Ford uses only heater codes for sensor 3. A failed heater (P0167) can cause it. When it fails, the downstream evaluation of that converter is suspended; there is no limp mode.
s: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Often together with P0167
Usually no noticeable change in driving

c: Engine module driver or software (Jaguar Land Rover)
P0167.d: Sensor 3 on bank 2 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick. It is rare – documented for Jaguar Land Rover's supercharged V6 and V8 (2013–2016), where it is the 'post-cat' sensor of the second bank, and for Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. P0167 concerns its heater. Ford checks the driver voltage continuously and the heater current once per drive cycle when the sensor is estimated above about 120 °C and has heated for 30 s; below 0.22–0.55 A (depending on sensor type) or above 3 A is a fault, and the heater resistance has its own code (P0061). Jaguar Land Rover lists P0167 for its post-cat sensor of the second bank. A cold sensor can lead to P0165/P0166. When it fails, the downstream evaluation of that converter is suspended; there is no limp mode.
s: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
P0165/P0166 may follow
Usually no noticeable change in driving

c: Fuel cooler (air or water cooler in the return) dirty or faulty, coolant circuit disturbed
Very little fuel in the tank at high load or heat
Excessive return flow from worn high-pressure pump or injectors, or faulty overflow valve
Fuel temperature sensor drifting and reading too high
P0168.d: P0168 is not a sensor fault but an operating condition, almost only on diesels: the fuel temperature sensor reports fuel hotter than a protective limit. The fuel heats up through the return flow from the high-pressure pump and injectors, especially with little fuel in the tank, at idle after full load, in hot weather or with a failed fuel cooler; one manufacturer patent names about 80 °C as the upper limit to protect seals, against a normal range of roughly 5–60 °C. On Saab's Bosch EDC16 diesels the code means an engine protection function is active and injection quantity is reduced. No manufacturer threshold was found, and GM's and Ford's diesel summaries do not use P0168. Whether the warning light comes on depends on the manufacturer.
s: Loss of power, limp mode (reduced injection quantity)
Warning light depending on manufacturer
Occurs in heat, at full load, with little fuel in the tank

c: Wrong fuel (E85 in a non-flex-fuel vehicle, ethanol content outside calibration)
Water or contamination in the fuel
Fuel composition sensor drifting (value in range but wrong)
P0169.d: According to its title, P0169 means the control module has detected a fuel composition outside what is expected – wrong fuel or an impermissible ethanol or water content – while the composition sensor itself works. None of the manufacturer OBD documents checked (GM, Ford) uses the code: GM reports water or conductive fuel via the ethanol sensor frequency as P2269, and Ford has had no composition sensor since 2000. Claims that diesel makers use it for misfuelling or water could not be verified. The description therefore rests on CARB, which lists the fuel composition sensor as a monitored component, and on component information. Unrecognised fuel usually also shows up as mixture adaptation codes.
s: Check engine light on
Poor cold start, stumbling, loss of power
Mixture adaptation codes (P0171/P0172)
Higher consumption

c: Oxygen sensor heater not working (fuse, fuse holder, wiring, heater element)
Engine not warming up (thermostat open, coolant sensor)
P016A.d: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. Closed loop needs a heated, working oxygen sensor and plausible engine data. P016A means the mixture control did not switch to closed loop within the calibrated time after starting; the engine then runs on map values with higher emissions but no actual limp mode. CARB requires this check, and since 2019 also after every automatic restart in start-stop systems. Bentley and other VW group petrol engines set it together with oxygen sensor heater codes when the heater fuse holder was damaged; Ram's 3.0 EcoDiesel listed it in bulletins fixed with new software and sensors. Time limits are not public.
s: Check engine light on
Higher consumption after cold start
Often with oxygen sensor or heater codes

c: Fuel pressure too high / high-pressure pump or regulator fault (direct injection)
Oxygen sensor or air flow/pressure sensor offset, control module software
P016B.d: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P016B means the mixture control as a whole has reached its lower limit: it already removes as much fuel as allowed and the mixture is still rich. In substance it matches P0172, but without a bank reference – for manufacturers whose strategy evaluates the control loop as a whole. CARB requires a fault once the adaptation has used up its range. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; Hyundai documents the lean counterpart P016C. Typical causes are those of a rich mixture: excessive fuel pressure, leaking injectors or an open purge valve.
s: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)
Poor cold start, rough idle
Higher consumption, fuel smell
Often together with P0172

c: Fuel pressure or delivery too low
Wrongly learned adaptation / control module software
Air flow or pressure sensor reading low, injectors clogged
P016C.d: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P016C means the mixture control as a whole has reached its upper limit: it already adds as much fuel as allowed and still cannot reach lambda 1. In substance it matches P0171, without a bank reference. Hyundai documents it on the 2021 Elantra 2.0: if the fuel adaptation was learned wrongly after starts below −10 °C, the engine could stall when stopping or at idle and set P016C; new engine software changed the learning logic. Otherwise the usual lean causes apply: air leaks, low fuel delivery or an air flow sensor reading low.
s: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)
Stalling when stopping or at idle
Rough idle, hesitation
Often together with P0171

c: Volume or pressure control valve sticking or worn
Unstable low-pressure supply (filter, lift pump, air in system)
Fuel leak or high injector return flow
P016D.d: Common-rail diesels regulate rail pressure in closed loop: the control module compares the rail pressure sensor with the target and adjusts a volume or pressure control valve, learning correction factors as it goes. CARB requires faults to be flagged when this feedback control does not start in time or runs out of authority. P016D means the pressure control has not settled into closed loop, or has not learned, in the time allowed. Ford's 2023 diesels (6.7 and 3.0 litre) set it when, within the learning conditions – target rail pressure 600–1300 bar, fuel at most 40 °C – no new adaptation factor has been learned after 300 s; the check only runs while the rail pressure sensor and its supply are fault-free. Ford reports adaptation at its limit separately as P228E/P228F. Use on petrol engines was not found. Often there are no noticeable symptoms.
s: Check engine light on
Often no noticeable symptoms
Occasional power reduction or rough idle

c: Rail pressure sensor or its contacts/wiring (corrosion) giving a falsely high signal
Pressure or volume control valve sticking (lets too much through)
Return line from control valve or rail blocked or kinked
P016E.d: Common-rail diesels regulate rail pressure in closed loop: the control module compares the rail pressure sensor with the target and adjusts a volume or pressure control valve, learning correction factors as it goes. CARB requires faults to be flagged when this feedback control does not start in time or runs out of authority. P016E means the controller is already at its limit in the 'reduce pressure' direction and the measured pressure is still above target. That can be real overpressure – a control valve that lets too much through or a blocked return – or a falsely high reading. Volvo and Mack document P016E on their 11 and 13 litre truck diesels together with P0194, caused by corroded contacts at the rail pressure sensor; the fix is a new sensor and internal harness. No public thresholds exist; Ford reports the comparable condition as P228F. Use on passenger-car diesels or petrol engines was not documented.
s: Check engine light on
Hard combustion noise, knocking
Power reduction (limp mode)
Sometimes no symptoms (intermittent sensor fault)

c: Weak low-pressure supply: lift/tank pump, pump control module, clogged filter
Connector or ground problems (corrosion, water) at pump module, low-pressure sensor or ground point
Pressure relief valve open or its control circuit interrupted
Worn high-pressure pump or internal leak
P016F.d: Common-rail diesels regulate rail pressure in closed loop: the control module compares the rail pressure sensor with the target and adjusts a volume or pressure control valve, learning correction factors as it goes. CARB requires faults to be flagged when this feedback control does not start in time or runs out of authority. P016F means the controller is at its limit in the 'more pressure' direction and the actual pressure still stays below target. Which circuit is meant depends on the manufacturer: Volvo and Mack use it for rail pressure, for example as a follow-up when their electronic pressure relief valve stays open (P009B); on FCA's 3.0 EcoDiesel it concerns the regulated low-pressure supply via the fuel pump control module and appears with P025C and P01C6, partly fixed by new engine software. No public thresholds exist. Weak supply pumps, clogged filters and corroded connectors or grounds are typical causes.
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power, sluggish acceleration
Hard starting, long cranking, stalling after start
Rough cold idle

c: Air flow sensor dirty or drifting
Air leak or crankcase ventilation leaking
Injection quantity error (diesel: injector drift, rail pressure sensor; petrol: injectors, fuel pressure)
P0170.d: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P0170 is the older, direction-neutral code for 'mixture adaptation of bank 1 out of range'; whether lean or rich has to be read from the trim values. Users are Mercedes-Benz petrol engines, which often set P0170/P0173 instead of P0171–P0175 – a Mercedes-Benz magazine for independent workshops reports that cleaning or replacing the air flow sensor most often cures it – and Ford's 6.7 litre diesel, where it flags a fuel quantity error above 15 % in either direction from its fuel mass observer. GM and Ford petrol engines do not use it. Two trips.
s: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)
Rough idle or hesitation
Higher consumption
Often no symptoms

c: Air leak after the air flow sensor (intake manifold gasket, vacuum hoses, throttle body gasket, brake booster line)
Crankcase ventilation leaking or faulty (PCV hose, diaphragm in valve cover, oil cap, dipstick)
Air flow sensor dirty or drifting (measures too little air)
Fuel pressure or delivery too low (weak pump, clogged filter, regulator, tank nearly empty)
Injectors clogged, or exhaust leak ahead of the oxygen sensor
P0171.d: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P0171 means long-term trim on bank 1 is at its upper limit: the module already adds the maximum fuel and the mixture still stays lean. GM sets it at a long-term factor of about 1.30–1.36 (+30–36 %, engine-specific), Ford above +25 % with short-term trim above +1 %; it needs two trips and is suspended during heavy purge flow or intrusive tests. GM bulletins repeatedly trace it to leaking crankcase ventilation hoses or pipes on V6 and V8 engines; Ford found leaking direct injectors. P0171 together with P0174 points to a shared cause. Diagnosis hint: trims very high only at idle and normal under load point to an air leak; trims rising with load point to fuel shortage or an air flow sensor reading low. The oxygen sensor only reports what is in the exhaust and is rarely the cause.
s: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)
Rough or unsteady idle, possibly stalling
Hesitation or lack of power when accelerating
Hissing or whistling from the engine bay (air leak, PCV)

c: Purge valve stuck open or charcoal canister saturated
Leaking or dripping injectors (also direct injection)
Fuel pressure too high (faulty regulator, blocked return, regulator vacuum hose)
Fuel in the engine oil (short trips, leaking injectors), vapour via crankcase ventilation
Clogged air filter or intake, air flow sensor reading high; flex-fuel: wrongly learned ethanol content
P0172.d: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P0172 means long-term trim on bank 1 is at its lower limit: the module already removes the maximum fuel and the mixture still stays rich. GM separates purge influence carefully: before the first purge it evaluates passively (factor 0.70 or below, i.e. −30 %), afterwards it closes the purge valve briefly for an active test, so a full charcoal canister is not counted as a fault. Ford only evaluates with purge off, at −25 %. Two trips. Bulletins name an open purge valve, leaking direct injectors and, on flex-fuel vehicles, a wrongly learned ethanol content. A permanently rich mixture can overheat the converter and dilutes the oil.
s: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)
Higher consumption, fuel smell
Black smoke, sooted spark plugs
Rough idle or starting problems after refuelling; converter damage possible later

c: Air flow sensor dirty or faulty
Air leak on bank 2 or at the crankcase ventilation
Exhaust leak ahead of the bank 2 oxygen sensor
P0173.d: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P0173 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0170: a direction-neutral trim fault, so whether bank 2 runs lean or rich has to be read from the trim values. It is mainly used by Mercedes-Benz V6 and V8 petrol engines instead of P0174/P0175; their workshop magazine names the air flow sensor as the most frequent fix. P0170 and P0173 together point to a common cause. No manufacturer threshold was found; the description rests on CARB's fuel system monitoring requirement and that publication. Two trips.
s: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)
Rough idle
Higher consumption
Often no symptoms

c: Air leak after the air flow sensor on bank 2 (intake manifold gasket, vacuum hoses, throttle body gasket, brake booster line)
Crankcase ventilation leaking or faulty (PCV hose, diaphragm in valve cover, oil cap, dipstick)
Air flow sensor dirty or drifting (measures too little air)
Fuel pressure or delivery too low (weak pump, clogged filter, regulator, tank nearly empty)
Injectors clogged, or exhaust leak ahead of the oxygen sensor
P0174.d: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P0174 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0171 and only exists on V and boxer engines with separate mixture control per bank. The limits match: GM a long-term factor of about 1.30 (engine-specific), Ford above +25 % with short-term trim above +1 %; an older Saab V6 flagged more than 25 % deviation for 20 s. Two trips, no limp mode. P0174 alone points to a leak, injector or exhaust leak on bank 2; together with P0171 to a shared cause such as the air flow sensor, fuel pressure or crankcase ventilation – exactly what several GM bulletins describe. Diagnosis hint: trims very high only at idle and normal under load point to an air leak; trims rising with load point to fuel shortage or an air flow sensor reading low. The oxygen sensor only reports what is in the exhaust and is rarely the cause.
s: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)
Rough or unsteady idle, possibly stalling
Hesitation or lack of power when accelerating
Hissing or whistling from the engine bay (air leak, PCV)

c: Purge valve stuck open or charcoal canister saturated
Leaking or dripping injectors on bank 2 (also direct injection)
Fuel pressure too high (faulty regulator, blocked return, regulator vacuum hose)
Fuel in the engine oil (short trips, leaking injectors), vapour via crankcase ventilation
P0175.d: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P0175 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0172: long-term trim at its lower limit, mixture still rich. GM evaluates it like bank 1 with a passive test before the first purge and an active test with the purge valve closed; Ford at −25 % with purge off. Two trips, no limp mode. P0175 alone points to a bank-specific cause such as a leaking injector on bank 2; together with P0172 to fuel pressure, purge, ethanol learning on flex-fuel vehicles or fuel in the oil. GM and Ford bulletins document wrongly learned ethanol content and a purge valve stuck open as causes.
s: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)
Higher consumption, fuel smell
Black smoke, sooted spark plugs
Rough idle or starting problems after refuelling; converter damage possible later

c: Flex-fuel sensor electrically failed (corrosion from road salt)
Connector or wire corroded, open or shorted
P0176.d: The fuel composition sensor is fitted only to flex-fuel vehicles that can run on petrol or ethanol up to E85. GM uses a capacitive sensor in the fuel line whose square-wave output frequency gives the ethanol content – 50 Hz for E0 up to 150 Hz for E100 – while the pulse width carries the fuel temperature. Ford has calculated the ethanol content from the oxygen sensor feedback after refuelling since model year 2000 and has no such sensor. P0176 is the general circuit fault of this sensor without telling low from high. GM's current documents use P0178/P0179 instead, so P0176 is mainly to be expected on older flex-fuel vehicles or other makes. GM issued a special coverage for 2013–2014 flex-fuel models (10 years/150,000 miles) because road salt could make the sensor fail electrically, turning on the MIL and disabling remote start. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the description rests on CARB's circuit monitoring requirement and component information.
s: Check engine light on
Ethanol content in scan data implausible or frozen
Starting problems on E85

c: Water or contamination in the fuel
P0177.d: The fuel composition sensor is fitted only to flex-fuel vehicles that can run on petrol or ethanol up to E85. GM uses a capacitive sensor in the fuel line whose square-wave output frequency gives the ethanol content – 50 Hz for E0 up to 150 Hz for E100 – while the pulse width carries the fuel temperature. Ford has calculated the ethanol content from the oxygen sensor feedback after refuelling since model year 2000 and has no such sensor. P0177 means the signal lies within the valid frequency range but is implausible – it jumps, changes without a refuelling event or does not match the mixture adaptation. Such sensors measure permittivity, conductivity and temperature and compare them with tables of known blends. GM's documents only list low, high and P2269, so no manufacturer threshold for P0177 was found; the description rests on CARB's rationality requirement and component information.
s: Check engine light on
Wrong ethanol value, stumbling or starting problems
Adaptation codes P0171/P0172

c: Signal wire open or shorted to ground
P0178.d: The fuel composition sensor is fitted only to flex-fuel vehicles that can run on petrol or ethanol up to E85. GM uses a capacitive sensor in the fuel line whose square-wave output frequency gives the ethanol content – 50 Hz for E0 up to 150 Hz for E100 – while the pulse width carries the fuel temperature. Ford has calculated the ethanol content from the oxygen sensor feedback after refuelling since model year 2000 and has no such sensor. P0178 means the frequency is too low. GM sets it below 45 Hz with 50 of 63 samples failing at 100 ms intervals (about 6 s), monitored continuously with the powertrain relay above 11 V; two trips. 'Low' refers to the frequency, not to the ethanol content: an open wire, missing supply or short to ground gives 0 Hz. The control module then uses a learned or substitute ethanol value. GM's road-salt special coverage for 2013–2014 flex-fuel models concerns exactly this kind of electrical failure.
s: Check engine light on
Ethanol value 0 % or frozen
Starting problems on E85
GM: remote start disabled

c: Interference or short on the signal wire
Water or conductive fuel near the P2269 limit
P0179.d: The fuel composition sensor is fitted only to flex-fuel vehicles that can run on petrol or ethanol up to E85. GM uses a capacitive sensor in the fuel line whose square-wave output frequency gives the ethanol content – 50 Hz for E0 up to 150 Hz for E100 – while the pulse width carries the fuel temperature. Ford has calculated the ethanol content from the oxygen sensor feedback after refuelling since model year 2000 and has no such sensor. P0179 means the frequency is above the physically possible range for E100 plus tolerance. GM sets it between 155 and 185 Hz (50 of 63 samples, two trips); above 185 Hz it sets P2269 instead, because such a high value indicates water or conductive fuel rather than a sensor fault. Typical causes of P0179 are failed sensor electronics or interference on the signal wire. With a falsely high ethanol value the mixture tends to run rich.
s: Check engine light on
Ethanol value implausibly high (100 %)
Rich mixture, stumbling, higher consumption

c: Wiring or connector open or corroded
P017A.d: The cylinder head temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor that measures the temperature of the cylinder head metal or of the coolant in the head. Some Ford engines use it instead of a coolant temperature sensor and calculate a coolant value from it; VW group V8 petrol engines use it as sender G407. CARB requires such sensors to be monitored like the coolant sensor. P017A is the general circuit fault without telling low from high. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found: VW uses P017B/P017C/P017E for its sensor, and Ford's summaries list its own codes. Ford's published summaries still use its own codes P1289/P1290 for this sensor (fault below 0.244 V or above 4.96 V for 5 s). The description rests on CARB and component information. On a sensor fault the control module typically uses a modelled temperature and runs the radiator fan.
s: Check engine light on
Coolant temperature warning or wrong gauge reading
Radiator fan runs loud or constantly
Cold-start problems possible

c: Genuine temperature problem (air in cooling system, thermostat)
P017B.d: The cylinder head temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor that measures the temperature of the cylinder head metal or of the coolant in the head. Some Ford engines use it instead of a coolant temperature sensor and calculate a coolant value from it; VW group V8 petrol engines use it as sender G407. CARB requires such sensors to be monitored like the coolant sensor. P017B means the signal is electrically valid but implausible – for example it does not fit other temperature sensors after a long standstill or does not rise as expected. Audi documents it on 2019–2021 V8 TFSI models and Bentley on V8 models from 2018 onwards, together with a cooling system fault code and a red coolant warning: a damaged O-ring at the sensor tip lets water into the housing and damages the sensing element, often intermittently; the fix is a new sender. GM lists P017B only as an exclusion condition in its diesel software. Thresholds are not public.
s: Check engine light on
Red coolant warning or overheating warning
Radiator fan runs loud or constantly
Possibly reduced power

c: Water or coolant inside the sensor (O-ring damaged)
P017C.d: The cylinder head temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor that measures the temperature of the cylinder head metal or of the coolant in the head. Some Ford engines use it instead of a coolant temperature sensor and calculate a coolant value from it; VW group V8 petrol engines use it as sender G407. CARB requires such sensors to be monitored like the coolant sensor. P017C means the signal voltage is too low – a short to ground of the signal wire or a short inside the sensor; the control module would read an implausibly hot cylinder head. 'Low' refers to the signal, not the temperature. Audi and Bentley document it as a short to ground, most often caused by water inside sender G407 after O-ring damage. Ford flags the same condition on its own code below 0.244 V for 5 s. A substitute value is used; an overheating warning with a cold engine is a typical sign.
s: Check engine light on
Overheating or coolant warning despite a cold engine
Radiator fan runs constantly

c: Sensor faulty (series fault on Ford 5.0 litre 2019)
Connector unplugged or corroded, wire open
P017D.d: The cylinder head temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor that measures the temperature of the cylinder head metal or of the coolant in the head. Some Ford engines use it instead of a coolant temperature sensor and calculate a coolant value from it; VW group V8 petrol engines use it as sender G407. CARB requires such sensors to be monitored like the coolant sensor. P017D means the signal voltage is too high – the sensor or wire is open or shorted to voltage, and the control module would read an implausibly cold head. Ford's published summaries flag this under its own code P1289 above 4.96 V for 5 s, but a 2019 bulletin for the F-150 and Mustang 5.0 litre names P1289 and/or P017D and replaces the sensor – so at least that calibration also sets the generic code. GM lists P017D only as an exclusion condition in its diesel software. The engine uses substitute values; the radiator fan typically runs constantly.
s: Check engine light on
Temperature gauge cold or missing
Radiator fan runs constantly
Cold-start or idle problems possible

c: Loose contact at connector or pin
Wire broken by engine movement or heat
P017E.d: The cylinder head temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor that measures the temperature of the cylinder head metal or of the coolant in the head. Some Ford engines use it instead of a coolant temperature sensor and calculate a coolant value from it; VW group V8 petrol engines use it as sender G407. CARB requires such sensors to be monitored like the coolant sensor. P017E covers intermittent interruptions or an erratic signal. The VW group explicitly uses it for 'open circuit or loose contact', not only for jumps: on Audi and Bentley V8 engines moisture inside sender G407 after O-ring damage makes it fail intermittently, and an improved part has been introduced. Loose contacts and wires broken by heat or engine movement are other causes. The detection logic is not public.
s: Check engine light on
Intermittent coolant or overheating warning
Temperature gauge jumps
Radiator fan intermittently loud

c: Leak detection pump filter dirty or blocked

P018F.d: Common-rail diesels have a pressure relief valve in the rail – usually a spring-loaded valve, on some truck engines electronically controlled. It opens on overpressure and then holds a low limp-home pressure; every opening wears the seat, and after many openings it may no longer close tightly. P018F means the valve has opened too often: the control module recognises openings from the rail pressure trace (overshoot, then a steep drop to the limp-home level) and counts them. The code therefore usually points to an underlying problem – the pressure control repeatedly lets overpressure build up. No manufacturer document describing P018F was found; the function and counting logic come from patents on large engines (example: opening at about 1950 bar, then about 800 bar).

P019A.d: Sensor 3 on bank 1 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick; it exists on Jaguar Land Rover's supercharged V6 and V8 (on both banks) and on Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. 'Delayed response' means the sensor starts reacting too late after a mixture change – unlike 'slow response' (P0145/P0165), where the transition itself is too flat. This code covers the rich-to-lean direction, tested during forced fuel cut-off. For sensor 2, GM checks whether the signal falls below 450 mV before a calibrated air mass has passed; behind two converters their oxygen storage buffers the change, so limits are wide. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found – the Jaguar Land Rover bulletins list only P0142ff/P0162ff for sensor 3 – so the description rests on CARB's response requirement and the sensor 2 logic. There is no limp mode; the converter monitor cannot complete.

c: Loose contact or corrosion at the connector

P01B8.d: These codes only apply to vehicles with a gaseous alternative fuel – compressed natural gas (CNG) or LPG – as bi-fuel models alongside petrol or as dedicated gas engines; on bi-fuel vehicles a fault usually blocks gas operation and the vehicle runs on petrol. The gas rail temperature sensor, often combined with the rail pressure sensor, measures the gas temperature at the injectors: gas cools strongly when it expands in the regulator, and the injected mass depends on density, i.e. on rail pressure and temperature, so the module corrects injection time with it. A Ford patent describes plausibility checks against engine bay temperature at idle and an expected cold rail at full load with a full tank. Roush propane systems report rail temperature faults as P0181–P0183; no manufacturer document using exactly this code was found. P01B8 covers brief dropouts or jumps in the signal, typically a loose contact or heat-damaged wiring near the engine.
s: Check engine light on
Gas operation blocked or switch to petrol
Mixture errors or stumbling in gas mode

c: Wiring or connector of sensor B
P01B9.d: The engine oil temperature sensor B is an NTC thermistor fed with 5 V through a resistor: the hotter the oil, the lower the signal voltage. The engine module uses the oil temperature for variable cam timing (Ford disables it with cold oil or a sensor fault), engine protection and the oil life monitor; many engines have no such sensor and use a calculated oil temperature instead. Sensor B is a second oil temperature sensor whose position is defined by the manufacturer. P01B9 is the general circuit fault of sensor B, the counterpart of P0195. No manufacturer document using the B-sensor codes was found, so it is unclear who fits a sensor B; the description follows sensor A and CARB's circuit monitoring requirement.
s: Check engine light on (depending on manufacturer)
Oil temperature reading possibly wrong
Usually no driving symptoms

c: Comparison sensor (oil sensor A, coolant) faulty
Thermal management or oil cooler fault (genuine deviation)

P01BE.d: The bank 2 rail pressure sensor measures the pressure in a second, separate high-pressure rail on V engines that have one rail with its own sensor per bank. Many V engines connect both rails and use only one sensor (P0190–P0194); the only documented user of the bank 2 codes is GM's 5.5 litre LT6 (Corvette Z06 2023–2024) with a digital sensor per rail. P01BE is the general circuit fault of the bank 2 sensor, the counterpart of P0190. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the logic follows the bank 1 sensor and CARB's circuit monitoring requirement. On a fault the module uses a substitute value and usually limits power.
s: Check engine light on
Limp mode or 'Reduced Engine Power'
Rough running

c: Water or corrosion at the bank 2 intermediate connector (GM LT6: wrong 12-pin connector)
Bank 2 rail pressure sensor faulty internally
Genuine pressure fault on bank 2 (pump, control valve)
P01BF.d: The bank 2 rail pressure sensor measures the pressure in a second, separate high-pressure rail on V engines that have one rail with its own sensor per bank. Many V engines connect both rails and use only one sensor (P0190–P0194); the only documented user of the bank 2 codes is GM's 5.5 litre LT6 (Corvette Z06 2023–2024) with a digital sensor per rail. P01BF is the plausibility fault of the bank 2 sensor, the counterpart of P0191. GM documents it on the LT6 as an 'internal component fault' of the sensor, appearing together with codes for low rail pressure at start (P00C6), pressure regulation at its limit and injector faults: a wrong 12-pin intermediate connector to the bank 2 rail let water in. The fix was a new engine/injector harness and rail pressure sensor. Thresholds are not published; GM's dual-channel comparison on bank 1 (1.0 MPa) suggests similar logic. On a fault the module uses a substitute value and usually limits power.

Reduced power

P01C0.d: The bank 2 rail pressure sensor measures the pressure in a second, separate high-pressure rail on V engines that have one rail with its own sensor per bank. Many V engines connect both rails and use only one sensor (P0190–P0194); the only documented user of the bank 2 codes is GM's 5.5 litre LT6 (Corvette Z06 2023–2024) with a digital sensor per rail. P01C2.d: The bank 2 rail pressure sensor measures the pressure in a second, separate high-pressure rail on V engines that have one rail with its own sensor per bank. P01C3.d: Fuel pressure sensor A is a fuel pressure sensor without 'rail' in its name and without a bank – unlike the rail pressure sensors P0190–P0194 and P01BE–P01C2; which sensor it is depends on the manufacturer. The only documented case is FCA, where sensor A is the low-pressure sensor in the supply line, read together with the fuel pump control module. GM calls its low-pressure sensor 'sensor B' (P018A–P018E). P01C3 is its general circuit fault without telling low from high. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the description rests on CARB's circuit monitoring requirement, the FCA sibling code P01C6 and GM's equivalent low-pressure sensor checks.
s: Check engine light on
Hard starting or stalling possible
Hesitation or lack of power under load

c: Genuine supply fault: weak pump, clogged filter

P01C4.d: Fuel pressure sensor A is a fuel pressure sensor without 'rail' in its name and without a bank – unlike the rail pressure sensors P0190–P0194 and P01BE–P01C2; which sensor it is depends on the manufacturer. P01C8.d: Some V engines have a separate high-pressure fuel circuit per bank, each with its own pump or rail – for example Audi's 4.0 TFSI V8 with a second high-pressure pump for bank 2. These codes are the bank 2 counterparts of the system pressure codes for bank 1. P01C8 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0087: the actual pressure stays below target over time. Typical causes are a weak high-pressure pump on bank 2, a faulty volume control valve, low supply pressure or a leak. No manufacturer using exactly this code was found; the logic follows P0087 and CARB's requirement for pressure control. Not every two-rail engine uses them: GM's LT6 reports bank 2 pressure problems under other codes.

P01C9.d: Some V engines have a separate high-pressure fuel circuit per bank, each with its own pump or rail – for example Audi's 4.0 TFSI V8 with a second high-pressure pump for bank 2. These codes are the bank 2 counterparts of the system pressure codes for bank 1. P01C9 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0088: the actual pressure is above target. P01CA.d: Some V engines have a separate high-pressure fuel circuit per bank, each with its own pump or rail – for example Audi's 4.0 TFSI V8 with a second high-pressure pump for bank 2. These codes are the bank 2 counterparts of the system pressure codes for bank 1. Long cranking or no start

Boost leak or loose injector clamp
P01CB.d: Diesel engines must detect when fuel can no longer be injected at the correct crank angle – CARB requires this for every injector individually, hence one code per cylinder. The start of injection is not measured directly: during overrun with fuel cut-off the control module fires a tiny test injection into one cylinder (GM: about 1.5 mm³) and evaluates the resulting speed change at the crankshaft sensor. From this it learns how much extra energizing time the injector needs (Bosch calls this zero fuel calibration). This code means injector 1 needs clearly more energizing time than intended, i.e. it opens too late – GM sets it above 80 µs of extra time, after two trips. Documented users are GM's 6.6 litre Duramax (LML, L5P) and FCA's 3.0 litre EcoDiesel; Ford reports the same function under P2B11ff. Bulletins often point away from the injector: GM fixed false settings on 2020–2021 L5P trucks with new software and warns that vibration, for example from off-road tyres, disturbs the evaluation; FCA lists wrong injector correction codes, boost leaks and loose injector clamps.
s: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)
Louder combustion noise or knocking
Rough idle
Possibly smoke

P01E3.d: Coolant temperature sensor 3 is a third NTC coolant sensor on engines with thermal management or split cooling circuits; its position is defined by the manufacturer – on Jaguar Land Rover's 2018–2019 Ingenium petrol engines it sits in the engine block water jacket, on Audi's 3.0 TFSI V6 it is part of the thermal management. As with every NTC sensor, a low signal voltage means hot and a high one cold. CARB requires such additional sensors to be monitored from model year 2019 onwards. P01E3 is the general circuit fault of this sensor without telling low from high. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; it is described by analogy with its documented sibling codes and the NTC principle.

P01E8.d: Engine coolant heater A is an electric coolant heater switched by the engine module, directly or via a relay or power stage, to shorten warm-up – less cold-start emissions and faster cabin heat; A and B denote two separately switched heaters or stages. It is not the same as a mains-powered block heater (which the vehicle does not control) or the electrically heated thermostat (P0597–P0599). CARB requires output components to be checked for correct response or at least for circuit faults. This code reports an open control circuit – the module detects missing continuity, typically with the driver switched off. No manufacturer using these codes was found in the GM, Ford or NHTSA documents checked; the typical driver diagnosis (open circuit detected with the driver switched off, as GM does for other outputs) is an analogy, and thresholds are unknown.

P01EF.d: Engine coolant heater B is an electric coolant heater switched by the engine module, directly or via a relay or power stage, to shorten warm-up – less cold-start emissions and faster cabin heat; A and B denote two separately switched heaters or stages. It is not the same as a mains-powered block heater (which the vehicle does not control) or the electrically heated thermostat (P0597–P0599). CARB requires output components to be checked for correct response or at least for circuit faults. This code reports that the heater circuit is electrically intact but the heater does not work as commanded – for example a sticking relay or a weak element. No manufacturer using these codes was found in the GM, Ford or NHTSA documents checked; the typical driver diagnosis (open circuit detected with the driver switched off, as GM does for other outputs) is an analogy, and thresholds are unknown.

P01F0.d: Since model years 2019–2021 CARB requires petrol engines to detect a thermostat fault not only during warm-up but also when the coolant, after reaching operating temperature, drops back below the temperature needed for other diagnostics. P01F0 is this check. GM sets it when coolant falls below 64 °C with a conventional thermostat or 70.5 °C with an electrically heated one (2019 Corvette: 65/78.5 °C) after having been above it, with at least 0.8 km driven, ambient above −7 °C, enough heat input and no long overrun downhill; two trips. GM also uses it on the 6.6 litre Duramax diesel as a 'stuck open thermostat' check. Ford does not use the code in the documents checked. Usual cause is a thermostat stuck open.

P0200.d: P0200 is the injector circuit fault without a cylinder assignment. The large US manufacturers do not use it – GM and Ford report injector faults per cylinder (P0201 ff) or as faults of the shared injector supply (P062D/P062E, P2146 ff). P0201.d: P0201 reports an electrical fault, mainly an open circuit, in the injector circuit of cylinder 1. On direct injection the affected injector is switched off; the cylinder misfires.

P020A.d: P020A reports a fault in the injection timing of cylinder 1 on a diesel engine. Unlike P01CB/P01CC ('over retarded/advanced', the result of the injector learning routine in overrun), this code has no direction, and what it checks is up to the manufacturer. GM uses it as an electrical check on a four-cylinder diesel and on the 6.6 litre L5P Duramax V8: at every injection the engine module measures how long the injector current takes to reach its pull-in level of 13 A. If on the V8 that time is outside 60–150 µs in 10 of 20 samples, the code sets and the warning light comes on in the first trip. FCA lists it for the 3.0 litre EcoDiesel V6 together with the learning codes: check injector coding, charge air leaks and the injector clamp, reset the zero fuel calibration and repeat the learning drive; if the code returns, the injector is replaced.

P0213.d: A cold start injector is an additional injector in the intake manifold that sprays extra fuel for a few seconds while a cold engine is cranked. In classic Bosch systems a thermo-time switch on the block powers it directly, without the engine module – such systems cannot set a code at all. P0215.d: The engine shutoff solenoid is the electric stop valve on older diesel injection pumps, mainly distributor pumps. It is energised with the ignition on and lets fuel into the pump; with no current a spring closes it, the pump runs dry and the engine stops – also as a safety backup if the governor fails. P0215 reports a fault in this solenoid or its supply, typically a broken coil, a sticking plunger, a blown fuse or relay, or a wiring fault. The result is either an engine that will not start or dies, or one that keeps running after switch-off. Newer diesels stop through the injectors or a fuel shutoff valve with its own codes P0005–P0007. No manufacturer document describing P0215 was found; the description rests on CARB's requirements for output components and a Bosch patent on the valve.

P0217.d: P0217 is a condition code: the engine module reports that coolant temperature has passed a protection threshold. The limit and the reaction depend on the manufacturer – Saab's 2.2 diesel sets it at 120 °C for over 10 s, limits fuel quantity and suspends EGR and boost diagnostics until the temperature drops; heavy-duty diesels cut power sharply and may shut down; Ford petrol engines use their own code P1299 and cut fuel to individual cylinders. Whether the warning light comes on varies, because CARB exempts overheat protection that only engages once the gauge reads red. Usual causes are low coolant, a thermostat stuck closed, a failed fan or water pump – but Ford traced some cases to a faulty coolant sensor or harness.

P0220.d: With electronic throttle control the throttle body carries two position sensors, A and B, usually with opposite or offset signals, and the engine module compares them (correlation code P2135). GM and Ford give the pedal sensors their own codes (P2120 ff), so B is in practice the second throttle sensor. P0220 is the general circuit fault of sensor B without telling low from high. Newer GM and Ford engines report sensor B faults as P0222/P0223. The module carries on with sensor A, limits throttle opening and power and switches off cruise control.

P022A.d: The charge air cooler bypass is a flap or valve that routes compressed air around the charge air cooler, so the engine and exhaust warm up faster after a cold start; when warm it closes or opens partly to control intake air temperature. The module then switches bypass control off and the flap stays in its rest position. No manufacturer document using this code was found – GM and Ford do not use the bypass codes; the description rests on CARB's component monitoring requirement and a Bosch patent on the bypass valve.

P024D is the plausibility fault: the signal is electrically valid but does not match the commanded position or the end stops. Bypass control is then switched off and the flap stays in its rest position. No manufacturer document using this code was found – GM and Ford do not use the bypass codes; the description rests on CARB's component monitoring requirement and a Bosch patent on the bypass valve.

P0251.d: These codes cover the electrically controlled fuel metering actuator on a diesel injection pump. On older distributor pumps it was a solenoid that set the injected quantity; on common rail it is usually an inlet metering valve on the high-pressure pump that lets only as much fuel into the pumping elements as the rail needs, instead of spilling the excess through a pressure valve. Manufacturers use different codes for this part: Ford P0001–P0004, GM Duramax P0090–P0092. P0251 is the general circuit fault of actuator A. Saab's 2011 9-5 diesel uses it for an open circuit of the pressure regulator on the high-pressure pump: if the control wire does not show the expected voltage with the driver off for more than 1 s, the code sets with the warning light at once. P0263.d: P0263 comes from the cylinder balance control of common-rail diesels: the engine module measures the crankshaft acceleration of each cylinder's power stroke, compares it with the average and gives a deviating cylinder more or less fuel. P026B.d: P026B is the engine-wide injection timing monitor: CARB requires diesels from 2010 to detect injection that is too early or too late overall, or a timing control at its limit. Unlike P020A ff (per cylinder) it concerns the engine as a whole. It is documented on the Ram 6.7 Cummins, together with the per-cylinder timing and balance codes; FCA describes it as set falsely by software and fixes it with an engine module update, without publishing thresholds. P026C.d: From 2010, CARB requires diesel engines to detect when the commanded injection quantity is not delivered. The module estimates the fuel actually burned from airflow and the measured lambda (from the NOx or oxygen sensor) and corrects the quantity; if that correction passes a limit, the code sets. P026C means the engine gets less fuel than commanded. GM's 6.6 litre LML diesel checks it at idle with the vehicle stationary and the engine warm, setting it at a correction of −20 to −35 mm³ per stroke for 12 s; later GM diesels use the learned correction value (10 of 20 samples); both need two trips. FCA lists it with an injector cleaning procedure for deposits. Ford diesels do not use it. Typical causes are coked injectors, wrong airflow or lambda measurement and weak fuel supply.

P026D.d: From 2010, CARB requires diesel engines to detect when the commanded injection quantity is not delivered. The module estimates the fuel actually burned from airflow and the measured lambda (from the NOx or oxygen sensor) and corrects the quantity; if that correction passes a limit, the code sets. P026F.d: P026F is a general functional code for the coolant thermostat. CARB requires that the coolant reaches the temperature needed for other diagnostics in the approved time and comes within 11 °C of the thermostat's regulating temperature; from model years 2019–2021 petrol engines must also detect it dropping back below that temperature, and electric pumps or valves controlling coolant flow are monitored like a thermostat. The module follows coolant temperature against a heat model. No manufacturer using P026F was found – GM and Ford report thermostat faults as P0128, P01F0 or P2181 – so the description rests on CARB and the thermostat's function.

P0272.d: P0272 comes from the cylinder balance control of common-rail diesels: the engine module measures the crankshaft acceleration of each cylinder's power stroke, compares it with the average and gives a deviating cylinder more or less fuel. The code sets when the correction for cylinder 4 reaches its limit and the cylinder still does not keep up – GM at 95 % of a limit of about ±12–17 mm³ for 30 s, Ford above 90 % of the allowed 3.5–15 mg per stroke for 7.5 s; GM needs two trips. The code does not say whether there is too much or too little fuel – the correction value for cylinder 4 shows the direction: strongly negative means a leaking injector, strongly positive a weak injector or low compression. VW and Ram traced some cases to over-sensitive software, so check for updates before replacing injectors.

P027A.d: On demand-controlled fuel systems the engine module does not drive the pump itself but sends a pump control module the desired pump output on a separate control line, usually as a duty cycle; the module reports back on a monitor line or via CAN. Module B is a second pump module, for example on dual-tank commercial vehicles. P027A is the counterpart of P025A: the control line from the engine module to pump module B is open or faulty. No manufacturer using P027A was found – Ford reports line faults of both modules together under P025A, GM only uses P025A; the description follows CARB's circuit monitoring requirement and Ford's module B check. If the second tank's pump gets no valid command, fuel may run short when running from that tank.
s: Check engine light (manufacturer-dependent)
Fuel shortage when running from the second tank
Starting problems, surging

P027B.d: On demand-controlled fuel systems the engine module does not drive the pump itself but sends a pump control module the desired pump output on a separate control line, usually as a duty cycle; the module reports back on a monitor line or via CAN. Module B is a second pump module, for example on dual-tank commercial vehicles. P027B means pump module B receives an invalid command or its feedback does not match. Ford's module signals this with a 20 % (±4 %) duty cycle on its monitor line, checked continuously at 11–16 V over 2–5 s; on Ford commercial vehicles the module B monitor line runs via the smart relay module and CAN to the engine module. Whether the warning light comes on depends on the vehicle.

No manufacturer using this code was found; the description follows CARB and the warm-running counterpart.

P028A.d: Some vehicles – mainly commercial and off-road machines, or cars with a separate cooler for a coolant-cooled charge air cooler – have their own fan for the charge air cooler; a Deere patent describes such a fan that the module switches and reverses to blow out dirt. P028A means the fan's control circuit is open or has a general fault, detected by the driver stage. Without the fan the charge air is cooled less at low speed or in heat, which can lead to P026A and boost limitation. No manufacturer document using P028A was found; the description rests on CARB's output component requirement.

P028B.d: Some vehicles – mainly commercial and off-road machines, or cars with a separate cooler for a coolant-cooled charge air cooler – have their own fan for the charge air cooler, switched by the engine module; a Deere patent describes such a fan that is also reversed to blow out dirt. P028B means the module commands the fan on but sees no effect – no speed or current feedback from a fan control module, or the charge air does not cool – although the circuit is electrically sound (circuit faults are P028A, P028D and P028E). The charge air then gets hotter, which can limit boost and power. No manufacturer document using this code was found; the description rests on CARB's output component requirement.

P028C.d: Some vehicles – mainly commercial and off-road machines, or cars with a separate cooler for a coolant-cooled charge air cooler – have their own fan for the charge air cooler, switched by the engine module; a Deere patent describes such a fan that is also reversed to blow out dirt. P028C means the fan runs although the module has switched it off – speed or current feedback, or the voltage at the output, does not match the off command. Typical causes are a welded relay contact or a shorted driver stage. The fan runs continuously and can drain the battery; the charge air tends to be too cold, which favours condensate. No manufacturer document using this code was found; the description rests on CARB's output component requirement.

P0290.d: P0290 comes from the cylinder balance control of common-rail diesels: the engine module measures the crankshaft acceleration of each cylinder's power stroke, compares it with the average and gives a deviating cylinder more or less fuel. The code sets when the correction for cylinder 10 reaches its limit and the cylinder still does not keep up – GM at 95 % of a limit of about ±12–17 mm³ for 30 s, Ford above 90 % of the allowed 3.5–15 mg per stroke for 7.5 s; GM needs two trips. The code does not say whether there is too much or too little fuel – the correction value for cylinder 10 shows the direction: strongly negative means a leaking injector, strongly positive a weak injector or low compression. Cylinder 10 only exists on diesels with ten cylinders; GM and Ford documents stop at cylinder 8, so the description follows CARB and the siblings.

P0297.d: P0297 is a condition code: the engine module detects that road speed – from the vehicle speed sensor or wheel and output shaft speed – exceeded the calibrated maximum. Electronic speed limiters cut fuel or throttle at that limit, and the event is stored. Ford uses the code on its petrol trucks and stores it without the warning light; no manufacturer publishes a threshold. Common triggers are descending with a trailer beyond the limiter speed, wheelspin on the driven axle, a wrongly programmed tyre size or axle ratio, or spikes in the speed signal. Unlike P0219 it concerns road speed, not engine speed.

P0298.d: P0298 is a protection code: engine oil temperature – from its own sensor, often combined with the oil level sensor, or modelled – has exceeded the protection limit. Saab's 3.0 diesel limits injection quantity when the oil stays at 135 °C or more for over 10 s, until it cools down; a heavy-duty bus engine warns in two stages and then derates. Ford stores the code without the warning light, in line with CARB's exemption for overheat protection. Usual causes are high load in heat, cooling problems, a clogged oil cooler or stuck oil thermostat, and occasionally a sensor reading too high.

P0299.d: P0299 means actual boost stays below target for a period although the control already demands more. Thresholds: GM petrol 30–55 kPa below target with the warning light in the first trip; GM diesels 10–50 kPa, two trips; Ford EcoBoost more than 4 psi (about 28 kPa) for 5 s with the wastegate already commanded fully closed; Ford diesels 30–40 kPa for 10–15 s, with a further underboost code P2263. Typical causes from manufacturer bulletins: a charge air leak, a wastegate that lost its preload or whose rod came off, a leaking bypass valve, sticking turbo vanes on diesels, and ice in the charge air cooler in winter. A faulty boost sensor can also fake underboost. Many engines then limit power.

P029A.d: These codes belong to an individual-cylinder fuel correction: a diesel's cylinder balance control measures each cylinder's crankshaft acceleration and adjusts its injection quantity; on petrol engines a cylinder-selective mixture control does the same. CARB requires the system to report when such a correction has used up its range or one cylinder causes an imbalance. P029A means the correction for cylinder 1 is at its upper limit: the module keeps giving this cylinder more fuel and still cannot even it out – a sign that the cylinder receives too little fuel or builds too little pressure. GM and Ford use other codes for this (P0263 ff, P219A ff); no manufacturer document describing this code with thresholds was found, so the description follows CARB and published patents.

P02CC.d: The engine module learns a small-quantity correction for each injector: on overrun it gives one injector a tiny test injection (GM about 1.5 mm³), measures the resulting crankshaft acceleration and corrects the injector's activation time per rail pressure step. P02CC means the learned correction for cylinder 1 has reached its lower limit at at least one pressure step: the injector needs much less activation time than nominal – it delivers too much at small quantities or opens early. GM diesels set it at limits of roughly ±66–182 µs after two trips. It is documented on GM's 6.6 litre L5P and 2.8 litre diesels – on the 2.8 a worn drive belt caused it to return after injector replacement – and on Land Rover's 5.0 V8 petrol, where a software update is the first step. It differs from P01CC (over advanced), which some systems derive from the same learning.

P02CD.d: The engine module learns a small-quantity correction for each injector: on overrun it gives one injector a tiny test injection (GM about 1.5 mm³), measures the resulting crankshaft acceleration and corrects the injector's activation time per rail pressure step. P02CD means the learned correction for cylinder 1 has reached its upper limit at at least one pressure step: the injector needs much more activation time than nominal – it delivers too little or opens late, for example from coking. GM diesels set it at limits of roughly ±66–182 µs after two trips. Older GM calibrations (LML) use only this code of the pair, for both directions. It is documented on GM's 6.6 litre L5P and 2.8 litre diesels – on the 2.8 a worn drive belt caused it to return after injector replacement – and on Land Rover's 5.0 V8 petrol, where a software update is the first step. It differs from P01CB (over retarded), which some systems derive from the same learning.

P02E0.d: The diesel intake air flow valve A is the throttle flap ahead of the intake manifold of a diesel engine: it creates the vacuum needed for high EGR rates, lowers airflow to heat the particulate filter and catalyst during regeneration and closes at switch-off against run-on shaking. A spring holds it open when unpowered; an electric motor positions it, with a position sensor reporting back. P02E0 means the motor circuit is open – cable, connector or motor winding. GM diesels detect more than 200 kΩ with the driver off, after about 1.5 s (6.6 litre LML: 7 s), two trips. On a fault the valve is switched off and the spring opens it: driving is usually little affected, but EGR control is restricted and filter regeneration may be blocked.

P02FB.d: Cold start fuel injection is an extra injection system for cold starts – for example on flex-fuel engines running on high ethanol blends, where a Hyundai patent describes a small auxiliary tank, a cold-start injector and a heater. CARB lists such heated fuel preparation systems among the monitored output components. P02FB means the control circuit of the cold-start injection is open or has a general fault – a broken coil, a loose or corroded connector or a broken wire. The engine then starts poorly or not at all in the cold; once warm it runs normally. No manufacturer document using this code was found; unlike the older P0213/P0214, these codes separate the fault types.

P0300.d: The engine module detects misfire from crankshaft speed: a cylinder that does not fire gives no acceleration impulse. At a catalyst-damaging rate (CARB: at least 5 % per 200 revolutions) the warning light flashes; at an emissions-relevant rate (at least 1 % per 1,000 revolutions – GM about 2–5 %, Ford 0.9–1.5 %) it comes on after two trips. Ford and GM may shut off a misfiring cylinder's injector to protect the catalyst. P0300 sets when the misfire cannot be assigned to one cylinder: several cylinders each account for more than 10 %, the cylinder changes randomly, or – at Ford – the cylinder cannot be identified at high speed. It often appears together with cylinder codes. Causes are usually systemic: false air, worn plugs on several cylinders, fuel pressure or fuel quality, valve timing – and false detection from a damaged tone wheel, rough roads or vibration. Bulletins name coils, cracked plug insulators and wrong plug gaps.

The code concerns the logic-level control signal, not the coil's primary current (that has its own codes, P0351 ff and P2300 ff). P030A means the control line is open – the module sees a voltage with its driver off that indicates high resistance. No manufacturer using these codes was found; GM reports coil control faults as P0351 ff (open above 30 kΩ, first trip), so the description follows CARB and that analogy. The affected coils fire wrongly or not at all, causing misfire; many modules then shut off injection to those cylinders to protect the catalyst.

P0310.d: The engine module detects misfire from crankshaft speed: a cylinder that does not fire gives no acceleration impulse. At a catalyst-damaging rate (CARB: at least 5 % per 200 revolutions) the warning light flashes; at an emissions-relevant rate (at least 1 % per 1,000 revolutions – GM about 2–5 %, Ford 0.9–1.5 %) it comes on after two trips. Ford and GM may shut off a misfiring cylinder's injector to protect the catalyst. P0310 means more than 90 % of the detected misfires fall on cylinder 10. Usual causes are the ignition coil or spark plug of that cylinder, its injector, or low compression; a quick test is to swap coil or plug with a neighbouring cylinder and see whether the misfire moves. Cylinder 10 exists on ten-cylinder engines such as Ford's 6.8 litre V10; there an under-torqued crankshaft pulley bolt and engine software caused false misfire codes on all cylinders.
s: Check engine light on, flashing at a catalyst-damaging rate
Rough idle, jerking, vibration
Loss of power, hesitation
Smell of unburnt fuel, higher consumption

c: Tank nearly empty – the fuel pump draws air (corners, gradients, braking)
Actual misfire cause (ignition, injector, false air) that happened at low fuel

Fuel level sender reading too low
P0313.d: When the tank is nearly empty the fuel pump can draw air in corners or on gradients, which causes misfires. CARB allows misfire detection to be switched off at 15 % fuel or less; some manufacturers instead report misfires detected in this state under P0313 rather than P030x. Ford's normal misfire monitor runs from 15 % fuel, Saab's ME9 from 12 %; Saab's T8 sets P0313 below 5 litres with the same tests as P0300 (3 % per 1,000 revolutions, flashing light at a catalyst-damaging rate). GM petrol engines simply suspend the monitor without their own code. After refuelling the symptoms usually disappear – if not, look for a real misfire cause.
s: Check engine light on (flashing at a catalyst-damaging rate)
Jerking or power loss with an almost empty tank, especially in corners or uphill
Usually no symptoms after refuelling

c: Injector of one cylinder clogged or leaking (diesel), or coil/plug (petrol)
Leaking high-pressure line, fuel bridge or injector washer
Air, water or petrol in the diesel, clogged filter, low supply pressure
P0314.d: P0314 means the misfire is attributable to a single cylinder, but the module does not say which one. CARB generally requires cylinder-specific codes and allows a general code only with approval where the cylinder cannot be identified reliably; for diesels identification is required only where possible without extra hardware. GM and Ford do not use P0314. It is documented on Saab's 2.2 TiD diesel with a Bosch distributor pump, as a mechanical misfire fault in two speed and quantity windows with the warning light and limp mode limiting injection quantity; the cylinder can still be read out with a scan tool. Typical causes are a faulty injector, leaking high-pressure lines, air or water in the fuel, or low compression.
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power, limp mode with quantity limit (Saab diesel)
Rough running, vibration

c: Relearn not performed after replacing sensor, crankshaft, damper, engine or engine module
Learned values lost through voltage loss (battery disconnected)
Tone wheel damaged or shifted, crankshaft runout, dirt on the sensor
Interference in the crankshaft sensor circuit
P0315.d: Manufacturing tolerances of the crankshaft tone wheel distort the speed fluctuations misfire detection relies on, so the engine module learns a correction for each tooth or segment. P0315 means these values have not been learned or are invalid. GM checks that the learned tooth angles add up to 360° (deviation above 0.001° sets the code in the first trip) and learns them with a scan tool: brakes held, full throttle in park until fuel cut-off. Ford learns the profile during up to three overrun phases from 60 to 40 mph and sets P0315 when that fails. Until relearned, misfire detection is suspended – at GM above 1,000 rpm – and misfire readiness stays incomplete. The relearn is needed after replacing the engine, engine module, crankshaft, damper or crankshaft sensor.
s: Check engine light on (GM; Ford depending on application)
Driving usually unaffected
Misfire readiness not set – emissions test fails

c: Moisture or water in the plug wells, coils arcing when cold or damp
Leaking injectors (fuel drips after switch-off, over-rich start)
Worn or sooted spark plugs that only fire cleanly when warm
Wrong temperature sensor value or engine software
P0316.d: P0316 concerns misfire within the first 1,000 revolutions after start. CARB requires a pending code here after the first exceedance of the emissions-relevant rate (later in the drive only after the fourth) and the warning light if it recurs at the next start. Ford sets P0316 in addition to the cylinder code; GM evaluates the start within P0300–P0308 without its own code. Typical causes are water in the plug wells (Mazda Tribute bulletin: blocked drain in the valve cover channel), coils that arc when cold and damp, injectors that drip after switch-off and over-rich starting – Ford traced cases on the 2.7 EcoBoost to engine software or leaking direct injectors.

Rough running right after a cold start, then normal
Delayed start, fuel smell at start

c: Module configuration does not match the equipment (after engine or ABS module replacement)
ABS/ESP module not responding (supply, CAN line)
Separate rough-road sensor missing or unplugged, where fitted
P0317.d: Misfire detection works from crankshaft speed fluctuations, which rough roads also cause. CARB therefore allows misfire detection to pause on rough roads; many engines take a rough-road signal from the wheel speeds of the ABS module, a Ford patent describes such a detector. P0317 means the engine module is calibrated for an external rough-road signal but does not find the hardware: the supplying module does not respond on the data bus, or the configuration does not match the equipment – for example after replacing the engine or ABS module. Without the signal misfire detection cannot separate road bumps from misfires. No manufacturer document using P0317 was found; the description follows CARB and GM's rough-road sources in its misfire monitor.
s: Warning light (manufacturer-dependent)
Misfire readiness not set
Possibly false misfire codes on rough roads

c: Wheel speed sensor or wiring faulty – the brake module passes on the fault
Communication between engine and brake module lost (CAN, connector, supply)
Separate rough-road sensor faulty, where fitted
P0318.d: Misfire detection works from crankshaft speed fluctuations, which rough roads also cause. CARB therefore allows misfire detection to pause on rough roads; many engines take a rough-road signal from the wheel speeds of the ABS module, a Ford patent describes such a detector. P0318 means rough-road signal A is missing or invalid. On GM engines (documented in Saab service information for the 1.6 turbo) the brake control module sends wheel speed over the data bus; the code sets between 1,520 and 4,000 rpm when that module reports a wheel speed sensor fault or no signal arrives for more than 5 s. GM files it without the warning light. Misfire detection then runs without its rough-road filter. ABS or stability warnings and further codes often appear at the same time.

Driving unaffected
