c: Crankshaft or distributor speed sensor faulty or wrong air gap
Wiring, connector or shielding disturbed (loose contact, interference from ignition or radios)
Tone wheel damaged or dirty (missing tooth, metal chips)
Ignition module faulty on older vehicles
P0320.d: P0320 originally covered the engine speed signal from the distributor or ignition module to the engine module (early OBD II); today Ford's engine module evaluates the crankshaft sensor directly and uses this code for it. Ford checks continuously from 200–500 rpm and sets it within 5 s when the number of teeth after the gap is wrong, the tooth time is implausible (below 30 or above 9,000 rpm) or the gap appears in the wrong place; fuel and spark are then cut briefly to resynchronise, and on electronic throttle P2106 limits power. Some Ford engines use P0339 instead. Typical causes are a faulty crankshaft sensor, interference in the wiring or a damaged tone wheel.
s: Check engine light on
Engine dies or stumbles briefly
Starting problems, tachometer twitching
Reduced power on electronic throttle (Ford P2106)

c: Crankshaft position sensor faulty or aged (weak, noisy signal)
Sensor loose or air gap wrong
Tone wheel damaged or clogged with metal chips
Interference, poor ground or damaged wiring
P0321.d: P0321 belongs to the same signal as P0320 and P0322: the speed and reference input of the ignition, formerly the distributor's Hall pickup, today practically always the crankshaft position sensor. Range/Performance means a signal is present but implausible – wrong number of teeth between the reference gaps, erratic tooth times, or a speed that does not fit the camshaft signal. No manufacturer document available to us describes P0321 by code: Ford runs these tooth checks under P0320 or P0339 (wrong tooth count after the gap, tooth time outside 30 to 9,000 rpm, gap at the wrong position) and GM under P0336. The description therefore follows that logic and CARB's rationality requirement for crank angle sensors.
s: Check engine light on
Jerking, misfire or brief stalling
Hard starting, long cranking
Tachometer flickers or drops out

c: Open or short in signal, ground or 5 V supply, corroded connector
Sensor loose, air gap too large or tone wheel damaged
5 V reference pulled down by another sensor on the same supply
P0322.d: P0322 means the speed and reference input of the ignition – today the crankshaft position sensor – delivers no signal although the engine is turning. Ford proves the rotation with the camshaft sensor: if it shows more than one engine revolution without a crank signal (from 500 rpm, detected within 5 s), Ford sets P0322 or, depending on the engine, P0335; with electronic throttle the throttle software adds P2106 and goes into limp mode. Without a crank signal there is no ignition or injection, so the engine stalls or does not start. Saab's Motronic 2.8.1 (900 V6) sets P0322 when the engine fails to start; its inductive sensor should measure 500–600 Ω and give 2–5 V AC while cranking. Systems without a camshaft-based check may store no code at all on a total failure.
s: Engine cranks but does not start
Engine stalls while driving
Tachometer shows zero
Check engine light on, with electronic throttle limp mode (P2106)

c: Loose contact or corrosion at the sensor connector
P0323.d: P0323 stands for a speed and reference signal at the ignition input – today the crankshaft position sensor – that drops out or is disturbed for moments and then recovers. None of the manufacturer documents available to us (GM 2014–2019, Ford 2012 and 2020–2023, Saab workshop information) uses P0323; the sporadic crank sensor check runs under P0339 at Ford and under P0336 at GM. Ford's logic shows what is evaluated: teeth missing or extra for a moment and the reference gap appearing at an unexpected position, after which the module briefly cuts fuel and spark and resynchronises. Typical causes are a loose contact, chafed wiring and electrical interference. The code itself is described only by its J2012 name and CARB's monitoring requirement for crank angle sensors.
s: Brief stumbling or stalling, then normal again
Sporadic misfire
Tachometer flickers
Check engine light on

c: Genuine knock: low-octane fuel, carbon deposits, high intake or coolant temperature, lean mixture
Mechanical noise taken for knock (loose parts, brackets, valve train, bearings)
Knock sensor damaged, wrongly torqued or mounted with sealant
P0324.d: P0324 concerns the knock control as a whole rather than a single sensor circuit. GM and Saab's GM-based engines set it when excessive knock persists on one cylinder – knock despite ignition retard, or mechanical noise taken for knock – for more than 8–10 s; GM's 2018 engines in the first trip, older ones after two. Older GM calibrations also flag an abnormally low or flat signal per cylinder here. Ignition is retarded. Typical causes are low-octane fuel, carbon deposits, high intake or coolant temperature, lean running, or loose parts and valve train noise. Ford does not use this code; GM reports internal processor faults separately (P06B6/P06B7).
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power from ignition retard
Audible pinging or knocking under load
Higher fuel consumption

c: Wiring or connector chafed, broken or corroded (sensor often under the intake manifold)
Knock sensor faulty (cracked piezo, moisture, heat damage)
P0325.d: The knock sensor is a piezoelectric structure-borne sound sensor bolted to the engine block; the module evaluates its signal per cylinder and retards ignition when it detects knock. Sensor A is the first sensor (bank 1 or a single sensor). With a fault the module retards ignition across the board as protection – noticeable loss of power and higher consumption. P0325 means the sensor circuit is open or the signal stays below the noise threshold. GM feeds a 20 kHz test signal into the circuit and detects an open circuit when it does not cancel out, setting the code in the first trip; Ford sees any open or short as a knock signal that is too small compared with the speed- and load-dependent noise level (at least 1,500 rpm, 35 % load, warm engine). Bulletins name moisture in the sensor (VW Touareg 3.6), engine software (GM Malibu 1.5) and chafed wiring (FCA).
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power, sluggish response from ignition retard
Higher fuel consumption

c: Sensor loose, wrongly torqued or mounted with sealant or on a dirty surface
Engine software or calibration (bulletins for some models)
Genuine knock on a whole bank or mechanical noise
P0326.d: The knock sensor is a piezoelectric structure-borne sound sensor bolted to the engine block; the module evaluates its signal per cylinder and retards ignition when it detects knock. Sensor A is the first sensor (bank 1 or a single sensor). With a fault the module retards ignition across the board as protection – noticeable loss of power and higher consumption. P0326 means the circuit is electrically sound but the signal is implausible. GM sets it when the filtered background noise stays below a threshold – typically a loose sensor or one not bolted down properly – in the first trip; Saab's GM-based engines also when excessive knock persists on several cylinders or a whole bank for 8–10 s. Ford does not use this code.
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power, sluggish response from ignition retard
Higher fuel consumption

c: Signal or return wire chafed to ground
Moisture or corrosion in connector or sensor
Sensor faulty internally (series issue on some models)
P0327.d: The knock sensor is a piezoelectric structure-borne sound sensor bolted to the engine block; the module evaluates its signal per cylinder and retards ignition when it detects knock. Sensor A is the first sensor (bank 1 or a single sensor). With a fault the module retards ignition across the board as protection – noticeable loss of power and higher consumption. P0327 means the diagnostic DC voltage at the sensor input is too low – the signal or return wire is shorted to ground. GM biases each input through a resistor network and sets the code below 8 % of 5 V in 50 of 63 samples, in the first trip; Ford checks actively once every 250 engine cycles on modules with this circuit. Subaru introduced a more durable sensor for this fault.
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power, sluggish response from ignition retard
Higher fuel consumption

c: Signal or return wire shorted to voltage
Corrosion or moisture in the connector
P0328.d: The knock sensor is a piezoelectric structure-borne sound sensor bolted to the engine block; the module evaluates its signal per cylinder and retards ignition when it detects knock. Sensor A is the first sensor (bank 1 or a single sensor). With a fault the module retards ignition across the board as protection – noticeable loss of power and higher consumption. P0328 means the diagnostic DC voltage at the sensor input is too high – typically a short to voltage. GM sets it above 39 % of 5 V in 50 of 63 samples, in the first trip; Ford checks actively once every 250 engine cycles on modules with this circuit.
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power, sluggish response from ignition retard
Higher fuel consumption

P0335.d: The crankshaft position sensor reads a tone wheel with a reference gap (GM 58X, i.e. 60-2; Ford 36-1, 40-1 or 60-2) and gives the engine module speed and crank angle for injection and ignition. P0335 means it delivers no pulses although the engine demonstrably turns. GM proves the rotation via starter, camshaft pulses or airflow above 1.5 g/s and sets the code after at least 4 s of cranking or 0.3 s while running without a crank pulse (2 of 10 revolutions); petrol engines after two trips, the LML diesel in the first. Ford compares with the camshaft: more than one revolution without a crank signal, detected within 5 s. Without the signal the engine stalls or does not start; GM Global A engines (Saab 9-5 2010) keep running only with learned cam positions. A hot sensor that fails and recovers after cooling is typical.

P033F.d: To know which stroke each cylinder is in, the engine module matches the crank angle with the camshaft phase. P033F means this synchronisation is lost while running or cannot be established. It is documented by code only at Ford (2020–2023): P033F, as an alternative to Ford's older own code, stands for a disturbed crank signal without crank/cam synchronisation, and then misfire detection is also impossible. Ford's 2012 description shows the reaction: on a crank sensor fault the module cuts fuel and spark and resynchronises – one revolution to find the gap, one more to confirm cylinder 1 via the camshaft sensor. FCA evaluates the same function in its own cam/crank synchronisation monitor under other codes. Besides the sensors, a jumped timing chain or belt can be behind it.

P0340.d: The camshaft position sensor, almost always a Hall sensor, tells the engine module which stroke cylinder 1 is in – one crank revolution alone is ambiguous – and measures the actual cam phase with variable timing. Sensor A is the intake camshaft, bank 1 the side with cylinder 1. P0340 means no or too few cam pulses arrive while the crankshaft turns in sync. GM sets it after 5.5 s (or 4 s) of cranking without a cam pulse or fewer than 4 pulses in 3 s running, petrol engines after two trips. Ford checks the ratio of cam to crank events from 200 rpm. The engine usually keeps running but starts longer and loses power as cam timing is held. Bulletins: corroded connectors on GM V8s (PIP5335C), moisture in the oil on short trips in Ford hybrids (SSM 48598).

P0341.d: P0341 means the intake camshaft sensor of bank 1 (or the only cam sensor) delivers pulses, but their number or pattern does not fit the crankshaft. GM counts the pulses while the crank is in sync: 4 to 6 in the first 12 reference events and 398 to 402 per 100 engine cycles on the 4X wheel of the cam phaser; outside that in 8 of 10 checks the code is set after two trips. Ford's 2023 diesel compares the detected segment profile of the cam wheel with the expected one (1.2 s); the Saab 9-4X V6 checks pulses per crank revolution and correlation with crank position. Ford petrol engines use P0344 instead. Result: cam phase uncertain, cam timing switched off, possibly hard starting. GM names corroded connectors at the timing cover as a sporadic cause (PIP5335C).

P0342.d: P0342 means the signal of the intake camshaft sensor of bank 1 (or the only cam sensor) stays at ground level without edges – signal wire shorted to ground, sensor supply missing or the Hall sensor faulty. Saab's Motronic 2.8.1 (900 V6) treats low and high together: no connection or short to ground or battery, about 4.5 V at idle, air gap at most 1.5 mm. c: Loose contact or corrosion at the bank 2 connector
Sensor dropping out when hot or due to oil moisture
P0349.d: P0349 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0344: the signal of the intake camshaft sensor on the side without cylinder 1 is disturbed for moments – edges are missing or appear at an unexpected angle. Ford checks this on the five-tooth wheel used with variable cam timing; if edges appear where none are expected, Ford sets P0349 and switches cam timing on bank 2 off, from 200 rpm, detected within 5 s. FCA also uses the code and asks for the cam/crank synchronisation event data to be saved before the sensor is replaced, because a disturbed crank reference can look like a cam fault. GM does not use P0349. Typical causes are a loose contact at the bank 2 connector, a sensor dropping out when hot or soaked with oil moisture, and a damaged tone wheel.
s: Check engine light on
Sporadic loss of power (cam timing off)
Rough running
Occasionally longer cranking

c: Direction-sensing crankshaft position sensor faulty or aged
Interference pulses in the sensor circuit during shut-off
Air gap or tone wheel – teeth not detected at low speed
P034A.d: Engines with start-stop or hybrid autostart store the crankshaft rest position when the engine stops, so that they can inject and fire correctly at once on restart. This needs a direction-sensing crank sensor, because a cylinder under compression can push the crankshaft backwards after shut-off. On restart the module compares the stored position with the one actually measured after the reference gap. GM sets P034A when they differ by more than 2 teeth in 2 of 3 autostarts or by at least 1 tooth in 4 of 5, after two trips; the diesel already at more than 1 tooth in 1 of 3. The check is suspended while a crank sensor fault is present. Result: start-stop is restricted, restarts take longer with conventional synchronisation, and the autostart may be rough.
s: Check engine light on
Start-stop restricted or off
Delayed or rough autostart
Rarely stalling after an autostart

c: Interference in the sensor circuit (wiring routed next to switching lines)
P034B.d: Direction-sensing (bidirectional) crank sensors count the rest position for start-stop even when the crankshaft rocks back after shut-off. In normal running the sensor must never report reverse rotation – if it does, the signal is disturbed. GM sets P034B after at least 3 direction reversals within 10 s at 400 to 2,000 rpm and an airflow of at least 1.5 g/s, after two trips; the diesel uses the same thresholds. GM bulletin 17-NA-317 describes the 3.6 V6 (LFY) in the 2018 Buick Enclave and Chevrolet Traverse: interference in the sensor circuit caused P034B with P0506, low idle or stalling after an autostart, transmission slip above 65 km/h and cruise control dropping out; the remedy was a revised sensor wiring. Result: start-stop disabled, possibly reduced power.
s: Check engine light on
Low idle or stalling after an autostart
Start-stop off, possibly reduced power
Follow-on effects such as transmission slip or cruise control dropping out (GM LFY)

c: Spark plugs sooted, oily or wrong type or gap

P034C.d: With ion current sensing the spark plug serves as a sensor after the spark: a measuring voltage across the gap drives a current through the ions in the flame, from which the module detects combustion, misfire and knock – a Delphi patent describes coils with built-in ion sensing, and Saab's Trionic engines detected misfire this way. P034C means this measuring system works implausibly, so misfire and knock detection are no longer reliable. It is documented on the Alfa Romeo Giulia and Stelvio 2.9 V6 biturbo, where three bulletins fix it mainly with engine software; limp mode is possible. Sooted plugs or a faulty coil with ion circuit are further causes.

Limp mode or reduced power possible
Often nothing noticeable otherwise

P0350.d: P0350 is the general ignition coil circuit code without assignment to a coil: the engine module detects a fault in the primary or secondary circuit of a coil but does not report which one. This typically concerns older systems with a shared output stage or ignition module, or a shared feedback line for all coils. The monitoring works as for P0351 ff – primary-current feedback for each ignition command, or the voltage at the driver. GM and Ford report coil faults individually (P0351 ff, P2300 ff) and do not use P0350; the description follows CARB's output monitoring requirement, which allows one collective code.

P0351.d: Modern engines have one coil-on-plug ignition coil per cylinder, with the output stage either in the engine module or in the coil itself. P0351 monitors the primary control circuit of coil A – the line from the engine module to the coil or its built-in output stage – for an open circuit or high resistance. GM's module measures the voltage with its low-side driver off and flags an open circuit above 30 kΩ in 50 of 63 samples (2018 engines in the first trip, older ones after two); Ford checks continuously within 1 s, expecting a primary-current feedback for every ignition command, and shuts off injection to that cylinder for 30 s at a time. Short circuits and the secondary side have their own codes (P2300 ff). Coil A usually serves cylinder 1, but the assignment is up to the manufacturer.

P035A.d: Ignition E is one of the control signal lines from the engine module to an ignition module, ignition output stage or group of coils; which cylinders it serves is defined by the manufacturer, not by the code standard. The code concerns the logic-level control signal, not the coil's primary current (that has its own codes, P0351 ff and P2300 ff). P035A means the control line is open – the module sees a voltage with its driver off that indicates high resistance. No manufacturer using these codes was found – neither GM nor Ford use the Ignition E to H codes; GM reports coil control faults as P0351 ff (open above 30 kΩ) – so the description follows CARB and that analogy. The affected coils fire wrongly or not at all, causing misfire; many modules then shut off injection to those cylinders to protect the catalyst.

P0363.d: P0363 is a reaction code: the engine module has detected misfire severe enough to damage the catalyst – through its crankshaft-based misfire monitor – and has therefore shut off injection to the affected cylinder or cylinders. CARB allows exactly this: a vehicle that cuts fuel immediately on catalyst-damaging misfire may turn the check engine light on steadily instead of flashing it, and may switch fuel back on to re-check at most every 30 s. The code names no cylinder; that comes from the accompanying P0301 ff. It is documented by code only at FCA: two reprogramming bulletins for the 2017–2018 Alfa Romeo Giulia 2.0 turbo list P0363 alongside misfire and mixture codes. Ford reacts in the same way without its own code, VW uses a manufacturer code (P130A) for the hidden cylinder, and GM does not list P0363.
s: Check engine light on steadily instead of flashing
Clearly rough running, one cylinder without power
Loss of power
Jerking or stalling, especially when cold

c: Control or enable line to the converter module disturbed (connector, wiring)
P0364.d: P0364 reports that the control circuit between the engine module and the control module of a DC/AC converter (inverter) behaves implausibly – the command or enable line is present but its signal does not fit what the engine module expects. The code is a late assignment in the P03xx block; the other DC/AC converter codes sit in the P2DAx range (P2DA8–P2DAB). Ford uses it on the 2021 F-150. On the 3.5 L PowerBoost hybrid, whose DC/AC converter module A feeds the Pro Power Onboard sockets, bulletin 21-2229 links P0364 in the PCM to a disabled Pro Power Onboard and a 'Pro Power Onboard Service Required' message; the cause was software parameters in the inverter and the PCM, fixed by reprogramming both. Bulletin 21-2087 lists P0364 among the codes that 3.5 L EcoBoost trucks built up to 2 March 2021 stored with the MIL on, cured by a PCM update alone. Without such a bulletin, check the enable and command wiring between PCM and inverter and the software levels of both modules.
s: Warning lamp depending on the manufacturer
Converter function restricted (for example power socket or hybrid drive)

c: Connector or wiring open or corroded, 5 V reference missing
Oil in the connector from a leaking sensor O-ring
Tone wheel on the exhaust phaser damaged or loose
P0365.d: Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor (bank 1 = side with cylinder 1), usually a Hall sensor on the exhaust cam phaser. P0365 means no or too few exhaust cam pulses arrive while the crankshaft turns in sync. GM sets it after 4 s of cranking or 5.5 s without a cam pulse, or fewer than 4 pulses in 3 s running, 8 of 10 samples, after two trips; on GM's 3.6-litre V6 (Saab 9-4X) also with no pulse in 800 of 1,000 engine cycles. Ford checks the ratio of crank to cam events from 200 rpm, detected within 5 s, and collects all electrical faults here. The exhaust phaser then goes to its park position; the engine keeps running but cranks longer and loses some power. FCA advises saving the cam/crank synchronisation data before replacing the sensor, as the fault is often elsewhere.
s: Check engine light on
Longer cranking before the engine starts
Loss of power or rough idle (exhaust cam timing in its base position)
Higher fuel consumption

c: Sensor faulty or dirty (metal debris on the magnet)
Wiring close to ignition coils or solenoids, loose contact
Tone wheel on the phaser damaged or loose, air gap too large
Sensor or phaser wrongly fitted after timing drive work
P0366.d: Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor (bank 1 = side with cylinder 1), usually a Hall sensor on the exhaust cam phaser. P0366 means its pulses arrive, but their number or position does not fit the crankshaft. GM expects 400 pulses per 100 engine cycles and sets the code outside 398–402, or with fewer than 4 or more than 6 pulses in the first 12 reference events at start, 8 of 10 samples, after two trips. On GM's 3.6-litre V6 in the Saab 9-4X the exhaust phaser then goes to its park position and ignition runs from the crankshaft alone; on the 2.8 turbo V6 (LAU) the fault must last 1 s, or 10 s cumulatively, below 2,520 rpm. Saab's workshop information names a damaged tone wheel, play, foreign matter and too large an air gap. Ford uses the code too but publishes no thresholds.
s: Check engine light on
Longer cranking before the engine starts
Loss of power or rough idle (exhaust cam timing in its base position)
Higher fuel consumption

c: Signal wire chafed through to ground
Oil or water in the connector
P0367.d: Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor (bank 1 = side with cylinder 1), usually a Hall sensor on the exhaust cam phaser. The engine module holds the signal line at about 5 V and the sensor pulls it to ground with each tooth. P0367 means the line stays low without edges – typically a short to ground of the signal wire or a sensor shorted internally. A code-specific manufacturer description exists only from GM: on the Saab 9-4X 2.8 turbo V6 (LAU) the signal must stay low without pulses for more than 1 s, or 10 s cumulatively, after more than 10 crank revolutions and below 2,520 rpm, and the code follows after two trips; with the sensor disconnected the signal wire should show 4.8–5.2 V. GM's other engines of 2014–2019 and Ford report such faults under P0365. The consequence is as for P0365: exhaust cam timing in its base position, longer cranking.

P0368.d: Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor (bank 1 = side with cylinder 1), usually a Hall sensor on the exhaust cam phaser. P0368 means the signal line stays high without edges. If the signal wire is open, the roughly 5 V the engine module applies to it simply remains; if the sensor's 5 V supply or ground is missing, the sensor never switches and the signal also stays high – and a short to positive has the same effect. A code-specific manufacturer description exists only from GM: on the Saab 9-4X 2.8 turbo V6 (LAU) the signal must stay high without pulses for more than 1 s, or 10 s cumulatively, and the code follows after two trips; GM lists exactly these causes. P0369.d: Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor (bank 1 = side with cylinder 1), usually a Hall sensor on the exhaust cam phaser. P0369 means its signal is basically present, but now and then a cam pulse arrives at a crank angle where none is expected, or pulses drop out. P036A.d: Ignition G is one of the control signal lines from the engine module to an ignition module, ignition output stage or group of coils; which cylinders it serves is defined by the manufacturer, not by the code standard. P0370.d: Some diesel systems give the injection control a finely divided angle signal in addition to the normal reference signal, to time and meter injection precisely – the high resolution signal. GM's 6.5-litre diesel (1997) had an optical sensor in the injection pump that delivers a high resolution track and one cam reference pulse per cylinder; P0370 is set if more than 8 consecutive cam pulses pass without progress on the high resolution counter, in the first trip. The engine then runs on backup fuelling with reduced power, and injection timing control is suspended. On the 2004 Duramax LB7 the injector driver module evaluates the 57X crank signal and reports 'no crank signal' over CAN; from 60 rpm, 100 of 120 samples sets P0370, also in the first trip. Petrol engines practically do not use the code.

P0371.d: Some diesel systems give the injection control a finely divided angle signal in addition to the normal reference signal – the high resolution signal – for precise injection timing and metering. P0371 means signal A delivers more pulses than expected within the reference window – for example more high resolution pulses per reference pulse than the nominal ratio, which on GM's 6.5-litre diesel is 64 ± 4 per cam pulse; the usual cause is interference pulses. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0371: GM's 6.5-litre diesel (optical sensor in the injection pump) reports all faults of its high resolution track under P0370 and the Duramax LB7 uses only P0370 and P0374. The description therefore follows the J2012 name, GM's description of the signal and CARB's monitoring requirement for crank angle sensors. Typically the engine loses power and runs roughly.

P037A.d: Diesel engines show the driver a wait-to-start lamp while the glow plugs preheat; the engine module switches it with a high-side driver. P037A means the lamp control circuit is too low – in practice a short to ground on the line to the instrument cluster. GM's diesels detect it in the driver itself: about 0.5 Ω to ground with the lamp commanded, only with a lamp configured, ignition on, more than 11 V and not while cranking. The 2015 engines need 3 s of fault, the 2016/2018 engines 10 of 15 samples; the check engine light follows after two trips. The glow plugs keep working; only the indication is missing, so the driver may start too early. CARB requires monitoring of the wait-to-start lamp circuit. Ford reports lamp faults under P0381 and does not use P037A.

Check engine light on (GM after two trips)

c: Lamp control wire chafed against battery or ignition positive
Fault in the instrument cluster feeding voltage back

Driver in the engine module faulty
P037B.d: P037B is the counterpart of P037A: the control circuit of the wait-to-start lamp is too high, i.e. the line carries voltage although the engine module's driver is off, or the driver sees a short to battery voltage. GM's 2015 diesels check in the off state and set the fault after 1 s with more than 11 V; the 2016/2018 engines evaluate a short of about 0.5 Ω to a voltage source in the driver, 10 of 20 samples at 100 ms. In both cases the check engine light comes on after two trips. The lamp then stays on permanently or cannot be switched off, so the driver no longer gets a usable preheat signal; the driver may protect itself when commanded. There is no limp mode. Ford and Saab do not use P037B; CARB requires monitoring of the lamp circuit and of output components for shorts.

c: Profile actuator (sliding cam pin) sticking or not switching

P037C.d: To heat the catalyst quickly after a cold start, some engines select a particular camshaft profile; CARB counts altered valve timing among these cold-start measures and requires components of the cold-start strategy to have their own diagnostics. P037C checks whether the requested profile is actually engaged during this phase. It is documented by code only at GM, on the 2.7-litre turbo four-cylinder (L3B) with a three-step sliding camshaft: while catalyst heating is active, the measured lift state is compared with the cold-start target, and if it is wrong in 100 of 120 cylinder events the code is set in the first trip. Two GM bulletins (19-NA-145 for 2019 Silverado/Sierra 1500 with stalling on remote start below −6 °C, 20-NA-174 for the 2020 Cadillac CT4) trace P037C to a software fault and reprogram the engine module.

P037D.d: To check the glow plugs, the engine module reads back the voltage or current of the glow plug supply through a sense circuit – CARB requires glow plug circuits to be monitored for correct current and voltage drop, and from model year 2010 the failure of a single plug to be detected. In the J2012 scheme P037D is the general code for this sense circuit, P037E and P037F its low and high counterparts. None of the manufacturer documents available to us uses P037D: GM's 2016/2018 diesels use only P037E/P037F, Ford 2023 its own glow plug codes (P0671 ff, P064C) and Saab reports the feedback of its glow plug control module as P0380/P0382. The description therefore follows CARB and the GM sister codes. Typically glow plug monitoring is inactive; glowing itself can work normally.

Possibly poor cold start if the cause also affects the glow plug supply
Further glow plug codes stored

P037E.d: P037E means the voltage read back from the glow plug supply is too low. GM's 2016/2018 diesels, whose glow plug output stages sit in the engine module, compare the feedback with the battery voltage while glowing: if it is lower by more than a calibrated, current-dependent threshold – excessive voltage drop or a short to ground of the sense line – a sample counts as faulty, and 60 of 120 samples in a 50 ms grid set the code, roughly 3 of 6 s. The check only runs with the engine running (afterglow), not while cranking, and is suspended if a single plug or the supply already has an electrical fault. GM classes the cause as internal to the module (measuring circuit) and turns on the check engine light after two trips. There is no limp mode; glow plug monitoring is restricted.

P037F.d: P037F means the voltage read back from the glow plug supply is too high. GM's 2016/2018 diesels set it when the feedback lies above a threshold derived from the run/crank relay voltage, with a feedback above 5.0 V – for example voltage is reported although the plugs are not energised, or the sense line is shorted to positive. The code needs 40 of 80 samples at 50 ms, about 2 of 4 s, only with the engine running, and turns on the check engine light after two trips; GM classes the cause as internal to the module. If there is a real short to positive or a stuck relay or output stage, the plugs can stay energised permanently, overheating them and draining the battery – then also check the single plug codes P0671 ff and P066x. CARB requires glow plug circuits to be monitored for correct current and voltage drop.

P0380.d: P0380 concerns glow plug circuit A – depending on the manufacturer the first group of plugs, glow relay 1 or feedback line A of the glow plug control module. Saab's 3.0 TiD (9-5, 2002) has two feedback lines from the control module; if line A at the engine module stays above 4.0 V for more than 3 s while glowing, the module is reporting a plug or circuit fault, checked once per drive cycle with the warning lamp on. In Saab's 1.9 TiD (EDC16) the glow plug control module drives two pairs of plugs, monitors them itself and reports faults over a diagnostic line that should switch inversely to the activation line. The 2010/11 Saab 9-5 2.0 TiD sets P0380 for implausible feedback or a missing supply of the module, there without check engine light. Newer GM and Ford diesels report single plugs under P0671 ff instead.

P0381.d: P0381 monitors the circuit of the wait-to-start lamp for an open circuit or, more generally, for faults that keep the lamp dark when commanded – CARB names a burnt-out bulb as the example, with exemptions for LCD clusters and for engines that only release the starter after preheating. GM's 2015–2018 diesels detect an open circuit in the driver by a high load impedance (about 200 kΩ in 2015), in 0.2 s or 10 of 15 samples, with the check engine light after two trips; on the 2014 Duramax LML P0381 still covered all lamp circuit faults including a short to ground. Ford's 2023 diesels check via the instrument cluster: if it reports the lamp off although on is commanded, P0381 is set within about 1 s at key-on. There is no limp mode; the risk is starting too early in the cold.

P0382.d: P0382 is the counterpart of P0380 for glow plug circuit B – depending on the manufacturer the second group of plugs, glow relay 2 or feedback line B of the glow plug control module. A code-specific manufacturer description exists from Saab: the 3.0 TiD V6 diesel in the 9-5 (2002) reads two feedback lines from its glow plug control module, and if line B stays above 4.0 V for more than 3 s while glowing, the module is reporting a fault in the second group of plugs; the check runs once per drive cycle, the warning lamp comes on and there is no further system reaction. Newer GM and Ford diesels report single plugs under P0671 ff and do not use P0382. CARB requires glow plug circuits to be monitored for correct current and voltage drop. P0383.d: Many diesels have a separate glow plug control module that the engine module commands over a control line. P0383 means this line is too low. In GM's logic for the 2010/11 Saab 9-5 2.0 TiD the engine module drives the module with a PWM signal and holds about 10 V on the line at rest (9.5–10.5 V at the signal terminal); if it reads too little voltage for more than 0.5 s – short to ground, or an open circuit or high resistance – it sets P0383, with ignition on, 9–16 V, once per ignition cycle. In that European version the code does not turn on the check engine light. Without a valid command the module does not glow, so the engine starts poorly when cold. Ford uses P0384 differently and not P0383; GM's 2016/2018 diesels have their output stages in the engine module and no such line. For US vehicles there is no code-specific source.

P0384.d: P0384 is the counterpart of P0383: the control line from the engine module to the glow plug control module is too high, i.e. shorted to positive. In GM's logic for the 2010/11 Saab 9-5 2.0 TiD the signal terminal should show 9.5–10.5 V; a higher voltage for more than 0.5 s, with ignition on and 9–16 V, sets the code, there without check engine light. Ford's 2023 diesels (6.7 and 3.0 litre) use P0384 differently from the J2012 name, for the supply voltage of the glow plug module: below 6.5 V, above 16.5 V or open, detected in about 1 s – today J2012 has P052F for that. So with Ford, check battery, alternator and the module's supply first. The consequence is missing or irregular preheating or a protective shutdown of the module, with a poor cold start.

P0385.d: Some engines have a second crankshaft sensor or a second track on the tone wheel, which the engine module checks against sensor A or the camshaft. P0385 means its signal is missing or does not match. GM's 2004 Northstar 4.6 V8 counts the crank pulses per cam pulse (target 48 ± 1, fault in 8 of 10 tests) and also flags 2 s while cranking or 0.4 s running without a match, after two trips; an active P0385 suspends the cam sensor check. GM's 3.8-litre V6 (2006) sets it when its low resolution track stays silent while the medium resolution track delivers 36 pulses, 40 of 50 samples. The Honda 3.5-litre in the 2004 Saturn Vue Redline sets it when the second crank signal is missing while the first runs, judged after 17 revolutions, in the first trip. The engine usually keeps running on sensor A.

P0386.d: P0386 means the signal of the second crankshaft sensor or second tone wheel track is present but implausible. GM's 2004 Northstar 4.6 V8 sets it after 5 resynchronisations within 10 s, after two trips. GM's 3.8-litre V6 (2006) expects exactly 0 or 6 low resolution pulses per 36 medium resolution pulses and one cam pulse; any other count in 40 of 50 samples sets the code, also after two trips. The Honda 3.5-litre in the 2004 Saturn Vue Redline counts implausible signals of its second crank sensor (target 44 crank pulses per 3 cam pulses, checked every half revolution, the counter dropping by one every 10 s) and sets the code at 30, about 2.2 s at idle, in the first trip. Typical causes are interference pulses, a dirty sensor or a wrong air gap; the result is jerking, misfire or longer cranking.

Jerking, misfire
Longer cranking

P0387.d: By its J2012 name P0387 means the signal of the second crankshaft sensor stays at a low level – typically a short to ground of the signal wire, a missing or shorted sensor supply, or with an inductive sensor an amplitude that is too small. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0387: the engines with a sensor B that we found (GM Northstar 4.6 and 3.8-litre V6, the Honda 3.5-litre in the Saturn Vue Redline) report its electrical faults under P0385 and implausible signals under P0386. The description therefore follows the J2012 name, the function of sensor B and CARB's monitoring requirement for crank angle sensors. As long as sensor A works, the engine usually keeps running; together with a sensor A fault it may not start.

P0388.d: Some engines have a second crankshaft sensor or a second track on the tone wheel – GM's 3.4/3.5/3.8-litre V6 use the low resolution track of a dual Hall sensor, the Honda 3.5-litre in the Saturn Vue Redline a second sensor – which the engine module checks against sensor A or the camshaft. By its J2012 name P0388 means the signal of sensor B stays above its upper limit – with a Hall sensor typically an open signal wire held high by the module's pull-up, or a short to positive. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0388: the engines with a sensor B report its electrical faults under P0385 and implausible signals under P0386. The description therefore follows the J2012 name, these component sources and CARB's monitoring requirement for crank angle sensors. The engine usually keeps running on sensor A; longer cranking is possible.

P038A.d: Ignition I is one of the control signal lines from the engine module to an ignition module, ignition output stage or group of coils; which cylinders it serves is defined by the manufacturer, not by the code standard. The code concerns the logic-level control signal, not the coil's primary current (that has its own codes, P0351 ff and P2300 ff). P038A means the control line is open – the module sees a voltage with its driver off that indicates high resistance. No manufacturer using these codes was found – neither GM nor Ford use the Ignition A to J codes; GM reports coil control faults as P0351 ff – so the description follows CARB and that analogy. The affected coils fire wrongly or not at all, causing misfire; many modules then shut off injection to those cylinders to protect the catalyst.

P0390.d: Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor; bank 2 is the side without cylinder 1, so the code only occurs on V and boxer engines with one exhaust cam sensor per bank. P0390 means no or too few exhaust cam pulses arrive from bank 2 while the crankshaft turns. GM's 3.0 twin-turbo V6 (LGW) sets it after 5.5 s without a cam pulse, 4 s of cranking or fewer than 4 pulses in 3 s, after two trips; for GM it collects all circuit faults. GM's 3.6-litre V6 in the Saab 9-4X also counts 800 of 1,000 engine cycles without a pulse. Ford checks the crank-to-cam ratio from 200 rpm within 5 s, and the 2004 Northstar counts missing signal changes up to 16. The bank 2 exhaust phaser then locks in its base position; the engine keeps running on the crank and intake cam sensors. FCA advises saving the synchronisation data before replacing the sensor.
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power (bank 2 exhaust cam timing in its base position)
Longer cranking
Rough idle

c: Tone wheel on the bank 2 exhaust phaser damaged, loose or wrongly fitted
Interference or loose contact producing extra edges
Sensor loose, wrong O-ring or gap, chips on the magnet
P0391.d: Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor; bank 2 is the side without cylinder 1, so the code only occurs on V and boxer engines with one exhaust cam sensor per bank. P0391 means the bank 2 exhaust cam signal is present, but the number or position of its pulses does not fit the crankshaft. GM's 3.0 twin-turbo V6 (LGW) expects 4 to 6 pulses in the first 12 reference events and 398 to 402 per 100 engine cycles on the four-tooth wheel, after two trips; the Saab 9-4X 2.8 turbo V6 (LAU) checks pulses per crank revolution below 2,520 rpm. The 2004 Northstar requires each edge within a window of crank teeth, and GM's 2004 3.6-litre V6 (LY7) counts implausible signals over two drive cycles. The phaser then goes to its base position and the engine cranks longer. Mechanical causes – damaged tone wheel, jumped chain – matter more here than with P0390.
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power (bank 2 exhaust cam timing in its base position)
Longer cranking
Rough idle
Occasional stalling

c: 5 V reference missing (shorted by another sensor on the same circuit)
P0392.d: Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor; bank 2 is the side without cylinder 1, so the code only occurs on V and boxer engines with one exhaust cam sensor per bank. P0392 means the bank 2 exhaust cam signal stays low without edges – typically a short to ground of the signal wire, a sensor output stuck low or a missing 5 V reference. Only manufacturers with separate low and high codes use it: on the Saab 9-4X 2.8 turbo V6 (GM LAU) the signal must stay low without pulses for more than 1 s, or 10 s cumulatively, after more than 10 crank revolutions and below 2,520 rpm, after two trips; GM's 2004/2005 3.6-litre V6 (LY7, LP1) counts the fault over two drive cycles. Newer GM petrol engines (2015–2020) and Ford report the same fault as P0390. The consequence is as for P0390: cam timing on bank 2 in its base position, loss of power, longer cranking.

Longer cranking

c: Signal wire open or connector off
P0393.d: Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor; bank 2 is the side without cylinder 1, so the code only occurs on V and boxer engines with one exhaust cam sensor per bank. P0393 means the bank 2 exhaust cam signal stays high without edges. Because the engine module pulls the Hall sensor's signal line up, an open wire leads to 'high' just like a short to positive – GM's 2004 3.6-litre V6 (LY7) therefore calls the fault 'circuit continuity or high' and counts it over two drive cycles. On the Saab 9-4X 2.8 turbo V6 (GM LAU) the signal must stay high without pulses for more than 1 s, or 10 s cumulatively, after two trips. Only manufacturers with separate low and high codes use it; newer GM petrol engines and Ford report the fault as P0390. The consequence is as for P0390: cam timing on bank 2 in its base position, loss of power, longer cranking.

P0394.d: Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor; bank 2 is the side without cylinder 1, so the code only occurs on V and boxer engines with one exhaust cam sensor per bank. P0394 means the bank 2 exhaust cam signal now and then appears at a position where it is not expected relative to the crank reference – sporadic extra or missing edges. Ford checks this in its camshaft ignition system test from 200 rpm and decides within 5 s. FCA also uses the code and asks dealers to save the cam/crank synchronisation event data before replacing parts, a hint that the sensor itself is often not the culprit. GM does not use P0394 and reports such faults under P0391. Typical causes are a loose contact, interference or a damaged tone wheel.
s: Check engine light on
Sporadic jerking or stalling
Occasionally longer cranking

c: Connector at the pressure-sensing glow plug loose or corroded
Reference, signal or ground wire open or shorted
Sensor electronics in the glow plug faulty
P0395.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P0395 is the general circuit code for this pressure sensor, meant for modules that do not separate open circuits and shorts into low and high. The only manufacturer we found using this code family – GM's European 2.0 CDTI diesel, documented in Saab 9-5 workshop information – splits the faults into low and high (P0397, P0398) and does not use P0395; VW's US 2.0 TDI engines with pressure-sensing glow plugs report such faults with their own codes (P13CE ff). The description therefore follows CARB's requirement to monitor input sensors for circuit faults. The sensor has three wires (5 V reference, ground, signal); without it the module drops combustion control for that cylinder.
s: Check engine light on (often after two trips)
Usually barely noticeable – combustion control for the cylinder is switched off
Possibly rougher running, more noise or slightly higher consumption

c: Sensor in the glow plug drifting (deposits, ageing)
Glow plug leaking or wrongly torqued (pressure transmitted wrongly)
Contact resistance in connector or ground
P0396.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P0396 means the sensor signal is electrically fine but does not fit the expected value. No manufacturer document available to us describes the code; a GM patent shows how such a check works: in overrun the measured peak pressure is compared with a compression pressure calculated from manifold pressure and compression ratio, and the pressure values are also compared with limits and with crankshaft speed fluctuation. GM's European diesel in the Saab 9-5 uses the peak pressure in overrun anyway to find top dead centre. Typical causes are sensor drift from combustion deposits or a glow plug that leaks or is wrongly torqued. CARB requires a two-sided plausibility check of input sensors where feasible.
s: Check engine light on
Combustion control for the cylinder off – slightly rough running, more noise
Possibly more smoke or consumption

c: 5 V reference wire open or shorted to ground
Sensor electronics of the glow plug faulty
P0397.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P0397 means the sensor signal stays below its lower limit. GM's European 2.0 CDTI diesel (Saab 9-5, 2010) sets it when the signal is below the threshold for more than 2 s with the engine running, checked once per drive cycle, with the check engine light after two trips; the displayed maximum combustion pressure then reads 0 kPa instead of the normal 0–9,000 kPa. Saab names an open or grounded 5 V reference and a signal wire shorted to ground as causes; the glow plug should measure 3–12 Ω between reference and ground. Without the signal, combustion control for this cylinder is switched off, which is usually barely noticeable.

P0399.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P039A.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P039A means the pressure measured in the cylinder is lower than expected while the sensor itself is electrically fine. No manufacturer document available to us describes the code; GM patents show how such an evaluation works: peak and minimum pressure are compared with limits and with a motoring pressure calculated from manifold pressure and compression ratio, and the ratio of measured to motoring pressure is compared between cylinders. A low value can mean weak combustion or compression – leaking valve, worn rings, leaking glow plug seat, an injector delivering too little – or a sensor drifting downwards. The usual consequence is rough running and more smoke.

P039B.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. It is documented by code at Audi, surprisingly on a petrol engine: on the 2015 S3 (2.0 TFSI, engine CYFB) the four 'pressure too high' codes came on with the EPC lamp, usually together with misfire codes P0300–P0304 and the manufacturer code for hiding a cylinder; the cause was a software fault that mis-detected misfire, and a software update fixed it. P039C.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P039E.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P03E3.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 8. P03E3 means the swing of the pressure signal is too large. The only manufacturer we found using this code family, GM's European 2.0 CDTI four-cylinder diesel (Saab 9-5, 2010), uses 'pressure variation too high' for cylinders 1 to 4: signal outside its range for more than 0.2 s with the engine running; what exactly is measured, Saab does not explain – presumably a noisy or overshooting signal, from faulty sensor electronics, interference or a combustion anomaly. For cylinder 8, which only engines with at least 8 cylinders have, no manufacturer document available to us uses the code; the description follows that logic and CARB. Usually there are no noticeable symptoms.

Usually no noticeable symptoms
Possibly rough running or combustion noise because control is off

c: Injector coked, leaking or delivering the wrong quantity

P03E4.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 8. P03E4 means the combustion quality in the cylinder, evaluated from the combustion pressure, is abnormal. No manufacturer document available to us describes the code; a GM patent shows the method: the ratio of measured to motoring pressure is turned into a measure of combustion energy, an inequality index against the neighbouring cylinders in firing order is formed, and a two-sided threshold detects partial combustion, misfire, injector and compression faults. CARB requires engines with a combustion or combustion quality sensor to detect misfire more sharply (5 % in 1,000 revolutions). Typical causes are a coked or leaking injector, compression loss or poor fuel; the engine runs roughly and smokes more.

P03E5.d: On some engines the intake cam phaser (camshaft position actuator A) has its own position sensors, which tell the engine module where the phaser actually is; sensor C is the third of them, bank 1 the side with cylinder 1. P03E5 is the general circuit code for this sensor: the module sees an open circuit or a signal outside its valid window on the supply, signal or ground line. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. GM's 2.7-litre engine monitors comparable position sensors on its sliding camshaft under other codes (P2C05 ff), with an open circuit above 200 kΩ and a short below 0.5 Ω in 4 of 5 samples – only as a comparison. The phaser is then usually held in its base position. CARB requires electronic parts of variable valve timing systems to be monitored as comprehensive components.

P03E9.d: Engines with cam profile switching move the intake camshaft between lift profiles with actuators – for example pins that shift a sliding cam – and position sensors report which profile is engaged. The engine module learns reference values of position sensor A, such as its end-position levels or the expected pulse position relative to the crankshaft and camshaft sensors; a Ford patent describes correcting this position for the cam phase. P03E9 means the learned value lies outside the permitted adaptation limit, so profile detection is no longer reliable and the module usually stays in a safe profile. No manufacturer document available to us describes the code or its limits; GM's 2.7-litre sliding cam has no learning-limit code. CARB lists a pin that does not reach its position among the faults to be detected.

P03EC.d: With a sliding camshaft, the intake camshaft (camshaft A) carries movable cam pieces with several lift profiles; solenoid actuators shoot a pin into a groove in the piece and shift it axially. P03FA.d: Ignition K is one of up to twelve control signal lines (A to L) from the engine module to an ignition coil with integrated output stage or to an ignition module – plausibly the 11th channel, but the code standard leaves the assignment to the manufacturer. The code concerns this logic-level signal, not the coil's primary circuit (coil K has its own codes, P0361 and P2330 ff). P03FA means the control line is open or high-resistance: with its driver switched off the module sees a voltage that indicates a missing load (GM uses more than 30 kΩ for comparable coil drivers). The coil fires wrongly or not at all; the misfire usually also sets P0300 ff, and many modules shut off injection to that cylinder to protect the catalyst. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code – it would only concern twelve-cylinder engines, whose makers publish no OBD summaries; GM and Ford tables stop at eight and ten cylinders.

P0400.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P0400 is the general flow fault of EGR system A, used where the module does not classify the error as too little (P0401) or too much (P0402). Ford petrol engines with a stepper-motor valve open and close the valve at steady part load and compare intake manifold pressure with and without EGR; too small a normalised difference (below 1.0) sets P0400, MIL after two trips. GM diesels use the code differently, for air-mass checks with excessive EGR rate. EGR is then usually switched off.
s: Check engine light on
Pinging under load or rough idle, depending on direction

c: EGR passages, valve or cooler carboned up
EGR valve faulty or stuck closed
Ford: DPFE sensor or its hoses blocked, cracked or swapped
Diesel: air mass meter drifting or air leak after the turbo
Vacuum control of the valve faulty
P0401.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P0401 means too little exhaust is recirculated. Petrol engines open the valve briefly and expect a rise in manifold pressure (GM 2004 V6, MIL on the first trip); older Ford systems measure the pressure drop across an orifice (DPFE sensor). Diesels balance the air mass: if the meter sees more fresh air than the target EGR rate allows, too little exhaust flows (GM, Ford, Saab, usually MIL after two trips). Diesel causes are mostly a coked valve or cooler, petrol causes blocked passages.

P040F.d: The two EGR temperature sensors measure the gas temperature in the EGR path, before and after the cooler – which is A and which is B depends on the maker. If they differ by more than the calibrated limit at start-up (GM Duramax LML table, at least 20 °C, with exclusions for block heaters), the code is set, MIL after two trips. P0410.d: After a cold start the secondary air (AIR) pump blows fresh air behind the exhaust valves so that unburnt fuel burns off and the catalyst heats up faster; a shut-off valve opens the path and stops exhaust from flowing back. P0410 is the general function code for secondary air system A. Many Bosch-managed engines check it passively: with the pump running, the front oxygen sensor must read lean or the fuel control must react; Pierburg lists P0410 as no lean signal, i.e. no air detected. Saab's Motronic 900, by contrast, uses it for too much air. GM's systems with a pressure sensor use P0411 and P2440 ff instead. The check runs once per trip after a cold start; driving is unaffected.

Secondary air readiness not set (emission test)

c: Pump weak or failed (water, filter debris)

P0411.d: After a cold start the secondary air (AIR) pump blows fresh air behind the exhaust valves so that unburnt fuel burns off and the catalyst heats up faster; a shut-off valve opens the path and stops exhaust from flowing back. P0411 means the measured air flow does not match the expected value. Passive systems judge it from the oxygen sensor or fuel control (Saab 900: less than 12 points of correction within 12 s). GM measures actively with a pressure sensor between pump and valve and compares it with a model while pump and valve are on – from 2018 a deviation above 5.0 kPa or below −4.9 kPa sets the code, MIL after two trips. The test needs a cold engine after a long stop, so short warm trips do not complete it.

Secondary air readiness not set (emission test)
Pump silent after a cold start, or unusually loud

P0412.d: The switching valve is the electrically driven valve of this path – a solenoid valve, or on Pierburg/VW systems an electric changeover valve that applies vacuum to the pneumatic combination valve; valve A serves the first path or bank 1, valve B the second. P0412 is the general electrical fault in the control circuit of valve A, detected by comparing the driver's feedback with its commanded state. GM has used it since about 2015 specifically for an open circuit (200 kΩ or more, 20 of 25 samples, MIL after two trips) and reports shorts as P041F and P044F; older GM systems and Toyota use it for any driver fault. The valve then stays shut, so secondary air is missing and P0411 or P2441 may follow.

Secondary air inactive
Secondary air readiness not set (emission test)
Driving normal

P0413 means the control circuit of valve A is open: with the driver switched off the module does not see the expected supply or pull-up level. The check runs continuously. P0414.d: The switching valve is the electrically driven valve of this path – a solenoid valve, or on Pierburg/VW systems an electric changeover valve that applies vacuum to the pneumatic combination valve; valve A serves the first path or bank 1, valve B the second. P0414 means the control circuit of valve A is shorted. A short to ground keeps the valve energized and open; a short to supply or a shorted coil overloads the driver, which many modules then switch off for the rest of the trip. An open valve with the pump running can also set P2440, and exhaust can reach the pump if the check valve leaks. Subaru names P0414 in its bulletin for the two-valve system.

P0420.d: The engine module checks whether the catalyst of bank 1 still converts enough. On petrol engines it estimates the oxygen storage capacity by comparing the sensors before and after the catalyst – a good catalyst smooths the rear signal. GM uses a test on overrun (ratio below 0.35 sets the code on the first trip), Ford an index ratio above 0.75 or fuel integration after fuel cut-off. On diesels P0420 concerns the oxidation catalyst, checked by its heat release during filter regeneration (GM Duramax LML, Ford below 45 % of the expected heat). Ford names oil-borne poisoning as the most common cause.

P0421 means it no longer converts enough. Mitsubishi V6 engines with manifold catalysts and GM's 3.0/3.2-litre V6 of 2004/05 with Bosch control report it: the rear sensor amplitude is compared with a model, and a quality factor above 0.625 (2004) or 0.375 (2005) sets the code after two trips. GM's small diesels use P0421 for the close-coupled oxidation catalyst, tested by heat balance during filter regeneration.

P043E.d: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. Systems with a leak detection pump (Bosch DM-TL at VW, Audi, BMW and Maserati, Denso's canister pump module at Toyota/Lexus) first measure a reference value with the pump working only through a built-in 0.5 mm (0.020 in) orifice; it is the yardstick for the small-leak test that CARB requires. P043E means the reference measurement shows too little flow – the vacuum (or with DM-TL the pressure and pump current) becomes stronger than expected, so the orifice or reference path is partly blocked, often by dirt or liquid after overfilling. GM and Ford do not use the code; Maserati fixed false triggering with software.

P043F.d: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. Systems with a leak detection pump (Bosch DM-TL at VW, Audi, BMW and Maserati, Denso's canister pump module at Toyota/Lexus) first measure a reference value with the pump working only through a built-in 0.5 mm (0.020 in) orifice; it is the yardstick for the small-leak test that CARB requires. P043F means the reference measurement shows too much flow – the reference vacuum or pressure does not reach the expected value, because the reference path or changeover valve leaks, the pump is weak, or air enters through leaking valves in the test path. The leak test can then not be judged, since a weak yardstick would hide leaks. GM and Ford do not use the code.

P0440 is the general code for a fault in this system without further narrowing down – leak, purge flow or component. Today most makers use the specific codes instead (P0441 ff, P0455–P0457, P0496); the GM and Ford tables of 2006–2023 do not contain P0440. P0441.d: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P0441 means the actual purge flow does not match the target – too little, or flow although the purge valve is closed. CARB requires a fault when no purge flow is detected. P0442.d: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P0442 reports a small leak; what size that means depends on the maker. Ford detects 0.040 in (1 mm) with the engine running: the vent valve closes, engine vacuum pulls the tank down, the purge valve closes and a pressure rise above 2.5 inH2O in 15 s sets the code (0.020 in is P0456). GM uses the natural pressure change after switch-off for 0.020 in and averages several tests. Pump systems at VW and Audi compare against a reference leak. A worn or loose fuel cap is the most common cause.

P0443.d: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P0443 is the electrical check of purge valve A, which the module switches to ground in pulses; it compares the driver's feedback voltage with the commanded state. Documented uses are the flap behind the particulate filter of VW's and Audi's 2.0 TDI, which raises back pressure for the low-pressure EGR, and the sound flaps of Audi and Bentley. P048C means valve A's position signal is electrically valid but does not match the commanded position or the learned end positions. It is documented only on VW's and Audi's 2.0 TDI of 2009–13, together with P047F, P048A, P048B and P0401, caused by the corroded, sticking flap shaft. After replacing the actuator, the end positions must be relearned.

Flap without function, exhaust sound changed

P048D.d: An exhaust pressure control valve is an electrically driven flap in the exhaust with a position sensor or end-position switch, usually inside the actuator. P0490.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P0491.d: After a cold start the secondary air pump blows fresh air behind the exhaust valves so that unburnt fuel burns off and the catalyst heats up faster; CARB requires the air flow to be monitored per bank. P0491 means too little air reaches bank 1 (the side with cylinder 1). VW and Audi calculate the injected air mass per bank from the front oxygen sensor's reaction during the cold-start phase; an Audi bulletin names values of 0.4–0.7 on both banks as too little together, often from coked air passages in the cylinder head. On VW/Audi V engines each bank has its own combination valve with a shared pump. Ford assigns the code to the bank 1 secondary air monitor; GM uses P0411 instead.

P0493.d: Two kinds of cooling fan carry these codes: electric fans switched by relays or driven by a PWM/LIN fan module with speed feedback, and engine-driven fans with an electronically controlled viscous clutch, whose speed a Hall sensor reports – GM calls them EV fans, meaning electro-viscous, not electric vehicle. Two counts set it, with the warning lamp on the first trip – unlike P0495, which needs two trips. Ford, FCA and GM from 2014 were not found to use it.

P0495.d: Two kinds of cooling fan carry these codes: electric fans switched by relays or driven by a PWM/LIN fan module with speed feedback, and engine-driven fans with an electronically controlled viscous clutch, whose speed a Hall sensor reports – GM calls them EV fans, meaning electro-viscous, not electric vehicle. P0496.d: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P0496 means vapour flows into the intake although the module is not purging – usually a purge valve that leaks or sticks open. GM and Saab seal the system after a cold start with the engine running; if tank vacuum exceeds 2491 Pa for 5 s, the code sets (fuel 10–90 %, MIL after two trips). Ford, which replaced its old code P1450 with P0496, also sets it for excessive vacuum during the leak test, for example with a vent valve stuck closed. Hard starting right after refuelling is typical.

P0497.d: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P049A.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. Circuit B is the second EGR path; on diesels with two circuits it is the low-pressure EGR, which takes exhaust after the particulate filter and feeds it in before the turbo compressor (GM diesels 2016–18, FCA's 2.2 and 3.0 diesels). P04AB.d: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. Purge valve B is a second electric purge valve, usually for the high-load purge line of a turbo engine, which purges to the compressor inlet when there is boost in the manifold (Ford patent). Many makers solve this path with one purge valve and passive check valves instead – Ford tests it as P04F0 – and then have no valve B. CARB requires every purge path to be checked. P04AB means the control circuit of purge valve B is open; the high-load path then does not purge. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB and the comparable purge valve A checks (for GM P0443/P0458/P0459).

P04AC.d: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. Purge valve B is a second electric purge valve, usually for the high-load purge line of a turbo engine, which purges to the compressor inlet when there is boost in the manifold (Ford patent). Many makers solve this path with one purge valve and passive check valves instead – Ford tests it as P04F0 – and then have no valve B. CARB requires every purge path to be checked. Many makers solve this path with one purge valve and passive check valves instead – Ford tests it as P04F0 – and then have no valve B. CARB requires every purge path to be checked. P04B4.d: Plug-in and some full hybrids keep the fuel tank sealed while driving, separated from the charcoal canister by a valve. P04CE.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. The code standard allows up to four EGR temperature sensors, A to D – for example before and after the cooler, or in the high- and low-pressure circuits; which is which depends on the maker. Sensor C is the third of them, usually an NTC whose low voltage means hot. P04CE is its general circuit fault, without separating low and high. FCA lists sensor C codes for its part 68142905A (Ram 2014 6.4 and 3.0 litre, Jeep and Dodge 3.6 Pentastar 2016) together with P040B, P0401 and P2457. Thresholds are not published. Without a valid temperature the EGR flow model is wrong, so the module uses a substitute value or switches EGR off.

P04D8.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. Where EGR is closed-loop controlled – on flow, valve position or pressure difference – CARB requires the control to start within a time set by the maker after starting; otherwise a fault is due, and P04D8 is that code. Typical prerequisites are coolant or cooler temperature, valid sensors and an operating range; Ford diesels, for example, run their EGR monitors only with EGR in closed loop. No manufacturer document available to us uses P04D8 – many monitor the inputs individually instead, as CARB permits.

P04D9.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P04D9 means the EGR control has used up its authority and still gets too little flow – CARB requires this to be detected. Ford's 6.7-litre diesel sets it when the desired minus the measured EGR rate stays above 50 points for 20 s. Volvo cars from 2022 also set it after long low-load driving and fix it with a software update and an activation drive; a Mack/Volvo truck bulletin traces it to wrong EGR temperature readings from worn connector contacts.

P04DA.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P04DA is the counterpart of P04D9: the control cannot lower the flow far enough even at the end of its range. CARB requires this for petrol engines from model years 2019–21 and for diesels. Ford's 6.7-litre diesel sets it when the desired minus the measured EGR rate stays below −60 points for 20 s with EGR in closed loop. Too much exhaust in the cylinder causes soot, rough running and, on petrol engines, misfire up to stalling at idle.

P04DB.d: The crankcase ventilation (PCV) system routes blow-by gas from the crankcase into the intake; CARB requires a disconnection between crankcase and intake to be detected. GM's 2.0-litre LSY has a pressure sensor in the PCV hose: with the hose connected it must see a pressure drop that grows with air flow, plus pressure pulses from the pistons. Ford reports the same sensor type as crankcase pressure sensor A (P051A ff). P04DB means a disconnection: without the pressure drop the clean-air side is off, without the pulses the crankcase side. GM's LSY uses the product of normalised offset and noise (below 0.63 kPa², MIL after two trips); Ford's EcoBoost checks the dirty side at cranking and the clean side above 5 lb/min of air. Engines without such a sensor may report a disconnection through mixture or load codes, as CARB allows. FCA bulletins cover it on the Alfa Romeo 2.0 turbo and the Ram 3.0 EcoDiesel.

P04DC.d: Plug-in and some full hybrids keep the fuel tank sealed while driving, separated from the charcoal canister by a valve. When the driver presses the fuel button, the system opens the valve, lets the pressure escape into the canister and only then unlocks the filler door. A switch reports whether the door is open or closed, so that the tank can be sealed again afterwards. P04DC means the door switch signal is electrically valid but implausible. A GM patent detects refuelling from a rising fuel level at standstill with low tank pressure; if the switch reported open for less than about 20 s, or closed for too long, it is faulty. A Ford patent sets a fault if the fuel level rose and the car drove off without the switch ever reporting open – the valve then stays open and the driver is warned. If the door state is unknown, the system leaves the tank open to the canister as a precaution and suspends the leak tests. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB's input component rules and patents for the door switch.

P04DE.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P04DF.d: Purge valve A is the main EVAP purge valve between charcoal canister and intake manifold (on turbo engines the low-load path); its electrical circuit faults are P0443, P0458 and P0459. P0500.d: The vehicle speed signal A comes, depending on the maker, from a sensor on the gearbox, the transmission output speed, the wheel speeds via ABS/ESP or a CAN message; CARB explicitly names it as an input to be monitored. P0500 is the general code for this signal. Ford checks plausibility: the car must be moving (high load, positive torque), yet the signal stays below 1–5 mph for 5 s; Ford diesels flag a missing CAN message after 0.5 s. GM's Saturn ION of 2004 used high load with below 3 mph for 6.2 s (MIL after two trips); GM's 2018 tables use P0502/P0503 instead. Cruise control is then disabled and substitute values are used.

P0505.d: CARB requires the idle speed control to be monitored: petrol engines must flag a fault if the target idle speed is not reached within +200/−100 rpm, diesels within ±30 %. Older engines use a separate idle air control valve that bypasses the closed throttle; with electronic throttle the throttle itself controls idle and no separate valve exists. P0505 is the general fault of the idle control, used where the maker does not separate too low from too high or the control is at its limit. P0506.d: CARB requires the idle speed control to be monitored: petrol engines must flag a fault if the target idle speed is not reached within +200/−100 rpm, diesels within ±30 %. P050A.d: After a cold start the engine module raises idle speed and air mass and retards the ignition so that much heat goes into the exhaust and the catalyst lights off quickly. CARB requires this cold-start strategy to be monitored with its own codes, separate from ordinary idle and ignition faults. Ford collects data during the first 15 s after a cold start (coolant and catalyst 20–100 °F) and judges after 300 s, once per trip. P050A checks whether the raised idle speed or air mass commanded at a cold start is actually reached: Ford sets it when the average deviation between target and actual speed exceeds 200 rpm, with the warning lamp. GM does not use P050A as its own monitor and reports cold-start system faults under its manufacturer code P1400.

c: Idle control takes back the retard because speed would drop (false air, dirty throttle)

P050B.d: After a cold start the engine module raises idle speed and air mass and retards the ignition so that much heat goes into the exhaust and the catalyst lights off quickly. CARB requires this cold-start strategy to be monitored with its own codes, separate from ordinary idle and ignition faults. Ford collects data during the first 15 s after a cold start (coolant and catalyst 20–100 °F) and judges after 300 s, once per trip. P050B checks the ignition part of the strategy – the retard for catalyst heating; CARB allows checking only the commanded value. Ford sets it when desired and commanded cold-start timing differ by more than 10°, for example because knock, torque or idle control take back the retard. Mostly MIL after two trips, some calibrations without MIL. Ford and FCA do not use P050D.

P050E.d: After a cold start the engine module raises idle speed and air mass and retards the ignition so that much heat goes into the exhaust and the catalyst lights off quickly.
