c: Idle valve faulty (coil open or shorted)
P0511.d: CARB requires the idle speed control to be monitored: petrol engines must flag a fault if the target idle speed is not reached within +200/−100 rpm, diesels within ±30 %. Older engines use a separate idle air control valve that bypasses the closed throttle; with electronic throttle the throttle itself controls idle and no separate valve exists. P0511 is the general circuit fault of the idle valve – open, short to ground or to positive – without separating low and high, which CARB permits. Ford (up to about 2012, engines with an idle valve) has the output stage report it via a diagnostic status bit, continuously. Valve types are PWM solenoid or rotary valves (two wires) or stepper motors (four wires, typical of GM). Without a working valve the engine runs on a fixed bypass or the mechanical stop and may stall.
s: Idle too high, too low or fluctuating
Engine stalls at idle
Check engine light on

c: Ignition or start switch, or start button, faulty or sticking
Harness chafed, short to ground or positive
Selector or clutch switch in the start path
P0512.d: The engine module reads a start request – from the ignition switch, a start button via the body module, or start-stop – and drives the starter relay with it. P0512 flags a fault in this signal. Subaru (also in the Saab 9-2X) checks plausibility: if the engine runs above 500 rpm and the start signal stays active for more than 3 minutes, a short or sticking switch is assumed, MIL after two trips. On a Jeep Cherokee diesel a chafed harness caused P0512 with a no-start. The starter then does not crank – or with a short to positive keeps running.
s: Engine does not start, starter does not crank
Starter keeps running after the start (noise)
Check engine light (Subaru after two trips)

c: Engine module replaced or reflashed and not taught to the immobiliser
Key or transponder not programmed or faulty
Immobiliser, body or RF hub module replaced or faulty
P0513.d: The engine module receives a secret code from the immobiliser or body module (Chrysler SKIM/SKREEM/RF hub, Saab CIM); if it does not match the stored code, P0513 sets and starting is prevented – Saab cuts fuel and blocks the starter. The most common trigger is a replaced or reflashed engine module that was not taught to the immobiliser (FCA, Saab), less often handshake timing on FCA hybrids or a key not programmed. FCA lists it as invalid SKIM key. It is not emission-related; CARB does not require immobiliser monitoring, and no source documents a warning lamp.
s: Engine does not start or stops after 1–2 s
Immobiliser or security lamp flashes
Starter does not crank (Saab)

c: Corrosion at sensor or connector near the battery acid
Sensor fitted wrongly after a battery change
P0514.d: The battery temperature sensor – usually an NTC in the battery tray or inside an intelligent battery sensor on the negative terminal – lets the module adjust the charging voltage (higher when cold, lower when warm) and supports battery management and start-stop. P0514 is the plausibility check of the temperature signal. On FCA/Alfa Romeo the temperature comes from the intelligent battery sensor on the negative terminal; P0514 means its value is implausible, and several cases on the Alfa Giulia 2.0 were fixed by engine module software. A fixed substitute temperature is then used; CARB requires plausibility faults to have their own code.
s: Possibly check engine light
Charging voltage too high or too low
Start-stop not working

c: Sensor not plugged in after a battery change
P0515.d: The battery temperature sensor – usually an NTC in the battery tray or inside an intelligent battery sensor on the negative terminal – lets the module adjust the charging voltage (higher when cold, lower when warm) and supports battery management and start-stop. P0515 is its general circuit fault – open or short – without separating low and high; the charging voltage is then fixed or conservative. No manufacturer document available to us names this code; the description follows CARB's input component rules. A fixed substitute temperature is then used.
s: Possibly check engine light
Charging voltage not temperature-compensated
Start-stop or battery management limited

c: Signal line shorted to ground (chafed at the battery tray)
Moisture or acid in the connector
P0516.d: The battery temperature sensor – usually an NTC in the battery tray or inside an intelligent battery sensor on the negative terminal – lets the module adjust the charging voltage (higher when cold, lower when warm) and supports battery management and start-stop. P0516 means the signal voltage stays below its limit for a minimum time; with an NTC in a voltage divider a low voltage means very hot, or more often a signal line shorted to ground or an internal short. The module then assumes a hot battery and may charge too little. No manufacturer document available to us names this code; the description follows CARB's input component rules. A fixed substitute temperature is then used.
s: Possibly check engine light
Charging voltage too low
Battery weak, starting problems in the cold

c: Sensor unplugged or forgotten after a battery change
Wire or connector open or corroded
P0517.d: The battery temperature sensor – usually an NTC in the battery tray or inside an intelligent battery sensor on the negative terminal – lets the module adjust the charging voltage (higher when cold, lower when warm) and supports battery management and start-stop. P0517 means the signal voltage is above its limit, close to the reference; with an NTC that means very cold, or more often an open circuit – sensor unplugged, wire broken – or a short to positive. The module then assumes a cold battery and may charge too high. No manufacturer document available to us names this code; the description follows CARB's input component rules. A fixed substitute temperature is then used.
s: Possibly check engine light
Charging voltage too high
Battery gassing or overcharged

c: Loose contact or corrosion at the idle valve connector
Broken or chafed wire in the harness
P0518.d: Older engines without electronic throttle have a separate idle air control valve bypassing the closed throttle; CARB requires its output to be checked but not the fault types to be coded separately. P0518 means its circuit fails sporadically – the signal or current briefly leaves its valid range and returns. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0518; GM and Ford report idle valve faults as P0505–P0507 and P0511. Engines with electronic throttle do not set it.
s: Fluctuating idle
Engine stalls when coasting or stopping
Check engine light (depending on the maker)

c: False air behind the throttle (intake, gasket, vacuum hose)
Throttle or idle valve stuck open (foreign body, coking)
Follow-on fault of other codes (sensors, pedal)
P0519.d: P0519 means the idle control fails functionally with an electrically sound circuit – the actual idle speed deviates strongly despite fully used control. It is documented only on Subaru (also in the Saab 9-2X, electronic throttle, around 2005): idle at least 1000 rpm above target with the control already at zero for 2 or 5 s sets the code with the warning lamp at once, and a fail-safe cuts fuel to cylinders to stop the engine racing. GM and Ford use P0506/P0507 instead; CARB's mandatory limit is +200/−100 rpm.
s: Idle far above target, engine races
Jerking from cylinder cut-off in limp mode
Check engine light on

c: Connector or supply, ground or SENT signal wire open or corroded
Oil or moisture in the connector
P051A.d: The crankcase pressure sensor measures pressure in the crankcase ventilation (PCV) against atmosphere; Ford's EcoBoost engines use it for the disconnection check P04DB, which needs a sound sensor. P051A is the sensor's general circuit fault. Ford uses it only for the digital SENT sensor, when the module receives invalid messages or signal patterns (together with U060E for lost communication); analogue sensors report P051B–P051D instead. It is checked continuously with 5 s to fault.
s: Check engine light on
Usually no change in driving
Disconnection check P04DB suspended

c: PCV or blow-by valve sticking, ventilation blocked or frozen (real overpressure)
P051B.d: The crankcase pressure sensor measures pressure in the crankcase ventilation (PCV) against atmosphere; Ford's EcoBoost engines use it for the disconnection check P04DB, which needs a sound sensor. P051B is its plausibility check. Ford flags a zero-point deviation above 0.15 inHg (about 0.5 kPa) from ambient with the engine stopped, and in operation at low air flow a pressure above 5 inHg (about 17 kPa) or below −0.6 inHg – so Ford also reports a real excess crankcase pressure under P051B. Maserati and Alfa Romeo bulletins name blow-by valves or software.
s: Check engine light on
Possibly oil leaks or oil mist (real overpressure)
Often no change in driving

c: 5 V reference or signal line open or shorted to ground
5 V reference pulled down by another sensor
P051C.d: The crankcase pressure sensor measures pressure in the crankcase ventilation (PCV) against atmosphere; Ford's EcoBoost engines use it for the disconnection check P04DB, which needs a sound sensor. P051C means the signal of the analogue ratiometric sensor is too low – Ford sets it below 0.44 V for 5 s. Typical is a signal shorted to ground, an open or shorted 5 V reference, or an open signal line pulled down.
s: Check engine light on
Usually no change in driving
Disconnection check P04DB suspended

P051D.d: The crankcase pressure sensor measures pressure in the crankcase ventilation (PCV) against atmosphere; Ford's EcoBoost engines use it for the disconnection check P04DB, which needs a sound sensor. P051D means the signal is too high – Ford sets it above 4.56 V for 5 s. Typical is a signal shorted to 5 V or battery voltage, an open sensor ground, or an open signal pulled up. A real excess pressure in the crankcase does not set P051D.
s: Check engine light on
Usually no change in driving
Disconnection check P04DB suspended

c: Loose contact at the sensor connector
Oil or water in the connector
P051E.d: The crankcase pressure sensor measures pressure in the crankcase ventilation (PCV) against atmosphere; Ford's EcoBoost engines use it for the disconnection check P04DB, which needs a sound sensor. P051E means the signal jumps or briefly drops below or above its limits – physically impossible changes, usually from a loose contact. No manufacturer document available to us uses P051E; Ford, Maserati and FCA use only P051A–P051D. The description follows CARB's input component rules.
s: Check engine light on
Usually no change in driving
Disconnection check P04DB suspended

c: Separator or filter clogged with oil, soot or sludge
Icing in the separator or hose on short winter trips
P051F.d: The crankcase ventilation has an oil mist separator or filter element that can clog; the crankcase pressure sensor then sees rising pressure at a given flow. P051F reports this restriction. No manufacturer document available to us uses it – Ford reports high pressure under P051B. BMW and GM bulletins describe the consequences of a blocked separator: oil pushed past seals, oil mist in the intake and charge air cooler, higher oil consumption. CARB requires the PCV system to be monitored.
s: Check engine light on
Oil leaks at seals or dipstick
Oil mist in the intake, higher oil consumption

c: Connector corroded or oily (oil creeping through a leaking sensor)
Signal line open or shorted to ground
5 V reference or supply faulty (usually with other sensor codes)
P0520.d: The oil pressure sensor matters for emissions control because modern engines use it as an input – for two-stage or regulated oil pumps, hydraulic cam phasers and GM's cylinder deactivation, whose lifters switch by oil pressure. P0520 is the general circuit fault, used differently: Ford petrol and diesel engines set it for the digital SENT sensor when it reports an internal fault, does not initialise or sends values out of range (lost communication is U0600), after 5 s. GM's 1.4 L turbo with an oil pressure switch sets it when the switch reports pressure although the engine has been off long enough to be pressureless – type C, without warning lamp.
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Oil pressure gauge or warning wrong
Cam phasing or cylinder deactivation possibly disabled

c: Oil pump control valve or two-stage pump stuck in the wrong stage
Wrong viscosity, low oil level or foaming oil
P0521.d: The oil pressure sensor matters for emissions control because modern engines use it as an input – for two-stage or regulated oil pumps, hydraulic cam phasers and GM's cylinder deactivation, whose lifters switch by oil pressure. P0521 is the plausibility check. With the engine off the sensor must read about zero (GM: above 40 kPa after 10 s is a fault, Ford diesel above 70 kPa); with it running the value is compared with a model of speed and oil temperature (GM single-stage pump ±50 kPa). GM checks two-stage pumps against limits per stage and calibrates P0521 with the pump valve – so a real pressure fault can also set it. GM type B, two trips.
s: Check engine light on
Oil pressure reading implausible or fluctuating
Cylinder deactivation or cam phasing possibly disabled

c: Signal line shorted to ground or open
P0522.d: The oil pressure sensor matters for emissions control because modern engines use it as an input – for two-stage or regulated oil pumps, hydraulic cam phasers and GM's cylinder deactivation, whose lifters switch by oil pressure. P0522 means the signal voltage is below its limit: GM 2018 below 5 % of the 5 V reference, Ford petrol below 0.25 V, Ford diesel below 0.018 V, about 5 s. As the sensor gives about 0.5 V at zero pressure, this is an electrical fault – real low pressure is P0524. GM's 2006 V8s used the warning lamp only with cylinder deactivation; GM's 4.6 L Northstar then allows cam phasing only above 1500 rpm.
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Oil pressure gauge at zero or warning despite normal pressure
Cam phasing or cylinder deactivation possibly disabled

c: Signal shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Oil or moisture in the connector
P0523.d: The oil pressure sensor matters for emissions control because modern engines use it as an input – for two-stage or regulated oil pumps, hydraulic cam phasers and GM's cylinder deactivation, whose lifters switch by oil pressure. P0523 means the signal voltage is above its limit: GM 2018 above 95 % of the 5 V reference, GM 2006 above 4.89 V, Ford petrol above 4.75 V, Ford diesel above 4.992 V, about 5 s. Typical are an open sensor ground or a signal shorted to 5 V or battery voltage. Real excess pressure is not reported here – Ford uses P055F for that. GM's 2006 V8s used the warning lamp only with cylinder deactivation.
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Oil pressure gauge at maximum
Cam phasing or cylinder deactivation possibly restricted

c: Oil level too low, oil loss or consumption
Too thin oil, fuel dilution or clogged pick-up screen
Oil pump or pressure control valve faulty or stuck
False setting by software in the cold (Ram EcoDiesel)
P0524.d: P0524 is not a sensor fault but a condition: the measured oil pressure is below a minimum depending on speed, load and temperature (Ford diesel 30–90 kPa) for about 5 s, with the sensor itself plausible. Its purpose is engine protection; Ford petrol engines with mid-lock cam phasers drive them into the locked position. GM's tables do not use it; FCA updated the Ram EcoDiesel software against false setting in the cold. Stop the engine, check the oil level and confirm with a mechanical gauge.
s: Oil pressure warning and/or check engine light
Engine noise (lifters, timing chain)
Possible power reduction

c: Servo worn or sticking, cable misadjusted
Vacuum leak at hose or diaphragm (vacuum servo)
Wiring, connector or fuse to the servo
Brake or clutch switch interrupting the servo release
P0525.d: P0525 concerns vehicles with a separate cruise control servo – a vacuum or electric actuator on the throttle cable driven by the engine module: the control circuit is electrically sound, but the response does not match the command. With electronic throttle the engine module controls the throttle itself, so the code hardly applies there. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0525. CARB names cruise control as the example of an emission-neutral diagnosis: switching it off as the default reaction suffices, so usually no warning lamp.
s: Cruise control inoperative or switches off
Speed not held or fluctuating
Usually no check engine light

c: Hall sensor at the fan clutch faulty
Wiring or connector (chafing at the shroud, corrosion)
P0526.d: Engine-driven fans with an electronically controlled viscous clutch (GM petrol SUVs and pick-ups 2004–2006, GM Duramax, Ford 6.7 L Power Stroke) have a Hall sensor reporting fan speed; the fan checks P0483, P0494 and P0495 need it. P0526 means no usable signal although the clutch is driven: GM Duramax below 500 rpm with fan duty at least 36 % for 2 s; the 6.6 L LML distinguishes a level stuck low or high; GM petrol V8s set it when no pulses arrive with the engine running. Type B, two trips. GM also reports a missing signal under P0526. A GM bulletin for 2011–2013 Duramax vans and pick-ups names loud fan noise and weak air conditioning at low speed.
s: Check engine light on
Fan permanently on or off, loud fan noise
Weak air conditioning at low speed, overheating under load

c: Sensor or trigger element damaged, wrong air gap
Interference or ground fault on the sensor line
Viscous clutch slipping or sticking (real speed off)
P0527.d: Engine-driven fans with an electronically controlled viscous clutch (GM petrol SUVs and pick-ups 2004–2006, GM Duramax, Ford 6.7 L Power Stroke) have a Hall sensor reporting fan speed; the fan checks P0483, P0494 and P0495 need it. P0527 means a signal is present but implausible – spikes, jumps or a speed that does not fit the clutch command and engine speed. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0527; GM covers implausibility through P0483 (target versus actual) and P0493. CARB requires input components used by other diagnoses to be checked for plausibility.
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Unsteady fan control
Fan permanently on

c: Fan or clutch really not turning
P0528.d: Engine-driven fans with an electronically controlled viscous clutch (GM petrol SUVs and pick-ups 2004–2006, GM Duramax, Ford 6.7 L Power Stroke) have a Hall sensor reporting fan speed; the fan checks P0483, P0494 and P0495 need it. P0528 means no pulses arrive from the sensor although the fan should be turning. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0528 – GM detects exactly this state (fan below 4 rpm with the engine running) but reports it as P0526. CARB requires input components to be checked for open and short circuits.
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Fan permanently on or not at all
Tendency to overheat

c: Loose contact at connector or wiring at the fan (vibration, chafing)
Sensor in the fan clutch intermittently faulty
P0529.d: Engine-driven fans with an electronically controlled viscous clutch (GM petrol SUVs and pick-ups 2004–2006, GM Duramax, Ford 6.7 L Power Stroke) have a Hall sensor reporting fan speed; the fan checks P0483, P0494 and P0495 need it. P0529 means the speed signal drops out or jumps at times. It is documented only for Ford's 6.7 L Power Stroke in the 2016–2019 Super Duty and F-650/750: a Ford service message lists it with P0480, P0494, P0495 and P0691–P0694 for fans running permanently or not at all, and warns against replacing the clutch too early – check wiring, connector and sensor first. Ford's summaries give no thresholds.
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Fan running permanently or not at all
Loud fan noise

c: Cam phaser sticking or lock pin not releasing
Low oil level, wrong viscosity or sludged oil
Oil control valve sticking or screen clogged
P052A.d: Some engines shift the intake (A) camshaft right after a cold start so that more exhaust heat reaches the catalyst; CARB requires each commanded element of this cold-start strategy to be monitored under its own codes. Documented only by Ford (from 2008): during the first 60 s it checks the cam position for 5 s and sets a code above 11° deviation, plus a stuck-pin test (10° commanded, under 2° movement) and an averaged deviation index. Warning lamp after two trips; afterwards the normal cam codes take over. P052A means bank 1 was too far advanced. Outside cold start, P0011 applies.
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable driving symptoms
Possibly rattle or rough idle on cold start
Higher cold-start emissions

c: Cam phaser sticking or lock pin not releasing (stuck in base position)
Low oil level, wrong viscosity or sludged oil
Oil control valve sticking or screen clogged
P052B.d: Some engines shift the intake (A) camshaft right after a cold start so that more exhaust heat reaches the catalyst; CARB requires each commanded element of this cold-start strategy to be monitored under its own codes. Documented only by Ford (from 2008): during the first 60 s it checks the cam position for 5 s and sets a code above 11° deviation, plus a stuck-pin test (10° commanded, under 2° movement) and an averaged deviation index. Warning lamp after two trips; afterwards the normal cam codes take over. P052B means bank 1 was too far retarded – typical for a phaser stuck in its locked base position.
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable driving symptoms
Possibly rattle or rough idle on cold start
Higher cold-start emissions

c: Cam phaser sticking or lock pin not releasing (bank 2)
Low oil level, wrong viscosity or sludged oil
Oil control valve sticking or screen clogged
P052C.d: Some engines shift the intake (A) camshaft right after a cold start so that more exhaust heat reaches the catalyst; CARB requires each commanded element of this cold-start strategy to be monitored under its own codes. Documented only by Ford (from 2008): during the first 60 s it checks the cam position for 5 s and sets a code above 11° deviation, plus a stuck-pin test (10° commanded, under 2° movement) and an averaged deviation index. Warning lamp after two trips; afterwards the normal cam codes take over. P052C means bank 2 of a V engine was too far advanced. Outside cold start, P0021 applies.
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable driving symptoms
Possibly rattle or rough idle on cold start
Higher cold-start emissions

c: Cam phaser sticking or lock pin not releasing (bank 2)
Low oil level, wrong viscosity or sludged oil
Oil control valve sticking or screen clogged
P052D.d: Some engines shift the intake (A) camshaft right after a cold start so that more exhaust heat reaches the catalyst; CARB requires each commanded element of this cold-start strategy to be monitored under its own codes. Documented only by Ford (from 2008): during the first 60 s it checks the cam position for 5 s and sets a code above 11° deviation, plus a stuck-pin test (10° commanded, under 2° movement) and an averaged deviation index. Warning lamp after two trips; afterwards the normal cam codes take over. P052D means bank 2 of a V engine was too far retarded. Outside cold start, P0022 applies.
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable driving symptoms
Possibly rattle or rough idle on cold start
Higher cold-start emissions

c: Diaphragm of the regulating valve torn or fatigued
Part-load ventilation valve blocked (oil carbon, sludge)
Elbow or hose at the valve cracked, clamp leaking
P052E.d: P052E is a function fault of the crankcase ventilation pressure regulating valve. Audi's 3.0 TFSI has a diaphragm valve whose torn diaphragm or elbow causes false air and whistling; Mercedes' M270/M274 have a switched part-load ventilation valve that blocks with oil carbon and lets oil into the intake – blue smoke, rough running, lack of power; Mercedes extended the emission warranty on the intake module. GM Europe's 2.0 diesel in the Saab 9-5 uses P052E differently, for PCV heater performance – which J2012 lists as P053D.
s: Check engine light on
Whistling or hissing in the engine bay
Rough idle, blue smoke or oil consumption, lack of power

c: Main feed to the module open or high-resistance (fuse, connector, corroded ring terminal)
Poor ground of the glow plug module
System voltage too low or too high (weak battery, regulator fault)
P052F.d: Diesel glow plugs are switched by a separate glow plug control module fed from the battery, with its own ground, a command from the engine module and a diagnostic line back. P052F means its supply voltage is out of range. Ford's 6.7 L and 3.0 L Power Stroke set it below 6.5 V, above 16.5 V or with an open supply, after about 1 s, continuously. An FCA bulletin shows P052F together with all six glow plug open codes P0671–P0676, because without supply no current flows – check main feed, connector and grounds first. GM does not use it.
s: Check engine light on
Hard cold start, long cranking, white smoke
Several glow plug codes at once

c: Connector or contacts corroded or loose
5 V reference shorted by another sensor
P0530.d: The engine module reads the high-side refrigerant pressure sensor (5 V reference, signal rising with pressure) to switch or regulate the compressor, raise the radiator fans at high pressure and pre-control the compressor load at idle. CARB therefore requires A/C components to be monitored where they alter fuel or ignition control or feed other diagnoses (from 2006–2008). P0530 is the general circuit fault; GM and the Saab 9-4X use the more precise P0532/P0533 instead. Saab's 2006 9-5 diesel (Bosch EDC16) assigns P0530 differently, to a short to ground below 0.1 V for 0.6 s, switching off the A/C relay. Warning lamp depends on the maker.
s: Air conditioning not cooling (compressor off)
Radiator fan running permanently
Check engine light (depending on the maker)

c: Refrigerant charge wrong (too little or too much)
Compressor or control valve delivering poorly
P0531.d: The engine module reads the high-side refrigerant pressure sensor (5 V reference, signal rising with pressure) to switch or regulate the compressor, raise the radiator fans at high pressure and pre-control the compressor load at idle. CARB therefore requires A/C components to be monitored where they alter fuel or ignition control or feed other diagnoses (from 2006–2008). P0531 means the signal is electrically valid but does not fit the expected pressure. GM compares the pressure rise after compressor engagement with a model of ambient and coolant temperature, road speed and fan speed, 100 samples of 100 ms, type X without warning lamp. Saab's 2006 9-5 diesel assigns P0531 differently, to a short to positive above 4.9 V with 101 kPa substitute value.
s: Weak or no cooling
Compressor cycling unusually
Usually no check engine light

c: Signal line open or shorted to ground
P0532.d: The engine module reads the high-side refrigerant pressure sensor (5 V reference, signal rising with pressure) to switch or regulate the compressor, raise the radiator fans at high pressure and pre-control the compressor load at idle. CARB therefore requires A/C components to be monitored where they alter fuel or ignition control or feed other diagnoses (from 2006–2008). P0532 means the signal voltage is too low – GM below 3 % of the 5 V reference in 80 of 100 samples (about 2 s), from a signal shorted to ground, an open signal line or a lost 5 V reference; an empty system at ambient pressure usually still reads in range. The compressor is locked out. Warning lamp: GM type C without, Saab 9-4X with, Ford depending on vehicle.
s: Air conditioning not cooling (compressor off)
Radiator fan running permanently
Check engine light (depending on the maker)

c: Signal line shorted to positive (e.g. 5 V reference)
Extreme overpressure (overcharge, blocked condenser, fan off)
P0533.d: The engine module reads the high-side refrigerant pressure sensor (5 V reference, signal rising with pressure) to switch or regulate the compressor, raise the radiator fans at high pressure and pre-control the compressor load at idle. CARB therefore requires A/C components to be monitored where they alter fuel or ignition control or feed other diagnoses (from 2006–2008). P0533 means the signal voltage is too high – GM above 98 % of the 5 V reference in 80 of 100 samples, from a signal shorted to positive or an open sensor ground. Real very high pressure normally leads to a pressure cut-out within range instead. The compressor is locked out. Warning lamp: GM type C without, Saab 9-4X with, Ford depending on vehicle.
s: Air conditioning not cooling (compressor off)
Radiator fan running permanently
Check engine light (depending on the maker)

c: Refrigerant leak (condenser, joints, compressor shaft seal, service ports)
Traction battery chiller faulty (electric and hybrid only)
P0534.d: P0534 reports too little refrigerant (a leak), not a sensor circuit: the module compares pressure or temperature in the circuit with a model, and the compressor is locked out for protection. FCA's 2020 Ram EcoDiesel sets it with the warning lamp; a software update fixed false setting. In GM's Volt, Spark EV and Lyriq the circuit also cools the traction battery – GM prescribes recovering and weighing the charge (Volt at least 800 of 950 g) and comparing the battery's refrigerant temperature sensors with ambient.
s: Air conditioning weak or not cooling
Compressor not engaging
Check engine light or high-voltage service message (electric)

P0535.d: The evaporator temperature sensor, an NTC thermistor behind the evaporator, prevents icing: near 0–3 °C the compressor is switched off or reduced. Usually the climate module reads it and reports body codes; P0535–P0539 only arise where the engine module controls the compressor and reads the sensor. P0535 is the general circuit fault; the compressor is usually locked out or run with a substitute value. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB's input component rules.
s: Air conditioning not or weakly cooling
Evaporator icing, airflow decreasing
Compressor cycling unusually

c: Sensor not seated correctly in the evaporator
P0536.d: The evaporator temperature sensor, an NTC thermistor behind the evaporator, prevents icing: near 0–3 °C the compressor is switched off or reduced. Usually the climate module reads it and reports body codes; P0535–P0539 only arise where the engine module controls the compressor and reads the sensor. P0536 means the signal is valid but implausible – for example it differs from other temperature sensors after standstill, or does not drop after compressor engagement. Hella compares it with the cabin sensor with A/C off. Icing protection then works wrongly. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB's input component rules.
s: Fluctuating or weak cooling
Evaporator icing
Compressor switching off too early

c: Condensate in the connector (leakage to ground)
P0537.d: The evaporator temperature sensor, an NTC thermistor behind the evaporator, prevents icing: near 0–3 °C the compressor is switched off or reduced. Usually the climate module reads it and reports body codes; P0535–P0539 only arise where the engine module controls the compressor and reads the sensor. P0537 means the signal voltage is below its limit; with the usual NTC voltage divider that is a signal shorted to ground or a shorted sensor, read as implausibly warm – icing protection may then fail. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB's input component rules.
s: Air conditioning not cooling
Possible icing
Compressor permanently on or locked out

c: Connector off or corroded, wire open
P0538.d: The evaporator temperature sensor, an NTC thermistor behind the evaporator, prevents icing: near 0–3 °C the compressor is switched off or reduced. Usually the climate module reads it and reports body codes; P0535–P0539 only arise where the engine module controls the compressor and reads the sensor. P0538 means the signal voltage is above its limit – an open sensor, signal or ground line, or a short to positive; with an NTC that reads as implausibly cold, so the system assumes icing and usually locks out the compressor. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB's input component rules.
s: Air conditioning not cooling (compressor locked out)
Vents blowing warm
Usually no check engine light

c: Loose contact or corrosion at the connector

No manufacturer document available to us uses P053E – Ford reports the same under P051B (above 5 inHg at idle air flow). Usually no noticeable driving symptoms

Ford watches the deviation with an averaged variance index for each direction; GM (Saab 9-4X V6) uses only the retard codes, above 6° for 1 s or 4 s cumulative, type B. P054E.d: Diesel only. At controlled idle the module compares the fuel quantity the idle governor needs for target speed with a model value; CARB sets the limit from 2013 at ±50 % of what a sound engine needs. Ford's diesel sets the codes beyond ±50 % for 5 s at standstill with warm engine and no filter regeneration; GM compares with 0.5 times a minimum map or 1.5 times a maximum map, 200 of 255 samples, type B. P0550.d: Hydraulic power steering has a pressure switch or sensor on the high-pressure line; when the wheel is turned at standstill, pump pressure and engine load rise sharply, so the engine module raises idle air in advance to stop the engine stalling. That makes it an input to idle control under CARB. Switches (Saab, Mitsubishi) ground a pull-up; analogue 5 V sensors (Toyota) give about 0.45 V at zero pressure. Without the signal the engine can drop or stall at full lock, or the module raises idle permanently as a substitute.

Unheated it opens late, for hot running at part load; the engine module heats it by map under full load or towing so it opens earlier. Often no noticeable symptoms

P05DB.d: Brake-by-wire and hybrid systems use a dual-channel pedal travel sensor; channel B runs opposite to A at Toyota (3.6–4.4 V at rest, falling when pressed), so a common fault of both channels shows up. It feeds brake assist and regenerative blending; CARB requires inputs used by other diagnoses to be monitored. A channel fault blocks the A/B correlation P05E0 and usually limits brake assist or regeneration. P05DB is the general circuit or open-circuit fault of channel B. Toyota's electronically controlled brake (RAV4 Hybrid 2024–25) reports channel B faults under it; while it is stored, the A/B correlation does not run.
s: Brake or regeneration warning light
Check engine light
Regeneration or brake assist reduced, pedal feel changed

P05E0.d: Brake-by-wire and hybrid systems measure brake pedal travel with a two-channel sensor; the channels often run in opposite directions (Toyota RAV4 hybrid 2024–25: one rises from about 1 V, the other falls from about 4 V). P05E0 means both channels are electrically fine but no longer match each other. Toyota sets it when the relationship is invalid for 0.2 s and lights the lamp at once; Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV adds the regenerative brake warning. Braking falls back to plain hydraulics, so the pedal may feel hard and regeneration is off. GM notes for the CT6, Bolt, Malibu and Volt 2016–18 that the code can also appear without a defect if the driver rests a foot lightly on the brake (1.8–5.6 mm travel) for 60 s while accelerating. Single-channel faults are P057A–P057E and P05DB–P05DF.

P05E1.d: The refrigerant pressure sensor (three wires, 5 V reference, signal rising with pressure) tells the engine module the A/C pressure; it uses it to switch the radiator fan, to block the compressor at too high or too low pressure and to pre-control idle load. CARB requires such inputs to be checked for circuit faults and plausibility, but they need not light the lamp if they do not affect emissions. 'Intermittent/Erratic' means the signal jumps implausibly fast or briefly leaves its valid range without staying low or high long enough for those codes. Sensor A is usually the high-pressure sensor; GM and Saab report it only as P0532/P0533 (circuit low/high, at GM below 3 % or above 98 % of 5 V) and P0531, so no manufacturer document available to us uses P05E1 itself. Typically the compressor is blocked and the fan runs. GM rates sensor A faults without the lamp, the Saab 9-4X with it.
s: A/C intermittently not cooling (compressor switched off)
Radiator fan runs unnecessarily or irregularly
Idle speed fluctuates when A/C engages
Warning lamp depending on the maker

c: Loose contact or corrosion at the sensor B connector
P05E2.d: The refrigerant pressure sensor (three wires, 5 V reference, signal rising with pressure) tells the engine module the A/C pressure; it uses it to switch the radiator fan, to block the compressor at too high or too low pressure and to pre-control idle load. CARB requires such inputs to be checked for circuit faults and plausibility, but they need not light the lamp if they do not affect emissions. 'Intermittent/Erratic' means the signal jumps implausibly fast or briefly leaves its valid range without staying low or high long enough for those codes. Sensor B is a second pressure sensor; which one depends on the maker – typically the low-pressure side or a second circuit in heat pump systems. Its other codes are P2515–P2518. No manufacturer document available to us uses P05E2, so this follows the sensor A family. Expect the A/C or heat pump to switch off intermittently.

P05E3.d: The engine module reads the park brake status, directly or via another module, because strategies depend on it: a parked diesel filter regeneration only runs with the park brake applied (Navistar), idle shutdown and PTO logic use it, and Ford delays an automatic restart while the electric park brake moves. CARB requires such inputs to be monitored. The only documented user of this code family is Volvo Trucks: since OBD 2021 a second park brake sensor (about 0.5 V applied, 3.5 V released) must agree with the old switch; the engine module reports the fault. No passenger car maker uses it verifiably. P05E3 is the general circuit fault – usually an open circuit or undefined state. Low and high signals are P05E4 and P05E5.

Park brake warning in the cluster

The only documented user of this code family is Volvo Trucks: since OBD 2021 a second park brake sensor (about 0.5 V applied, 3.5 V released) must agree with the old switch; the engine module reports the fault. No passenger car maker uses it verifiably. P05E6 is the one code of the family with a manufacturer description: at Volvo both signals must change together and agree; if they contradict each other or one changes late, the code sets. Volvo advises starting the diagnosis with the brake released.
s: Check engine light or OBD warning (heavy-duty)
Park brake warning in the cluster
Parked regeneration cannot be started
Stop-start or idle shutdown not working

c: Loose contact or corrosion at connector or splice
P05E7.d: The engine module reads the park brake status, directly or via another module, because strategies depend on it: a parked diesel filter regeneration only runs with the park brake applied (Navistar), idle shutdown and PTO logic use it, and Ford delays an automatic restart while the electric park brake moves. CARB requires such inputs to be monitored. The only documented user of this code family is Volvo Trucks: since OBD 2021 a second park brake sensor (about 0.5 V applied, 3.5 V released) must agree with the old switch; the engine module reports the fault. No passenger car maker uses it verifiably. P05E7 means the signal jumps briefly without being permanently low or high – changes without operation, while driving or too quickly in a row. The status is then discarded and regeneration or stop-start is blocked.

Running parked regeneration aborts
Stop-start occasionally blocked

c: Connector at the valve loose, corroded or spread
Output driver in the module faulty
P05E8.d: The engine oil bypass valve is an electrically switched solenoid that, according to patents (Hyundai/Kia), routes oil around the oil cooler when cold so the engine warms up faster with less friction, and through the cooler once the oil is hot. It is not the purely mechanical oil filter bypass. CARB requires output components to be checked for circuit faults. No manufacturer document available to us uses P05E8–P05EA, and no vehicle with these codes was found. If the circuit fails, the valve stays in its unpowered position – depending on design oil may run too hot under load or warm up slowly. P05E8 means the control circuit is open: the driver sees missing voltage or high resistance.
s: Check engine light (if rated as emission related)
Oil too hot under load or slow warm-up, depending on rest position
Usually no noticeable driving symptoms

c: Control wire chafing against ground (block, bracket)
Moisture or oil in the connector

It is not the purely mechanical oil filter bypass. CARB requires output components to be checked for circuit faults. c: Engine module software or calibration (false trigger)
Exhaust temperature sensor before the SCR reads low or slow
Heating measure not effective: throttle, EGR cooler bypass or turbo vanes sticking
Post or retarded injection not effective (injectors)
Exhaust leak before the sensor or extremely cold conditions
P05EB.d: After a cold start a diesel heats its exhaust actively – retarded and post injection, intake or exhaust throttling, higher idle, EGR cooler bypass – so the SCR catalyst quickly reaches the temperature at which urea dosing can start (around 180–200 °C). P05EB sets when the measured temperature at the SCR inlet stays below the expected or modelled value within a set time after the start: the heating strategy is not working. CARB requires this 'catalyst warm-up' monitor for light-duty diesels from model year 2026 (20 %) to 2028 (100 %); GM 2025 and Ford 2023 tables do not contain the code yet. Volvo Trucks used it on 2016–17 heavy-duty engines and advised a software check instead of replacing parts. The lamp comes on; no power limitation from this code alone is known.
s: Check engine light on
Usually no driving symptoms
Higher NOx emissions after cold start (not noticeable)

c: Engine module software or internal fault (request and execution differ)
Cold start mode blocked by other faults (coolant or fuel temperature, rail pressure)
P05EC.d: To heat the exhaust after a cold start, a diesel shifts its start of injection, usually later, plus post injections. CARB requires faults of such elements during the cold start strategy to be reported under codes separate from normal operation – hence P05EC. GM's 2025 diesels compare the start of injection requested by the application software with the timing actually scheduled for the injector drivers, during cold start only; a deviation beyond ±4 or ±5 in 88 of 176 or 8 of 16 samples sets the code and the lamp in the first trip. Ford's 2023 diesel instead checks whether the cold start operating mode is really activated when requested (10 s). Mechanical injector timing faults in normal operation are P01CB ff and P020A ff; the petrol counterpart for ignition timing is P050B.
s: Check engine light on
Usually no driving symptoms
Possibly more white smoke or rougher running after cold start

c: Main fuse or feed wire to the heater module faulty, connector corroded (splash zone)
Weak battery or charging fault (system voltage too low or too high)
P05ED.d: Some diesels use a separate control module or power stage for the DEF heaters in tank, pump and lines; without heating, frozen fluid cannot thaw in winter and dosing stays blocked. P05ED reports that this module's supply voltage is outside its allowed window – a blown main fuse, an open feed or ground, or system voltage too low or too high. Chrysler (FCA) lists this code among those that trigger the DEF inducement: a 'Service DEF System' warning, a countdown after 50 miles and no restart after 150 miles (P241D). Thresholds are not published; GM's L5P monitors the comparable heater supply under its own codes and flags a drop of more than 3 V below battery voltage while heating is requested. Start with fuse, feed, ground and battery or charging system.
s: Check engine light on
DEF/AdBlue warning, possibly countdown to no-restart
In cold weather: DEF frozen, dosing blocked, further heater codes

c: Connector at the pump or tank module corroded or loose
Open wire in the harness to the tank
Fuse or relay of the pump supply faulty
Pump or tank module open internally
P05EE.d: The electric supply pump in the diesel exhaust fluid (DEF, AdBlue) tank module builds the dosing pressure for the SCR catalyst. Its supply voltage is monitored separately from the pump control circuit (P208A ff); CARB requires SCR components and their outputs to be checked for circuit faults and function. P05EE means the supply circuit is open: when the supply is switched on, no voltage or current reaches the pump branch. Ford's comparable check flags a pump controller voltage below 6 V. Chrysler (FCA) lists this code among those that trigger the DEF inducement: a 'Service DEF System' warning, a countdown after 50 miles and no restart after 150 miles (P241D). Without supply the pump cannot build pressure, dosing stops and NOx rises; pressure or SCR efficiency codes may follow.
s: Check engine light on
DEF/AdBlue warning, possibly countdown to no-restart
Follow-up codes for low DEF pressure or SCR efficiency

c: Supply line shorted to ground (chafed against the frame)
High contact resistance or corrosion in the connector
Pump shorted internally or stiff (high current)
P05EF.d: The electric supply pump in the diesel exhaust fluid (DEF, AdBlue) tank module builds the dosing pressure for the SCR catalyst. Its supply voltage is monitored separately from the pump control circuit (P208A ff); CARB requires SCR components and their outputs to be checked for circuit faults and function. P05EF means the supply voltage is too low or the supply line is shorted to ground. GM's 6.6 L diesel monitors the same high-side driver under P1043 (short to ground with driver on, about 0.5 Ω, 3 s, first trip); Ford flags its pump controller voltage below 8.5 V. No manufacturer document available to us uses this exact code; GM and Ford monitor the same function under their own codes. Without supply the pump cannot build pressure, dosing stops and NOx rises; pressure or SCR efficiency codes may follow.
s: Check engine light on
DEF/AdBlue warning, possibly countdown to no-restart
Follow-up codes for low DEF pressure or SCR efficiency

c: Pump supply shorted to battery positive in the harness
Overvoltage from the charging system or a jump start
Moisture or corrosion causing leakage current in the connector
Relay or driver does not switch off
P05F0.d: The electric supply pump in the diesel exhaust fluid (DEF, AdBlue) tank module builds the dosing pressure for the SCR catalyst. Its supply voltage is monitored separately from the pump control circuit (P208A ff); CARB requires SCR components and their outputs to be checked for circuit faults and function. P05F0 means the supply voltage is too high, or voltage is present although the supply is switched off (short to battery). GM's 6.6 L diesel monitors this as P1044 (two trips); Ford flags pump voltage above 16 V or controller voltage above 19 V. No manufacturer document available to us uses this exact code; GM and Ford monitor the same function under their own codes. Without supply the pump cannot build pressure, dosing stops and NOx rises; pressure or SCR efficiency codes may follow.
s: Check engine light on
DEF/AdBlue warning, possibly countdown to no-restart
Follow-up codes for low DEF pressure or SCR efficiency

c: External voltage or short to positive in the harness
P05F1.d: The electric supply pump in the diesel exhaust fluid (DEF, AdBlue) tank module builds the dosing pressure for the SCR catalyst. Its supply voltage is monitored separately from the pump control circuit (P208A ff); CARB requires SCR components and their outputs to be checked for circuit faults and function. P05F1 means the pump supply stays on although the module switches it off – typically detected after the switch-off command, e.g. during after-run, when the feedback still shows voltage. A welded relay or a shorted semiconductor switch is the usual reason. Chrysler (FCA) lists this code among those that trigger the DEF inducement: a 'Service DEF System' warning, a countdown after 50 miles and no restart after 150 miles (P241D). Without supply the pump cannot build pressure, dosing stops and NOx rises; pressure or SCR efficiency codes may follow.
s: Check engine light on
DEF/AdBlue warning, possibly countdown to no-restart
Follow-up codes for low DEF pressure or SCR efficiency
Pump keeps running after switch-off, battery drains

c: Relay does not pull in or fuse blown
Open in the relay control or load circuit
Output driver in the engine module faulty
Electronics of the tank module faulty (no feedback)
P05F2.d: The electric supply pump in the diesel exhaust fluid (DEF, AdBlue) tank module builds the dosing pressure for the SCR catalyst. Its supply voltage is monitored separately from the pump control circuit (P208A ff); CARB requires SCR components and their outputs to be checked for circuit faults and function. P05F2 means the pump supply cannot be switched on: after the switch-on command no voltage or feedback appears at the pump branch, so no pressure builds up. Chrysler (FCA) lists this code among those that trigger the DEF inducement: a 'Service DEF System' warning, a countdown after 50 miles and no restart after 150 miles (P241D). Without supply the pump cannot build pressure, dosing stops and NOx rises; pressure or SCR efficiency codes may follow.
s: Check engine light on
DEF/AdBlue warning, possibly countdown to no-restart
Follow-up codes for low DEF pressure or SCR efficiency

c: Relay missing, coil open or not seated properly
Output driver in the engine module faulty
P05F3.d: A power relay, switched by the engine module through an output driver, feeds aftertreatment consumers such as the DEF pump, tank and line heaters and possibly NOx sensors or the SCR module. CARB requires such outputs to be checked for circuit faults and function. P05F3 means the driver detects an open relay control (coil) circuit. Ford's comparable relay check flags 'driver on but 0 V' or a heater relay current below 0.2 A, within 5 s. Chrysler (FCA) lists this code among those that trigger the DEF inducement: a 'Service DEF System' warning, a countdown after 50 miles and no restart after 150 miles (P241D). If the relay fails, heaters, pump and SCR control drop out and dosing stops.
s: Check engine light on
DEF/AdBlue warning, possibly countdown to no-restart
Follow-up codes for heaters, pump or NOx sensor supply

c: Output driver in the engine module faulty
P05F4.d: A power relay, switched by the engine module through an output driver, feeds aftertreatment consumers such as the DEF pump, tank and line heaters and possibly NOx sensors or the SCR module. CARB requires such outputs to be checked for circuit faults and function. P05F4 means the relay control circuit is shorted to ground or its voltage is too low. No manufacturer document available to us uses this exact code; GM and Ford monitor the same function under their own codes. Output driver in the engine module faulty

CARB requires such outputs to be checked for circuit faults and function. P05F5 means the relay control circuit is shorted to battery positive: the voltage stays high although the driver is off. No manufacturer document available to us uses this exact code; GM and Ford monitor the same function under their own codes. c: External voltage on the load side (short to positive)
Output driver in the engine module faulty
P05F6.d: A power relay, switched by the engine module through an output driver, feeds aftertreatment consumers such as the DEF pump, tank and line heaters and possibly NOx sensors or the SCR module. CARB requires such outputs to be checked for circuit faults and function. P05F6 is a function check on the load side: the relay stays closed although it is switched off, so the consumers keep their supply, e.g. during after-run. A patent by Delphi describes this kind of check via the voltage at the heater node. No manufacturer document available to us uses this exact code; GM and Ford monitor the same function under their own codes. If the relay fails, heaters, pump and SCR control drop out and dosing stops.

DEF/AdBlue warning, possibly countdown to no-restart
Follow-up codes for heaters, pump or NOx sensor supply

c: Relay contacts burnt or coil faulty, relay does not close
Fuse on the load side blown
Output driver in the engine module faulty
P05F7.d: A power relay, switched by the engine module through an output driver, feeds aftertreatment consumers such as the DEF pump, tank and line heaters and possibly NOx sensors or the SCR module. CARB requires such outputs to be checked for circuit faults and function. P05F7 is the opposite function check: the relay does not close although it is commanded on, so the load side stays without voltage. No manufacturer document available to us uses this exact code; GM and Ford monitor the same function under their own codes. If the relay fails, heaters, pump and SCR control drop out and dosing stops.

DEF/AdBlue warning, possibly countdown to no-restart

c: Engine module software (Chrysler 3.0 L 2014: diagnostic revised by reflash)
Heater element or line in tank or hose with abnormal current
P05F8.d: P05F8 is the function check of the DEF heater control module: its feedback does not match the command – heating current or power, temperature rise, or an internal module fault. The code is documented for Chrysler's 3.0 L EcoDiesel in the 2014 Ram 1500 and Jeep Grand Cherokee: several bulletins list it together with the heater codes P20BA, P20BE and P20C2, and the fix in each case was only reprogramming the engine module – a diagnostic that was too sensitive rather than a hardware defect. It is not on Chrysler's inducement list. Ford checks the same function under heater plausibility codes. Thresholds for P05F8 are not published. If it returns after a software update, check the heater elements in tank and lines and the module supply (P05ED).
s: Check engine light on
Usually no driveability issue
DEF warning in cold weather, possible heater codes P20BA/P20BE/P20C2

c: Open status line or connector problem
Sending module without supply or faulty
Wrong software or variant coding (stop-start set without hardware)
P05F9.d: A discrete stop-start status line tells the engine module (or another module) whether stop-start is active, inhibited or has just stopped the engine. On most current cars this status travels over CAN instead, so a hard-wired line and these codes are rare; no manufacturer document available to us uses P05F9–P05FB. CARB names stop-start as its example of an 'emissions neutral' reaction: a module that simply disables stop-start when a fault appears may report it without the check engine light, which is what Ford does for its stop-start codes. P05F9 is the general circuit fault or open line. The typical reaction is that stop-start is disabled; the driver-operated stop-start switch has its own codes.
s: Stop-start does not work
Stop-start indicator or message in the cluster
Check engine light only with some makers

c: Sending module pulls the line to ground permanently (faulty output)
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
P05FA.d: A discrete stop-start status line tells the engine module (or another module) whether stop-start is active, inhibited or has just stopped the engine. On most current cars this status travels over CAN instead, so a hard-wired line and these codes are rare; no manufacturer document available to us uses P05F9–P05FB. CARB names stop-start as its example of an 'emissions neutral' reaction: a module that simply disables stop-start when a fault appears may report it without the check engine light, which is what Ford does for its stop-start codes. P05FA means the status line stays below its lower limit – a short to ground or a missing pull-up supply. Stop-start is then disabled.
s: Stop-start does not work
Stop-start indicator or message in the cluster

c: Open status line or connector off
Sending module faulty or without ground
P05FB.d: A discrete stop-start status line tells the engine module (or another module) whether stop-start is active, inhibited or has just stopped the engine. On most current cars this status travels over CAN instead, so a hard-wired line and these codes are rare; no manufacturer document available to us uses P05F9–P05FB. CARB names stop-start as its example of an 'emissions neutral' reaction: a module that simply disables stop-start when a fault appears may report it without the check engine light, which is what Ford does for its stop-start codes. P05FB means the status line stays above its upper limit – an open line pulled up or a short to voltage. Stop-start is then disabled.
s: Stop-start does not work
Stop-start indicator or message in the cluster

c: High-pressure pump or volume control valve of bank 2 weak or sticking
Rail pressure sensor of bank 2 inaccurate
Leaking injector or pressure relief on bank 2
P05FC.d: During a cold start, direct injection petrol engines usually raise rail pressure for finer atomisation with multiple injections while the catalyst heats up. P05FC monitors whether the actual rail pressure of bank 2 stays within the target window during this phase – only engines with separate rails and pressure sensors per bank (V or boxer engines with two high-pressure circuits) can set it. CARB lists fuel pressure as a cold start component that must respond measurably beyond what would happen without the strategy. No manufacturer document available to us uses P05FC; Ford checks the single-rail counterpart P053F and flags a fault when the share of cold start time inside the pressure window is 0.70 or less, and Kia replaced the engine module of the 2018 Stinger 2.0T for P053F with stumbling during warm-up. GM uses P2C1E–P2C20 instead.
s: Check engine light on
Stumbling, hesitation or rough idle during warm-up
Poorer cold start
Usually normal once warm

c: Vane mechanism sooted or stiff, actuator works constantly against resistance
Electric actuator faulty internally (shorted turns, bearing)
High ambient heat at the actuator (missing heat shield, exhaust leak)
P05FD.d: Electric variable-geometry turbo actuators use a DC motor with gearing, driven by an H-bridge in the engine module or in the actuator itself. Constant high load – sooted or stiff vanes, running against a stop, an internal motor short – drives up current and temperature. GM's 2025 diesels set P05FD when the H-bridge driver exceeds 170 °C in 240 of 300 samples (about 3 s) and light the lamp in the first trip. The driver then shuts off for protection, the actuator stops or returns to its rest position, and boost control is limited – underboost or overboost and reduced power can follow. GM Europe's earlier 2.0 diesels reported the same protection under P0046. Circuit faults of the actuator are P0045–P0048, the position sensor P2563 ff.
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power or limp mode
Possibly underboost or overboost codes (P0299/P0234)
More smoke under load

c: Debris or ice blocking the louvres
P05FE.d: Active grille shutters close the air inlet when little cooling is needed, to reduce drag and speed up warm-up. P05FE is the performance check of a third shutter C – target and actual position do not match, as P059F does for shutter A and P05AE for shutter B. Only vehicles with three separately driven shutters could set it, and no manufacturer was found that uses a shutter C: GM and Ford use only A (upper) and B (lower). This description therefore follows A and B: control is suspended and the shutter stays where it is or opens; if it sticks closed, cooling air is missing under load. GM and Ford light the lamp for A and B after two trips. Ice and debris are frequent causes, and GM fixed false A/B codes in snow by software on the 2025 Equinox. Stuck on is P2C73.
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Higher coolant temperature under load or slower warm-up
Slightly higher fuel consumption
Often no noticeable symptoms

c: Brake pedal position sensor or switch misadjusted or faulty
Master cylinder pressure sensor in the ABS unit faulty
Network communication or software between ABS module and engine module
Air in the brake system or hydraulic fault (long pedal travel without pressure)
P05FF.d: Stop-start decides when to stop and restart the engine from the brake: Ford stops it when the pedal switch is on and master cylinder pressure is high enough, and restarts when pressure falls below a filtered reference. P05FF means brake pressure (from the sensor in the ABS unit, sent over the network) and brake pedal position do not agree – for example pedal pressed without pressure build-up, or pressure without pedal. Ford's 2020–23 petrol vehicles check this continuously in the section 'Brake Diagnostics for Stop-Start Dependability' and set the code within 1 s, without the check engine light; stop-start is blocked so the engine is not stopped or started unexpectedly. Ford gives no threshold for the deviation. GM monitors the pedal travel sensor under P057x instead. Brake switch disagreement is P0504.
s: Stop-start disabled
No check engine light at Ford, possibly wrench or service warning
Possible related codes P0504 or brake pressure codes

c: Internal module fault in the processor-to-processor link
Open or short in a dedicated serial line between engine and transmission module (e.g. Subaru)
Low voltage, voltage dips or a poor ground or supply at the module
Fault in the transmission module at the other end of the line
P0600.d: P0600 means a serial data link that the module relies on has failed. At Ford it is the internal link between the main processor and the monitoring processor ('quizzer') of the electronic throttle safety concept: if data cannot be exchanged or check bytes are invalid, the code sets within about a second (diesel: 5 s), usually with the check engine and wrench lamps and a throttle failure mode such as an RPM limit. Subaru (also sold as Saab 9-2X) uses it for the dedicated serial line between engine and transmission module. GM does not use P0600. Lost CAN messages from a named module are reported separately as U0100 and following. Before replacing anything: check battery, grounds and supply, look for a software bulletin, reprogram with a stable power supply, and replace the module only if the code returns.
s: Check engine light, at Ford also the wrench lamp
Reduced power or RPM limit (throttle failure mode)
Harsh shifts or transmission limp mode where the line links engine and gearbox
Other monitors such as the catalyst monitor do not run

c: Defective flash memory in the module
Low voltage, voltage dips or a poor ground or supply at the module
P0601.d: The module continuously calculates a checksum over its program and calibration memory (flash) and compares it with the stored value; on newer units the flash error correction also reports bit errors it cannot repair. A mismatch means the stored software is corrupted. GM sets P0601 in the engine module after one failed pass (or five once the first pass is complete) and turns on the lamp in the first trip; in body modules after two trips. Ford reports the same check as P0605, while GM, VW and Mazda use P0601. Typical causes are an interrupted reflash and manufacturer software errors – VW (2.0 TFSI) and Mazda (MX-5 2013) fixed it by reprogramming. The code alone does not say which module set it – the scan tool shows whether it is the engine, transmission, brake or body module.
s: Check engine light on
Often no change in driving
Possibly no start or limp mode if the software is badly damaged
Transmission limp mode if the transmission module is affected

c: Programming interrupted by a voltage dip or lost connection
Wrong or incompatible software, calibration or configuration block
Internal memory defect in the module
P0602.d: P0602 reports that the module is not, or not completely, programmed for this vehicle. GM checks at power-up and then every second whether a service replacement module still carries no calibration, and sets the code in the first trip; in brake modules a missing calibration set or a sensor ID that does not match also counts. Ford uses P0602 when the checksum of the vehicle identification block (tyre size, axle ratio, VIN) is wrong. Typical triggers are a new module that was never programmed, a reflash interrupted by a voltage dip or lost connection, or wrong software. Depending on the maker the engine may not start, run with reduced power or only show the lamp; GM Europe engines show a service lamp instead of the check engine light. The fix is almost always reprogramming with a stable power supply; replace the module only if the code returns.
s: Check engine light or service lamp
Engine may not start or runs in limp mode
Reduced engine power
Appears right after a module replacement or software update

c: Battery disconnected, deeply discharged or replaced
Interrupted constant power feed to the module (fuse, wire, corrosion)
Main relay drops out too early, memory not saved completely at shutdown
P0603.d: Keep alive memory holds learned values – fuel trim, idle and shift adaptation, readiness status – while the engine is off, as long as the module has constant battery power; CARB defines it as memory that is lost when the battery or fuse is disconnected. The module stores a checksum of this memory at shutdown and compares it at the next start (Ford, GM Europe); GM calls the check 'long term memory reset', and the Ford diesel watches the supply of its engine-off timer chip (below 0.25 V). By far the most common trigger is outside the module: a disconnected, flat or replaced battery or an interrupted constant feed – Nissan bulletins name exactly this and ask for at least 11 V before clearing. Learned values then start from default and the readiness monitors are reset. Whether the lamp comes on depends on the maker.
s: Check engine light on (depending on the maker)
Rough idle or changed shifting until values are relearned
Readiness monitors reset
Often right after battery work

c: Internal hardware defect of the module (RAM)
Low voltage, voltage dips or a poor ground or supply at the module
Moisture or corrosion in the module or at its connector
P0604.d: P0604 means the module's working memory (RAM) failed its self-test: a value written to a cell does not read back correctly, a built-in hardware test fails, error correction reports faults, or protected memory is written without permission. GM's engine module scans the whole RAM within 30 s of start-up and then keeps checking in the background, setting the code after repeated failures with the lamp in the first trip; Ford tests RAM during initialisation, the GM gateway with error correction at start (two trips). Unlike most memory codes, P0604 is used the same way by GM, Ford, Chrysler and Saab. Consequences depend on the module: a transmission module goes into limp mode with maximum line pressure and a fixed gear, an engine module may reduce power. The code alone does not say which module set it – the scan tool shows whether it is the engine, transmission, brake or body module.
s: Check engine light on
Limp mode or transmission limp mode
Intermittent stalling or starting problems
Several module codes at the same time

c: Program memory corrupted by an interrupted reflash
Low voltage, voltage dips or a poor ground or supply at the module
P0605.d: P0605 reports an error in the module's program memory (ROM, today flash), found by a checksum or error-correction check at start-up or in the background. Ford is the main user: its engine and transmission modules compare a ROM checksum and set P0605 with the check engine light; the diesel transmission module tests once per trip at start. GM's engine module does not use P0605 and reports the same fault as P0601; the GM gateway (2025) uses it for uncorrectable ROM bit errors with two-trip logic, and GM Europe's 1.6 L engine even assigns it to processor faults of the throttle control. Which of P0601 and P0605 appears is therefore the manufacturer's choice. The usual repair is reprogramming, which restores the memory contents; replace the module only if the code returns.
s: Check engine light on
Possibly starting problems
Transmission limp mode if the transmission module is affected
Reduced power (GM Europe assignment)

c: Low voltage, voltage dips or a poor ground or supply at the module
Internal hardware defect (processor, voltage regulator, output stage chip)
Short on a 5 V sensor reference loading the internal supply
P0606.d: P0606 means the module doubts the integrity of its own processor. Checks include a question-and-answer game between main and monitoring processor (GM: new seed via SPI within 450 ms; Ford: 'quizzer' level 3), arithmetic unit and register tests, stack overflow, the order in which safety-critical software runs, and the internal voltage supply (Ford diesel: 5 V rail outside 4.7–5.3 V). Because it belongs to the electronic throttle safety concept, the module usually reacts with a failure mode – reduced power, RPM limit or throttle default position – and the lamp in the first trip. Many cases are software issues fixed by reprogramming (Chrysler 3.6 L 2014, VW Routan, GM brake module 2024), so check bulletins before replacing hardware. The code alone does not say which module set it – the scan tool shows whether it is the engine, transmission, brake or body module.
s: Check engine light, at Ford also the wrench lamp
Limp mode with reduced power or RPM limit
Poor throttle response
Rarely stalling or no start
Often together with voltage codes P0562/P0563

c: Internal module defect (processor, clock, monitoring chip)
Low voltage, voltage dips or a poor ground or supply at the module
Electrical interference, e.g. from a faulty alternator or ignition
P0607.d: P0607 is the general 'module not working correctly' code, used when no specific memory or processor part is named. Ford sets it for wrong instruction execution or too many processor resets in engine and transmission modules; the Ford diesel after five communication errors with its monitoring chip within 20 s (a complete loss of that link is P0600). GM introduced it in the engine module only recently: the 2025 tables evaluate the results of built-in self-tests and error-correction counters, with the lamp in the first trip. Resets can cause brief stumbling or stalling, and some systems switch to limp mode. Software updates fixed it on the Alfa Romeo Giulia 2.9 V6 and Ram 6.7 Cummins, so check bulletins first. The code alone does not say which module set it – the scan tool shows whether it is the engine, transmission, brake or body module.
s: Check engine light on
Limp mode or reduced power
Brief stumbling or stalling (module reset)
Several implausible codes at once

c: Short or open in the output line A to the receiving module
Corroded or spread connector pins at the module or receiver
Faulty receiving module pulling the line to ground
Internal driver fault in the module
P0608.d: Many engine or powertrain modules turn the raw wheel or output-shaft speed into a cleaned-up vehicle speed signal and pass it on through their own driver – a square-wave signal whose frequency rises with speed – to the instrument cluster, cruise control, radio or steering. P0608 concerns output A: the module compares the commanded driver state with the actual line state and reports a short to ground or voltage, an open circuit or an internal driver fault, as CARB requires for output components. Output A is the first such output, usually the speedometer feed. If the speed sensor itself fails, P0500–P0503 set instead. No manufacturer table available to us gives thresholds; GM lists the code in older vehicles. On modern cars speed is shared over CAN, so the code mainly affects older vehicles with a hard-wired speedometer signal.
s: Speedometer dead or jumping
Cruise control not working
Odometer stops counting
Speed-dependent functions (steering, radio volume) disturbed

c: Short or open in the output line B to the receiving module
Corroded or spread connector pins at the module or receiver
Faulty receiving module pulling the line to ground
Internal driver fault in the module
P0609.d: Many engine or powertrain modules turn the raw wheel or output-shaft speed into a cleaned-up vehicle speed signal and pass it on through their own driver – a square-wave signal whose frequency rises with speed – to the instrument cluster, cruise control, radio or steering. P0609 concerns output B: the module compares the commanded driver state with the actual line state and reports a short to ground or voltage, an open circuit or an internal driver fault, as CARB requires for output components. Output B is a second output; which device hangs on it (cruise module, radio, body builder interface) depends on the wiring diagram. If the speed sensor itself fails, P0500–P0503 set instead. No manufacturer table available to us gives thresholds; GM lists the code in older vehicles. On modern cars speed is shared over CAN, so the code mainly affects older vehicles with a hard-wired speedometer signal.
s: Speed-dependent function of the receiver on output B disturbed
Cruise control or add-on device without speed signal
Often no noticeable driving symptom

c: Unstable supply voltage or poor ground at the module (weak battery, voltage spikes)
Moisture or corrosion in the module or connector
P060A.d: Electronic throttle systems use three levels: level 1 runs the engine, level 2 recalculates key values independently on the same processor, and level 3 is a separate monitoring processor that quizzes the main one and can shut down the throttle outputs. P060A means this monitoring processor (level 3) or its cooperation with the main processor is faulty: the question-and-answer game fails, an operating system call ends with an unrecoverable error, or the self-test of the monitoring module fails (Ford diesel: 5 s). Ford sets it with the check engine and wrench lamps since generation 3 throttle systems (older generation 2 without the check engine light); GM Europe's 1.6 L turbo rates it type C with a service lamp and reduced power. GM North America does not use P060A. Nissan (Rogue 2021) and Ford (Explorer 2.3 2025) fixed it by reprogramming – often there are no driving symptoms at all.
s: Check engine light, at Ford also the wrench lamp
Reduced power or limp mode
Often no driving symptoms
Rarely stalling or starting problems

c: Unstable supply voltage or poor ground at the module (weak battery, voltage spikes)
Internal defect of the converter or its chip
Shorted sensor input pulling the converter reference
P060B.d: The analog-to-digital converter turns every analog sensor voltage into a number, so a faulty converter can falsify many values at once. The module checks it by timing its start-up calibration (GM 6.6 L diesel: 0.30 s or longer is a fault), by converting fixed internal reference voltages (about 4.73–4.83 V must be read), by grounding a test channel that must then read near 0 V (Ford diesel: over 249 mV is a fault) and by comparing with a second converter. GM sets it in the first trip, Ford with the check engine and wrench lamps as a level 3 check; the module usually enters limp mode. Ford fixed an F-150 2.7 L case (with misfire codes) by reprogramming. GM also uses P060B in the brake module – then ABS warnings appear and the engine module is not the culprit. The old wording 'A and D' simply spelled out 'A/D'.
s: Check engine light, at Ford also the wrench lamp
Reduced power or limp mode
Several sensor or misfire codes at the same time
ABS/ESC warning if the brake module set the code

c: Unstable supply voltage or poor ground at the module (weak battery, voltage spikes)
Overheating or moisture in the module
P060C.d: P060C reports a fault in the main processor that actually runs the engine, found either by the monitoring processor (Ford 'quizzer', level 3) or by duplicate storage and recalculation (GM). Typical findings are corrupted RAM or ROM data, arithmetic unit errors, memory address violations, a wrong program sequence or internal supply or temperature out of range (Ford diesel: internal voltage outside 1.3–3.3 V, 5 s). GM's 2025 petrol table flags a torque compensation outside ±52.9 Nm for 475 ms and sets the code in the first trip. Reactions range from reduced power to engine shutdown. Software is the most common cause: GM (2022 full-size trucks and SUVs), VW (Tiguan 2021, with cruise control faults), Nissan and Mercedes (transmission module, E-Class hybrid) fixed it by reprogramming.
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power or limp mode
Driver assistance such as adaptive cruise unavailable
Rarely stalling or no start
Transmission limp mode if the transmission module is affected

c: Short between the two pedal sensor signal lines or moisture in the pedal connector
P060D.d: The accelerator pedal has two sensor tracks. With P060D the module's own cross-check of the pedal value fails: two processors (GM: main and 'motor' processor) calculate pedal position independently and must agree, and an active test briefly pulls one track to ground – the other must not follow, otherwise the tracks are shorted together. Thresholds: GM 2005 difference over 0.142 V or track 2 over 2.05 V during the test; GM 2006 over 5 %; Ford diesel compares track 1 against twice track 2 (half slope), fault above 547 or 1055 mV for 5 s. GM sets it in the first trip, Ford since 2020 with the check engine and wrench lamps (2012 only the wrench lamp). Unlike P2138, where the two pedal tracks disagree outside the module, P060D is the internal plausibility check.
s: Reduced power, engine barely responds to the pedal
Check engine light or wrench lamp
Cruise control disabled
Raised idle or limp mode

c: Short between the throttle sensor signal lines or moisture in the throttle connector
Internal module fault (test circuit, second processor)
P060E.d: P060E is the throttle counterpart of P060D. The throttle body also has two position sensor tracks, and the module checks whether it can still detect a short between them: during an active test one track is influenced briefly, and the second processor (GM 'motor processor') confirms that the test actually ran. GM 2005 sets the code when track 2 exceeds 1.75 V during the test or no test activity is seen for 500 ms, GM 2006 at 2.05 V or 498 ms, each after two counts of about 155 ms, with the lamp in the first trip; GM Europe rates it type C with reduced power. Ford does not use P060E. The throttle opening is limited or set to its default position. External disagreement between the two tracks is P2135; circuit faults of single tracks are P0120–P0123 and P0220–P0223.
s: Reduced power
Check engine light (GM) or service lamp (GM Europe)
Hesitant or jerky throttle response
Cruise control not working

c: Internal module fault in a converter or processor path
Loose contact at the coolant temperature sensor that jumps between samples
Unstable supply voltage or poor ground at the module (weak battery, voltage spikes)
P060F.d: Coolant temperature feeds the torque model of the engine (friction, cold start), which the level 2 monitoring of the electronic throttle concept recalculates.
