P0657 is the open-circuit code; it is documented at Ford: the high-side switch of the 5R110W and 6R80 automatics feeds all shift solenoids, and the 2023 diesels split them into two supplies (P0657 and P2669), checked continuously. On a fault the solenoids are de-energised and the transmission falls back to a mechanical limp gear with maximum line pressure – harsh shifts and a single forward gear. Ford's 6.8 L V10 reports it with or without the lamp depending on the variant. GM does not use P0657 and reports opens together with ground faults under P0658.
s: Transmission limp mode (fixed gear)
Harsh shifts, no upshift
Check engine light (depending on the variant)
Codes for individual shift solenoids

c: Actuator supply wire shorted to ground
Transmission harness or connector (also open, in transmission modules)
Module internal (main cause on the Saab diesel)
P0658.d: Actuator supply A is a high-side switch feeding several actuators together; its use differs by maker (Ford transmission solenoids, GM shared high-side driver, GM Europe 2.0 CDTI internal 5 V supply). P0658 means the supply output is too low with the driver on – a short to ground (0.5 Ω or less). GM's engine module checks its shared high-side driver in 20 of 25 samples; the lamp rating changed from none (2016) via two trips (2017–18) to the first trip (2025). GM's transmission modules include an open circuit here, set it in the first trip and block the solenoid diagnostics, so the gearbox goes into limp mode. On GM Europe's 2.0 CDTI it means the internal 5 V supply is too low – no MIL, and if it recurs, the engine module is replaced.
s: Transmission limp mode or fixed gear
Several actuators not working
Check engine light (GM from 2017)
Codes for individual solenoids

c: Actuator supply wire shorted to battery or ignition voltage
Harness chafed against a 12 V line
Module (driver shorted; internal on the Saab diesel)
External voltage fed back through a faulty actuator
P0659.d: Actuator supply A is a high-side switch feeding several actuators together; its use differs by maker (Ford transmission solenoids, GM shared high-side driver, GM Europe 2.0 CDTI internal 5 V supply). P0659 means a short to voltage on the supply output, checked with the driver off – the output should then be dead (GM: 0.5 Ω or less to the supply, 20 of 25 samples; lamp after two trips in 2017–18, none in 2016). The driver can then no longer switch the actuators off; GM's transmission modules block their solenoid diagnostics while P0658/P0659 are active, and limp mode follows. On GM Europe's 2.0 CDTI it means the internal 5 V supply is too high, without MIL – the engine module is replaced.
s: Check engine light (GM from 2017)
Transmission or actuator limp mode
Actuators cannot be switched off
Follow-up codes

c: Electrical fault in another module (lighting, wipers, blower) disabling smart charging
Loose or corroded B+ or high-current connection
P065A.d: Demand-controlled (smart) charging lets the module vary alternator voltage; the charging system is not an emission component, so these codes usually come without the check engine light. P065A is the function check of the whole charging strategy. Chrysler (Stellantis) explains it as a non-MIL code: the engine module switches off demand-controlled charging and falls back to normal charging because of electrical faults in other modules – returned alternators replaced for P065A were found to be fine. Other Stellantis cases trace it, together with P2503/P2504, to loose B+ or high-current connections, and the Ram 1500 3.0 EcoDiesel Gen 3 received a software update. The result is a constant charging voltage instead of smart charging, possibly with a battery lamp; there is no power limitation. Check codes in other modules and the main battery connections before replacing the alternator.
s: Battery warning lamp (in some cases)
Fluctuating charging voltage reading
No check engine light (Chrysler)
Fault codes in other modules

c: LIN or control wire between alternator and module (connector, corrosion, open)
Weak battery, jump start or external charging
P065B.d: Demand-controlled (smart) charging lets the module vary alternator voltage; the charging system is not an emission component, so these codes usually come without the check engine light. P065B is the plausibility check of the control channel to the alternator regulator (LIN or a dedicated smart-charge line): command and feedback do not match, or the signal is out of range (too low or too high). A manufacturer table published via NHTSA for a gateway with LIN alternator shows the battery lamp and disabled stop-start, notes that jump starting or charging can set it briefly, and says to check P065C (belt) first; Ford's 6.8 L V10 reports it with or without the lamp depending on the variant. The regulator then falls back to a default target voltage. Circuit faults are P0620; L and F lines are P0621/P0622.
s: Battery warning lamp on
Stop-start not working
Battery drains
Usually no check engine light

P065C.d: Demand-controlled (smart) charging lets the module vary alternator voltage; the charging system is not an emission component, so these codes usually come without the check engine light. P065C points to the alternator's mechanical drive: the alternator does not deliver as commanded or its feedback does not match engine speed, typically because the belt slips. The only manufacturer document found – a table for a gateway with LIN alternator published via NHTSA – shows the battery lamp and disabled stop-start and names checking and adjusting the drive belt tension as the fix, to be checked before P065B. Thresholds are not published. Belt wear or oil contamination, a weak tensioner, a faulty overrunning pulley or a stiff alternator bearing are the obvious mechanical causes. Hybrid starter-generators use other codes.
s: Battery warning lamp
Stop-start disabled
Belt squeal
Low battery voltage

c: Wire or connector between module and receiver open, corroded or shorted
Driver in the engine or SCR module faulty
P065D.d: The engine module switches this hard-wired output with its own driver and checks the circuit electrically (open, short to ground or voltage) – it cannot see whether the lamp lights; on CAN-based cars such faults appear as U codes. On SCR diesels a separate lamp or symbol warns of low DEF/AdBlue level, poor quality or system faults and announces speed or start restrictions (inducement). P065D reports a fault in the control circuit of this lamp. CARB requires inputs and outputs of the inducement strategy to be monitored on diesels from model years 2019–2021, and US federal rules define the inducement stages; Detroit Diesel, for example, shows the symbol below 1/8 tank and flashes it with a speed limit when empty. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB and the component. Without the lamp the driver may run into an inducement stage without warning; the code itself is not known to trigger one.
s: AdBlue warning lamp does not light at ignition on, or stays on
No early warning of low AdBlue (risk of speed limit or no-restart without notice)
Check engine light possible (depending on the maker)

c: Valve shaft or linkage stiff or sooted (oil mist from crankcase ventilation or EGR)

P0666.d: Control modules measure their own circuit board temperature with an internal sensor to protect output stages (overtemperature is P0634) and, in GM transmission modules, as a substitute for fluid temperature. In GM's 6T70/6T75 and related automatics the sensor sits in the transmission module inside the valve body, with no external wiring – so the repair is practically always the module or valve body assembly. P066A.d: Modern diesel glow systems switch each glow plug through its own power semiconductor (in a glow plug module or the engine module), so current and faults can be measured per plug; a faulty channel is switched off. CARB requires glow plugs to be checked for correct current and voltage drop and, since model year 2010, a single plug outside specification to be detected and named. P066A means the circuit to the cylinder 1 glow plug is shorted to ground or draws overcurrent. GM's engine-module drivers flag a circuit impedance to ground below 0.11 Ω (10 of 20 samples at 100 ms) with the check engine and glow plug lamps after two trips; Ford's 2023 Power Stroke checks during heating for more than 22 A for 0.3 s or 20–22 A for 2 s. The channel is switched off, so plug 1 no longer heats – harder cold starts and white smoke follow. A plug shorted internally is the usual cause; a wrong plug type is another.
s: Check engine and glow plug lamp

Rough running and white smoke right after a cold start
Possibly blown glow system fuse

Wrong plug type (resistance or voltage rating)
Driver in the glow or engine module faulty, or software (GM bulletins)
P067A.d: Modern diesel glow systems switch each glow plug through its own power semiconductor (in a glow plug module or the engine module), so current and faults can be measured per plug; a faulty channel is switched off. CARB requires glow plugs to be checked for correct current and voltage drop and, since model year 2010, a single plug outside specification to be detected and named. P067A means the circuit to the cylinder 4 glow plug is shorted to ground or draws overcurrent. GM's engine-module drivers flag an impedance to ground below 0.11 Ω (10 of 20 samples) with the check engine and glow plug lamps after two trips; Ford's 2023 Power Stroke checks during heating for more than 22 A for 0.3 s or 20–22 A for 2 s. The channel is switched off and plug 4 no longer heats – harder cold starts and white smoke follow.
s: Check engine and glow plug lamp
Harder cold start, especially in frost
Rough running and white smoke right after a cold start

c: Cylinder 4 plug wire touching battery positive (chafing in the harness)

P067B.d: Modern diesel glow systems switch each glow plug through its own power semiconductor (in a glow plug module or the engine module), so current and faults can be measured per plug; a faulty channel is switched off. A permanently powered plug can overheat and burn through.

c: Communication or feedback wire between glow and engine module open, chafed or connector corroded
Glow module without supply or ground (fuse, main cable) – does not answer

P0683.d: Glow plug module 1 reports to the engine module over a feedback wire (Bosch-type systems expect it inverse to the activation line) or the bus; GM and Ford report a lost bus link as U0106, Saab as P0380/P1380, and no manufacturer document available to us uses P0683/P0684 themselves. P0683 means communication or feedback from the glow module to the engine module is missing or the line is open or shorted. The engine module then no longer receives plug status reports, so the individual plug monitoring fails; depending on design the glow module keeps glowing on its own timing or not at all. The activation line in the other direction is P0670/P0383/P0384.
s: Check engine light (glow plug lamp may flash or stay on)
Harder cold start, long cranking in frost
Rough running and white smoke after a cold start
No individual plug reports any more

P0684.d: Glow plug module 1 reports to the engine module over a feedback wire (Bosch-type systems expect it inverse to the activation line) or the bus; GM and Ford report a lost bus link as U0106, Saab as P0380/P1380, and no manufacturer document available to us uses P0683/P0684 themselves. P0684 means communication exists but is implausible: wrong level or duty cycle, implausible content or a feedback that does not match the activation state – as in the Saab logic, where the feedback must be the inverse of the command. The engine module can then no longer rely on the glow system status; individual plug faults may go unreported. Contact resistance at the pins and voltage dips at the glow module during high glow currents are typical causes.

P0685.d: The engine module switches its main relay coil to ground (control circuit), reads the switched voltage back on a sense line and keeps the relay on briefly after ignition off to save learned values. P0685 means the relay control circuit is open: GM measures with the driver off and flags 200 kΩ or more to ground. GM checks with run/crank voltage above 11 V and sets the code after 8 of 10 samples at 250 ms, with the lamp after two trips. GM Europe's 2.0 L turbo compares commanded and actual state for 2 s, Ford's 2023 diesel checks continuously within 0.5 s. A real open keeps the relay from pulling in – no start; on Saab's V6 there is then no communication with the engine module and the MIL flashes. GM notes P0686 may set alongside.
s: Check engine light
Engine does not start or stalls
No communication with the engine module (Saab)

c: Control wire between relay and module chafed to ground

P0686.d: The engine module switches its main relay coil to ground (control circuit), reads the switched voltage back on a sense line and keeps the relay on briefly after ignition off to save learned values. P0686 means the control line is shorted to ground: with the driver off it should carry battery voltage through the coil, but it sits at ground (0.5 Ω or less). The relay then stays energised and the module can no longer switch it off – after-run and shutdown are disturbed and the battery can drain. GM checks with run/crank voltage above 11 V and sets the code after 8 of 10 samples at 250 ms, with the lamp after two trips. The former obdex title (the wording of P0685) was a shifted entry; P0686 is the 'low' code.
s: Check engine light
Relay stays on after ignition off, battery drains
Possibly P068B as well

c: Control wire shorted to positive (harness, external voltage)
P0687.d: The engine module switches its main relay coil to ground (control circuit), reads the switched voltage back on a sense line and keeps the relay on briefly after ignition off to save learned values. P0687 means the control line is shorted to voltage: when the driver switches on and should pull it to ground, it stays high (0.5 Ω or less to positive) or the driver goes into overcurrent protection, so the relay does not pull in – no supply to the loads, no start or stalling. GM checks with run/crank voltage above 11 V and sets the code after 8 of 10 samples at 250 ms, with the lamp after two trips. The former obdex title (a sense-circuit wording) was a shifted entry; P0687 is the 'high' code of the control circuit. A high voltage on the sense line is P0690.

Engine does not start or stalls

P0688.d: The engine module switches its main relay coil to ground (control circuit), reads the switched voltage back on a sense line and keeps the relay on briefly after ignition off to save learned values. P0688 means the expected switched voltage does not arrive on the sense line – the line is open, a fuse in the monitored path has blown or the contact does not close. Chrysler (Stellantis) calls the relay 'auto shutdown (ASD) relay'; a service case for intermittent no-starts with P0688 points first to spread or pushed-back terminals in the ASD circuit connector. GM does not use P0688 and reports an open sense line as P0689. The former obdex title (a duplicate of P0690) was a shifted entry.
s: Check engine light
Engine cranks but intermittently does not start (Stellantis)

High resistance or corrosion in relay carrier, connector or wire
P0689.d: The engine module switches its main relay coil to ground (control circuit), reads the switched voltage back on a sense line and keeps the relay on briefly after ignition off to save learned values. P0689 means the sense voltage is too low although the relay is commanded on – the contact does not close or has high resistance, the sense line is open or grounded, or a fuse in the load circuit has blown. GM sets it at 5 V or less with more than 9 V supply in 5 of 6 samples at 1 s, lamp after two trips; GM Europe's V6 below 6 V for 1 s and the 2.0 L turbo below 5 V, both without the lamp. GM includes an open sense line here. Starting problems or stalling follow, and on Saab the throttle control, which uses this voltage, may go into limp mode.
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Starting problems or no start
Engine stalls or stumbles
Possibly electronic throttle limp mode

Open, high resistance or short to ground in the relay coil or contact supply
Relay faulty (drops out with vibration or heat)
P068A.d: The engine module switches its main relay coil to ground (control circuit), reads the switched voltage back on a sense line and keeps the relay on briefly after ignition off to save learned values. P068A means the relay dropped out before the module released it. Ford explains it as the non-volatile memory write after ignition off not being completed before the module lost power; the 2023 diesel checks continuously within 0.5 s. GM Europe's 2.0 diesel checks with the engine running for an unexpected loss of relay voltage (no MIL). VW (2017–18 Jetta 1.4 T) and Stellantis (2026 Dodge Charger 3.0 twin turbo) fixed false reports by software updates. Often no noticeable symptoms

P068B.d: The engine module switches its main relay coil to ground (control circuit), reads the switched voltage back on a sense line and keeps the relay on briefly after ignition off to save learned values. P068B is the counterpart of P068A: after ignition off and the module's switch-off command the relay voltage remains – the relay drops out late or not at all. GM Europe's 2.0 diesel runs this check from ignition off until the module shuts down and names a control line shorted to ground (coil stays energised), an output line shorted to voltage or a sticking contact as causes, without lighting the MIL. Modules and loads then stay powered and the battery drains. GM reports the same electrical faults as P0686/P0690 instead. A Ford diesel table lists 'P068B' for a memory error, which is evidently a typo for P06B8.

Battery drains

P0697.d: The engine module feeds sensors from several regulated 5 V reference circuits; a short at one sensor pulls the whole circuit down, so all its sensors report at once – unplug them one by one to find the culprit. Which sensors hang on circuit C depends on the maker – pedal sensor 2 is common to all: GM 2016–2025 feeds only pedal sensor 2 from it, the Saab 9-4X also the MAP sensor, the Saab 9-5 2.0 L turbo also throttle, crankshaft and A/C pressure sensors, and Bentley's 2026 Bentayga V8 lists its own set. P0697 is the general code for circuit C. GM puts all faults into it: reference outside 4.875–5.125 V or jumping, 19 of 39 counts or 0.19 s, lamp in the first trip; GM Europe's 2.0 L turbo also uses P0698/P0699.

P069A.d: Modern diesel glow systems switch each glow plug through its own power semiconductor (in a glow plug module or the engine module), so current and faults can be measured per plug; a faulty channel is switched off. CARB requires glow plugs to be checked for correct current and voltage drop and, since model year 2010, a single plug outside specification to be detected and named. P069A means the circuit to the cylinder 9 glow plug is shorted to ground or draws overcurrent. GM's engine-module drivers flag an impedance to ground below 0.11 Ω (10 of 20 samples) with the check engine and glow plug lamps after two trips; Ford's 2023 Power Stroke checks during heating for more than 22 A for 0.3 s or 20–22 A for 2 s. The channel is switched off and plug 9 no longer heats – harder cold starts and white smoke follow. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code for cylinders 9 and above; the description follows cylinders 1–8.

P06A0.d: Variable-displacement A/C compressors change their swash-plate stroke via an electric control valve: a PWM current sets the crankcase pressure and thus the output. Where the engine module drives this valve (Ford's 'EVDC' compressors 2013–2019), it monitors the circuit; where the climate control module drives it (Hyundai, VW/Audi, GM), faults appear in that module instead. P06B6.d: To detect an open knock sensor circuit, GM's engine modules feed a 20 kHz test signal into the sensor circuit and check whether it returns. P06B6 checks the internal test circuit or knock signal processor for sensor 1: it sets when the returned 20 kHz component lies between the open-circuit thresholds, so the module cannot decide 'connected' or 'open'. GM rates it type B (two trips), type A in some 2025 modules; Saab retards ignition timing as a reaction. GM bulletin 22-NA-229 calls for reprogramming only, not part replacement. Ford uses P06B6 for lost communication with its knock chip (more than 200 cylinder events). Knock sensor circuit codes are P0325–P0328.

Often no other symptoms

c: Interrupted shutdown (battery disconnected, voltage dip, main relay too early)
P06B8.d: Non-volatile RAM keeps its content without power; among other things it stores the permanent fault codes CARB requires, which cannot be cleared with a scan tool. Ford sets P06B8 when the checksum of this permanent-code memory is wrong; a common companion is P068A (main relay dropped out too early, memory write incomplete). Ford's commercial and propane variants list it with or without the check engine light depending on the vehicle; Ford's 2023 diesel table misprints it as 'P068B'. GM and Saab do not use P06B8. Typical causes are interrupted shutdowns (battery disconnected, voltage dips), software faults and, rarely, a memory defect. After a software check, clearing and an ignition cycle with normal shutdown often resolve it.

P06B9.d: The glow module calculates each plug's resistance from voltage and current while glowing. 'Range/performance' means the circuit is electrically intact but the resistance or current lies outside the specified window – typically an aged, high-resistance or wrong plug or contact resistance at the connector. Glow module software or check during cranking (false report)
Contact resistance at the plug connector
P06C5.d: A glow plug has no identification; the control unit recognises its type only from its electrical behaviour – cold resistance at switch-on and how resistance rises during heating (R = U/I). A Beru patent describes how steel and ceramic plugs are told apart this way so the right heating profile is used and a wrong or mixed type is reported. A low-voltage plug on an 11 V control burns out, an 11 V plug on a low-voltage control glows too weakly. GM uses 'incorrect' for any resistance outside the window: the 2025 diesels check 0.22–2.00 Ω (15 of 25 samples, two trips), the L5P glow module a ramp-dependent window. P06C5 reports this for cylinder 1. VW's 2.0 TDI (Jetta, Golf, Passat 2011–13) checks the type 2 s after ignition on – starting during that time caused false codes from the voltage dip, fixed with new glow module software.

c: Coil driver chip or internal communication in the engine module faulty
Supply or ground problem at the module
P06D1.d: On ignition systems where the coils are driven through a separate driver chip inside the engine module, P06D1 reports that this internal coil control does not work correctly. Ford checks the communication with the coil driver chip continuously and sets the code within 1 s at 200–3200 rpm, positive torque and 11–16 V. GM Europe's V6 (Saab 9-5 2.8 T) reports it as an internal engine module fault with the lamp after two trips. Misfires or rough running can follow if coils are no longer fired correctly. Primary circuit faults of individual coils are P0351–P0360, driver shorts P2300 ff. Check supply and ground, look for software updates; otherwise the module is the likely cause.
s: Check engine light
Misfires or rough running
Possibly no start

c: Short in the wire or sensor of a connected sensor
Chafing or water in harness or connector
Module internal voltage regulator or components
P06D2.d: The engine module feeds sensors from several regulated 5 V reference circuits; a short at one sensor pulls the whole circuit down and all its sensors report at once – unplug them one by one to find the culprit. P06D2 is the general code for circuit E. GM uses it as the collective code for its fifth 5 V reference: petrol engines 2015–2019 flag a reference outside 4.875–5.125 V in 19 of 39 samples with the lamp in the first trip, the 6.6 L Duramax LML/LGH 4.6 V or less for 0.1 s with two trips; GM includes it in its 'engine power limited' group. Which sensors are on circuit E is not listed. GM's hybrid control module uses P06D2 for a separate 12 V reference.
s: Check engine light
Several sensor codes at once
Reduced power or limp mode
Possibly starting problems

c: Short in the wire or sensor of a connected sensor
Chafing or water in harness or connector
Engine module internal fault (e.g. leaking capacitor, Ram 2023)
P06D3.d: The engine module feeds sensors from several regulated 5 V reference circuits; a short at one sensor pulls the whole circuit down and all its sensors report at once – unplug them one by one to find the culprit. P06D3 means reference E is too low – typically a short to ground. Ram's 2023 6.7 L Cummins set P06D3 together with P0642/P0652 because of a leaking capacitor in the engine module; the fix was replacing the module. GM reports circuit E under the collective code P06D2.

P06D4 means reference E is too high – often a sensor signal wire shorted to 12 V. P06DA.d: A switchable or variable oil pump saves fuel by lowering its output at part load; a solenoid valve sets the stage. GM and Ford design it so the pump runs at full output, i.e. high pressure, when the valve is unpowered – the safe default – and at the low stage when powered. P06DA means the control circuit of this valve is open: it can no longer be powered, so the pump stays at high pressure. GM measures the voltage with the driver off and flags more than 200 kΩ after two trips; some GM modules set P06DB instead. GM checks the low-side driver at 11 V or more relay voltage over 40 of 50 samples (100 ms); Ford's smart driver reports output faults after 5 s with the battery at 11 V or more. Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander uses the same code. The engine is not at risk, the pump just can no longer be regulated.

P06DB.d: A switchable or variable oil pump saves fuel by lowering its output at part load; a solenoid valve sets the stage. GM and Ford design it so the pump runs at full output, i.e. high pressure, when the valve is unpowered – the safe default – and at the low stage when powered. P06DB means the control wire behind the valve is shorted to ground. With a low-side driver the valve is then powered all the time, so the pump stays at the low stage even at high load and speed. That endangers the engine, so GM flags a short below 0.5 Ω after just one trip, unlike open circuit and short to positive. P06DD.d: A switchable oil pump changes its output via a solenoid valve; unpowered it delivers high pressure. To test it, the module switches the pump between stages (GM up to 15 times, with oil at 50–110 °C and 1350–2500 rpm, expecting more than 100 kPa difference) and watches the oil pressure sensor; Ford checks each switch-over of a two-stage pump within 1 s, or a variable pump over 10 s, from 30 s after start. P06DE.d: A switchable oil pump changes its output via a solenoid valve; powered it runs at the low stage. P06E9.d: On cars with stop-start or keyless start the engine module operates the starter relay itself and watches the start: if cranking is commanded but the engine does not turn, turns too slowly or the start is aborted, it sets P06E9. Bulletins show both sides: VW traces P06E9 on the Tiguan to dirt inside the starter that opens its contacts intermittently, and on the Atlas has relays, battery and voltage drop checked; Audi's SQ5 and FCA's Jeep Compass need module software instead. P06EA.d: A modern NOx sensor is a smart sensor: a ceramic sensing element with pump cells and heater plus its own control unit with a microcontroller, which regulates the pump currents, calculates NOx and oxygen and sends them to the engine module over CAN. P06EA means this control unit of sensor 1 (before the SCR catalyst) reports an internal fault – its self-tests of RAM and ROM or EEPROM checksums fail – so the electronics, not the sensing element, are at fault. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code: Ford's 2023 diesels run exactly these checks continuously, with a fault after 5 s, but report them as P2200; GM uses the P2200 family and U029D/U029E. The NOx value is then invalid, so SCR dosing runs on a model or stops, a warning appears and, depending on market, a countdown to a start lock.

c: Glow plug control module 2 faulty internally
Poor supply or ground of module 2
P06F5.d: SAE J2012 provides a complete code family for a second glow plug control module, mirroring module 1 code for code. P06F5 is the general or internal fault of module 2, the counterpart of P064C. For module 1, GM's L5P groups driver faults (under 3.2 A with 0 V at the plug for 3.5 s) and a ROM checksum error under P064C, after two trips; Ford's 2023 Power Stroke lists P064C among the module checks with detection in about 1 s. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P064C). The plugs fed by module 2 then heat poorly or not at all.
s: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp
Hard cold start, long cranking in frost
Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only
Usually no symptoms when warm

c: Line from engine module to glow module 2 open, connector loose or corroded
Input of glow module 2 faulty or module not connected
P06F6.d: P06F6 means the command line from the engine module to glow plug control module 2 is open or has a general circuit fault – the counterpart of P0670 for module 1. The engine module's output driver detects an open load while the driver is off. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P0670). Shorts on the same line are P06F7 (to ground) and P06F8 (to positive); the feedback line back to the engine module is P06FC/P06FD. The plugs of module 2 then heat poorly or not at all, typically on one bank.
s: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp
Hard cold start, long cranking in frost
Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only
Usually no symptoms when warm

c: Command line to glow module 2 chafed through to ground
Moisture or corrosion in the connector bridging to ground
Input of glow module 2 or engine module driver faulty
P06F7.d: P06F7 means the command line from the engine module to glow plug control module 2 is too low, typically shorted to ground – the counterpart of P0383 for module 1. The engine module's output driver detects the short by its current when switched on or by the line voltage when switched off. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P0383). An open line is P06F6, a short to positive P06F8. The plugs of module 2 then heat poorly or not at all, typically on one bank.
s: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp
Hard cold start, long cranking in frost
Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only
Usually no symptoms when warm

c: Command line shorted to positive or supply
Corrosion in the connector bridging to a B+ pin
P06F8.d: P06F8 means the command line from the engine module to glow plug control module 2 is too high, typically shorted to positive – the counterpart of P0384 for module 1. Note that Ford's 2023 diesels use P0384 differently, for the supply voltage of the glow module (below 6.5 V or above 16.5 V); in J2012 that is P052F, and for module 2 P06F9. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P0384). An open line is P06F6, a short to ground P06F7. The plugs of module 2 then heat poorly or not at all, typically on one bank.
s: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp
Hard cold start, long cranking in frost
Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only
Usually no symptoms when warm

c: Main feed to glow module 2 open or high-resistance (fuse, fusible link, B+ wire)
Weak battery or discharged auxiliary battery
P06F9.d: P06F9 means the supply voltage of glow plug control module 2 is out of range – the counterpart of P052F for module 1. For module 1, Ford's 2023 Power Stroke flags below 6.5 V, above 16.5 V or an open supply after about 1 s; GM's L5P checks the same under P163C (below 6.0 V with ignition above 9 V, or implausible against ignition voltage, 4 s). An FCA bulletin shows P052F together with the glow plug open codes, because without supply no current flows. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P052F). Check main feed, fuses and ground first.
s: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp
Hard cold start, long cranking in frost
Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only
Usually no symptoms when warm

c: Glow module 2 faulty internally (drivers do not switch)
Poor supply or ground of module 2
P06FA.d: P06FA means glow plug control module 2 does not respond correctly to the glow command – the counterpart of P06E5 for module 1. For module 1, Ford's 2023 Power Stroke flags internal drivers that fail to switch or overheat for more than 1 s; GM's L5P files the same check under P064C (under 3.2 A with 0 V at the plug for 3.5 s, two trips). No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P06E5). Internal checksum errors are P06FB, overheating P263F. The plugs of module 2 then heat poorly or not at all, typically on one bank.
s: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp
Hard cold start, long cranking in frost
Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only
Usually no symptoms when warm

P06FB.d: P06FB means glow plug control module 2 has found a memory checksum error – the counterpart of P06DF for module 1. The module forms a checksum over its memory at power-up and compares it with the stored value. For module 1, Ford's 2023 Power Stroke checks the RAM checksum at power-up (about 1 s); GM's L5P checks the ROM checksum (4.5 s, two trips) and reports it as P064C. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P06DF). The usual remedy is reprogramming or replacing the module. The plugs of module 2 then heat poorly or not at all, typically on one bank.
s: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp
Hard cold start, long cranking in frost
Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only
Usually no symptoms when warm

c: Feedback or bus line open or shorted, connector corroded
Glow module 2 without supply (does not transmit)
Glow module 2 or engine module interface faulty
P06FC.d: P06FC means the feedback or communication from glow plug control module 2 to the engine module is missing, or the line is open or shorted – the counterpart of P0683 for module 1. Depending on design the module reports over a single feedback wire (Bosch-type systems expect it inverse to the command line) or over the bus; GM and Ford report a lost bus link as U0106 rather than P0683. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P0683). The engine module then loses the plug status reports; implausible messages are P06FD. The plugs of module 2 then heat poorly or not at all, typically on one bank.
s: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp
Hard cold start, long cranking in frost
Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only
Usually no symptoms when warm

c: Loose contact or contact resistance in the feedback or bus line
Ground offset between module and engine module from glow currents
Software mismatch between modules or module faulty
P06FD.d: P06FD means signals or messages from glow plug control module 2 arrive at the engine module but are implausible – wrong duty cycle or pattern, feedback not matching the command, or single messages timing out. It is the counterpart of P0684 for module 1; Saab's Bosch-based diesels, for example, expect the feedback signal to be inverse to the command line. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P0684). A missing signal or open line is P06FC, a lost bus link usually U0106. The plugs of module 2 then heat poorly or not at all, typically on one bank.
s: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp
Hard cold start, long cranking in frost
Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only
Usually no symptoms when warm

c: Intake throttle coked with soot and oil (EGR, crankcase ventilation)
Throttle motor or gear stiff, position sensor faulty
Ice or condensate in the intake in frost
Contact resistance in connector or wiring, low voltage
P06FE.d: 'Diesel intake air flow control' is the diesel's electric intake throttle with position sensor (P02E0 ff). During cold start many diesels close it partly: the extra load raises exhaust temperature so the catalysts light off sooner. CARB requires such cold start elements to be monitored, with their own codes separate from normal operation. P06FE means the throttle does not reach its target position while the cold start strategy is active – it is not the intake air heater. No manufacturer document available to us uses P06FE: GM's 2025 diesels run this check under P2957 (deviation above 16 % or 10 %, two trips), Ford's 2023 diesels under P02E4 in cold start mode. Cold start emissions rise; driveability usually stays normal.
s: Check engine light, usually after two trips
Hardly any change in driveability
Possibly more smoke or smell while warming up
Further throttle codes (P02E1/P02E4/P02E5) possible

c: Wire or connector to the lamp open or shorted
P06FF.d: When the engine module switches a lamp through its own wire, it checks the output driver electrically like other lamp outputs: with the lamp off the line must carry supply voltage, with it on nearly 0 V – GM's MIL driver, for example, flags an open circuit at 200 kΩ or more. It cannot see whether the bulb lights, and on cars that send the lamp command over CAN such faults appear as U codes. P06FF concerns an economy indicator such as an ECO lamp that the engine module switches directly; the code reports a fault in its control circuit. It should not be confused with a body electrics 'economy mode' that saves battery energy. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB's output check and other lamp circuits. Driving is not affected.
s: ECO indicator not working or permanently lit
No effect on driving

c: Actual fault stored in the transmission module (sensor, solenoid, ratio, speed sensor)
Wrong transmission fluid level or condition causing slip or ratio codes
Harness or connector at the transmission corroded or damaged
Low system voltage or weak battery
P0700.d: P0700 is a notice code: the separate transmission control module has stored an emission-related fault of its own and asks the engine module to switch on the check engine light. The actual fault – a sensor, solenoid, ratio or speed sensor code – is stored in the transmission module and must be read with a tool that can address it; simple OBD readers often show only P0700. GM's engine module reads the request message from 3 s after start; Subaru-based systems (Saab 9-2X) light the MIL at once and clear it after three fault-free cycles. Ford's engine modules with integrated transmission control do not use P0700. Any limp mode comes from the transmission fault, not from P0700.
s: Check engine light, possibly transmission warning
Depending on the transmission fault: limp mode, harsh or delayed shifts
Often no symptoms if the fault was intermittent
Simple OBD reader shows only P0700

c: Transmission control faulty internally or software
Implausible input signals (speed or range sensor) without own circuit fault
Wrong fluid level or quality – hydraulics do not respond
Harness or connector with contact resistance
P0701.d: P0701 means the transmission control system works outside its expected range or its function is implausible – without a circuit fault. What exactly is checked is up to the manufacturer; no GM, Ford, Saab or bulletin document available to us describes the strategy. The only manufacturer evidence is Ford's engine module list for 6.8 L E- and F-Series trucks, where P0701 is stored without the check engine light. Typically the control cannot plausibly achieve the requested gear, pressure or torque, and the transmission goes into limp mode. Individual components have their own codes (P0705 ff range sensor, P0715 ff speed sensors, P0750 ff solenoids).
s: Transmission warning (at Ford no check engine light)
Limp mode with fixed gear or missing gears
Harsh or irregular shifts

c: Transmission actuator supply interrupted (fuse, relay, ground)
Harness or connector at transmission or module damaged, corroded or oil-soaked
Transmission module output stage or supply switch faulty
P0702.d: P0702 reports an electrical fault in the transmission control system as a whole – typically the supply of the transmission actuators (solenoid supply, transmission relay, supply switch in the module) or a circuit fault not assigned to a single component. No manufacturer document available to us describes it in detail; Ford's engine module list for 6.8 L E- and F-Series trucks stores it without the check engine light. If the solenoid supply is lost, transmissions usually fall back to a hydraulic limp gear. Individual solenoids have their own codes (P0750 ff); actuator supply is P0657 ff.
s: Transmission limp mode with fixed gear
Transmission warning; check engine light depending on the maker
No or harsh shifts, further solenoid codes

c: Brake light or double switch worn, corroded or misadjusted
Wiring or connector at the pedal damaged, fuse blown
CAN message from the body module disturbed (GM: software, bus fault)
Aftermarket LED lamps or trailer module distorting the circuit
P0703.d: Brake switch A is usually the brake light switch, B a second, redundant contact or signal used to cancel cruise control, release the converter clutch, check 'brake before throttle' and for stop-start. Since about 2014 GM receives it as a CAN message from the body module and checks its integrity (rolling counter, protection value: 3 of 10 faulty in 2014, 9 of 17 in 2025) without the check engine light; cruise control is disabled. Subaru-based systems (Saab 9-2X) check the circuit electrically during stops and starts and light the MIL after two trips. An NHTSA investigation of Hyundai and Kia brake light switches lists P0703 with a brake light that stays on. Brake switch A codes are P0571–P0573, disagreement between A and B is P0504.
s: Cruise control cannot be engaged or drops out
Brake light stays on or does not work
Selector cannot be moved out of P (shift lock)
Check engine light depending on the maker

c: Clutch switch faulty or misadjusted (does not switch or too late)
Connector or wiring at the pedal box damaged or corroded
Floor mat or pedal stop shifted, switch bracket broken
Driving style (pulling away or shifting without fully depressing the clutch)
P0704.d: Only on cars with a clutch pedal: the clutch switch tells the engine module that the clutch is depressed, used to cancel cruise control, smooth load changes when shifting and for stop-start. The check is a plausibility test over driving events rather than a voltage check: Saab's Trionic T8 expects a change of state every time the car pulls away from 3 to 50 km/h (four misses in a row), the EDC16 diesel at gear changes (25 in a row, above 35 km/h and 1500 rpm), and Ford compares its two clutch switches continuously. None of them lights the check engine light; cruise control is disabled. Separate clutch pedal switch codes are P0830–P0835.
s: Cruise control not working or not cancelling when declutching
Jerks or rev hang when shifting
Stop-start inactive
Usually no check engine light

c: Range sensor worn, dirty or with oil or water ingress
Sensor misadjusted or selector cable out of adjustment
Harness or connector at the transmission damaged, short to ground
Transmission or engine module input faulty
P0705.d: The transmission range sensor (selector or multifunction switch, PRNDL) reports the selected range; it may be a multi-contact switch with a bit pattern per position, an analog sensor with two opposing voltages adding up to 5 V, or a contactless PWM sensor. Its second channel has its own codes (P2801–P2805). P0705 is the circuit or pattern fault: the module receives a combination that matches no valid position. Ford flags an invalid pattern after 5 s (digital sensor) or 200 ms (4-bit sensor), checking continuously with the check engine light; Saab's 9-5 (9600) detects an impossible combination of its four contacts and goes into limp mode with the gearbox warning. The transmission no longer knows the range reliably – limp mode, start interlock or reversing light may be affected. Check the harness for shorts to ground before replacing the sensor.
s: Check engine and/or transmission warning lamp
Transmission limp mode, fixed gear, harsh shifts
Starting problems in P/N or start interlock
Wrong gear indication, reversing light not working

c: Range sensor or transmission module with integrated sensor faulty
Selector cable or sensor misadjusted (position between two ranges)
Contact resistance in sensor supply or ground
Moisture or oil in harness or connector
P0706.d: The transmission range sensor (selector or multifunction switch, PRNDL) reports the selected range; it may be a multi-contact switch with a bit pattern per position, an analog sensor with two opposing voltages adding up to 5 V, or a contactless PWM sensor. Its second channel has its own codes (P2801–P2805). P0706 means the signal is present but implausible. Ford uses it per transmission: for its PWM sensor when the frequency leaves 100–175 Hz (nominal 125 Hz), for the 6F digital sensor when it stays in the transition zone between two positions. Saab's 9-5 (9650), whose sensor sits in the transmission module, flags a sum of the two opposing channels more than 0.29 V away from 5 V, with the lamp in the first trip; adaptations are frozen, the gearbox holds 2nd gear in D and the engine may not restart after switch-off.
s: Check engine and/or transmission warning lamp
Transmission limp mode, fixed gear, harsh shifts
Starting problems in P/N or start interlock
Wrong gear indication, reversing light not working

c: Signal wire shorted to ground (chafing at the transmission case)
Sensor supply missing (5 V reference, fuse)
Connector corroded or oil in the connector
P0707.d: The transmission range sensor (selector or multifunction switch, PRNDL) reports the selected range; it may be a multi-contact switch with a bit pattern per position, an analog sensor with two opposing voltages adding up to 5 V, or a contactless PWM sensor. Its second channel has its own codes (P2801–P2805). P0707 means the sensor A signal is too low – usually a short to ground or lost supply. GM's T87A transmission module flags a PWM duty cycle below 8.8 % for 0.5 s within 1.5 s, with the lamp in the first trip; Ford flags a duty cycle below 10 %, an analog sensor below 0.2 V for 5 s or a dual-analog channel below 0.127 V for 200 ms; Saab's 9-5 (9650) below 0.127 V for 100 ms twice. 'Low' refers to the signal, not to a gear.
s: Check engine and/or transmission warning lamp
Transmission limp mode, fixed gear, harsh shifts
Starting problems in P/N or start interlock
Wrong gear indication, reversing light not working

c: Sensor connector off or signal/ground wire open
P0708.d: The transmission range sensor (selector or multifunction switch, PRNDL) reports the selected range; it may be a multi-contact switch with a bit pattern per position, an analog sensor with two opposing voltages adding up to 5 V, or a contactless PWM sensor. Its second channel has its own codes (P2801–P2805). P0708 means the sensor A signal is too high – a short to voltage or, depending on the circuit, an open line pulled up. GM's T87A transmission module flags a PWM duty cycle above 91.2 % for 1.8 s within 2.25 s, lamp in the first trip; Ford flags a duty cycle above 90 %, an analog sensor above 4.8 V for 5 s, a dual-analog channel above 4.84 V for 200 ms, and explicitly an open circuit on its digital sensor (all switches open, e.g. unplugged); Saab's 9-5 (9650) above 4.87 V for 100 ms twice, with 2nd gear held and a restart interlock.
s: Check engine and/or transmission warning lamp
Transmission limp mode, fixed gear, harsh shifts
Starting problems in P/N or start interlock
Wrong gear indication, reversing light not working

c: Loose contact or corrosion in the range sensor connector
Worn sliding contacts in the selector switch
Harness chafing on transmission or bracket, breaking when moved
Misadjusted sensor or selector cable (position at the limit)
P0709.d: The transmission range sensor (selector or multifunction switch, PRNDL) reports the selected range; it may be a multi-contact switch with a bit pattern per position, an analog sensor with two opposing voltages adding up to 5 V, or a contactless PWM sensor. Its second channel has its own codes (P2801–P2805). P0709 means the sensor A signal jumps briefly to invalid values or drops out without being permanently low or high. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0709 – Ford catches short invalid states under P0705 and P0706 instead – so the description follows the sibling codes. Sliding contacts in older selector switches are a typical source; the transmission may briefly lose the range and go into limp mode.
s: Intermittent transmission warning or check engine light
Gear indication flickers, brief shift jolts
Occasional starting problems in P/N
Occasional limp mode

c: Wire or connector to the sensor (often through the sump or transmission connector) open or oil-soaked
P070A.d: Fluid level sensors in the transmission sump (capacitive or voltage-based) report the oil level to the transmission module; measurements are only valid under defined conditions – an Allison patent names fluid temperature, vehicle at rest, low input speed and a tilt correction. Such sensors are mainly found in heavy automatic transmissions. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. P070A is the general circuit fault of this sensor (open or fault in the signal circuit). Because the oil level does not usually affect emissions directly, a rating without the check engine light is likely; expect a transmission warning or a missing level display. An actually low oil level is not a P070A fault. Range, low, high and intermittent are P070B–P070E; fluid temperature has its own codes (P0710 ff).
s: Transmission warning or 'check fluid level' message
Fluid level display missing
Usually no driveability problems

c: Fluid level sensor drifting or dirty (wear debris, sludge)
Fluid level actually wrong (over- or underfilled) or wrong fluid
Contact resistance in connector or wire
Faulty tilt or temperature compensation (fluid temperature sensor fault)
P070B.d: Fluid level sensors in the transmission sump (capacitive or voltage-based) report the oil level to the transmission module; measurements are only valid under defined conditions – an Allison patent names fluid temperature, vehicle at rest, low input speed and a tilt correction. Such sensors are mainly found in heavy automatic transmissions. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. P070B means the signal is present but implausible – it does not change, does not fit temperature or operating state, or lies outside the physically possible range. Such checks only make sense within the valid measuring window. A truly wrong oil level (overfilled, underfilled) or the wrong fluid can also appear as an implausible signal. The circuit fault is P070A.
s: Warning or message about transmission fluid level
Fluid level display implausible or unavailable
Usually no driveability problems

c: Signal wire to the level sensor shorted to ground (chafing, transmission connector)
Transmission connector soaked in oil or corroded
P070C.d: Fluid level sensors in the transmission sump report the oil level to the transmission module as a voltage; an Allison patent converts it to millimetres and only accepts readings with the vehicle at rest, warm fluid, low input speed and a tilt correction. Such sensors are mainly found in heavy automatic transmissions. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. P070C means the sensor signal is below its lower limit – typically the signal wire shorted to ground or a sensor shorted internally. Because the oil level does not usually affect emissions directly, a rating without the check engine light is likely; expect a transmission warning or a missing level display. An actually low oil level is P070F.
s: Fluid level display missing or warning to check transmission fluid
Usually no driveability problems
Transmission warning lamp depending on manufacturer

c: Wire or connector to the level sensor open
P070D.d: Fluid level sensors in the transmission sump report the oil level to the transmission module as a voltage; an Allison patent converts it to millimetres and only accepts readings with the vehicle at rest, warm fluid, low input speed and a tilt correction. Such sensors are mainly found in heavy automatic transmissions. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. P070D means the sensor signal is above its upper limit – typically an open signal or ground wire, pulled up inside the module, or a short to positive. Because the oil level does not usually affect emissions directly, a rating without the check engine light is likely; expect a transmission warning or a missing level display. The opposite fault is P070C.
s: Fluid level display missing or warning to check transmission fluid
Usually no driveability problems
Transmission warning lamp depending on manufacturer

c: Loose contact in transmission connector or harness
Contaminated or foaming fluid at the sensor
P070E.d: Fluid level sensors in the transmission sump report the oil level to the transmission module as a voltage; an Allison patent converts it to millimetres and only accepts readings with the vehicle at rest, warm fluid, low input speed and a tilt correction. Such sensors are mainly found in heavy automatic transmissions. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. P070E means the level signal drops out briefly or jumps unrealistically – usually a loose contact or a wire breaking under movement. Sloshing and tilt also make readings vary, which is why valid measurements need the vehicle at rest. Because the oil level does not usually affect emissions directly, a rating without the check engine light is likely; expect a transmission warning or a missing level display.
s: Fluid level display jumps or drops out at times
Intermittent warning message

c: Leak (pan gasket, shaft seals, cooler lines)
Underfilled after fluid change or repair
P070F.d: P070F is not a circuit fault but a condition: a working fluid level sensor reports a level below the target band. In the Allison patent the module compares the measured height in millimetres with a tilt-dependent band and reports at least a quart too little or too much – only with the vehicle at rest, fluid above about 30–40 °C and low input speed. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. Take it seriously: real fluid loss leads to slipping, overheating (P0218) and ratio errors. Leaks at the pan gasket, seals or cooler lines and wrong filling after service are the usual causes.
s: Warning: transmission fluid level low
Slipping gears, delayed engagement
Transmission overheating
Oil spots under the vehicle

c: Fluid temperature sensor faulty (often part of the internal harness or valve body)
Transmission connector leaking or corroded, oil in the connector
P0710.d: The transmission fluid temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor whose resistance falls as the fluid warms; the module feeds it with 5 V through a resistor. A low signal therefore means very hot or a short to ground, a high signal very cold or an open circuit. P0710 is the general circuit code used when a manufacturer does not separate low and high. Subaru-based systems (Saab 9-2X) flag 0.1 V or less or 4.7 V or more, light the MIL after two consecutive trips and use 80 °C as substitute. Ford's 2023 diesels use P0710 alongside P0712/P0713 for open and short circuits, without MIL, after 5–12 s, substituting coolant temperature. GM uses only the split codes. With the substitute value the shift quality suffers: harsh shifts and a late converter clutch.
s: Harsh or late shifts
Torque converter clutch applies late or not at all
Check engine or transmission lamp depending on manufacturer
Implausible fluid temperature in the scan tool

c: Fluid temperature sensor drifting or stuck
High contact resistance in connector or harness (oil, corrosion)
Very cold weather or short trips (fluid does not reach warm-up threshold)
P0711.d: P0711 means the fluid temperature signal is electrically valid but implausible. Manufacturers check three things: the fluid does not warm up as expected (GM 2025 still below 15 °C after the calibrated warm-up time, Saab's AF40 below 20 °C after 10 minutes of driving), the value is stuck (Ford: within ±2 °F for about 2.5 minutes below 70 or above 225 °F), or it jumps unrealistically. GM's 6T70 compares it with the module's internal temperature. The MIL rating varies: GM's newer modules after two trips, Saab AF40 none, Ford none; a 2013 Ram 6.7 bulletin moved P0711–P0714 from one to two trips. A substitute value then limits adaption and converter clutch control.
s: Harsh or late shifts
Torque converter clutch applies late or not at all
Check engine or transmission lamp depending on manufacturer
Implausible fluid temperature in the scan tool

c: Signal wire shorted to ground (internal harness, chafing)
P0712.d: The transmission fluid temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor whose resistance falls as the fluid warms; the module feeds it with 5 V through a resistor. A low signal therefore means very hot or a short to ground, a high signal very cold or an open circuit. P0712 means the signal is too low – the sensor reads extremely hot, or the signal wire is shorted to ground. GM's 2025 transmission modules flag below 13.5 Ω for 5 of 6 s after two trips; the 2018 LT4 engine module below 17.88 Ω (over 150 °C) without MIL; the 2007 Allison 1000 150 °C or more for 2.5 s; Saab's AF40 over 200 °C; Ford below 0.05 V for 5–12 s without MIL. The module substitutes a value (coolant temperature, 80 °C or a hot mode) and may shift with hot-fluid strategy. Real overheating with a good sensor is P0218.
s: Transmission in hot mode (early converter clutch, changed shift points)
Harsh shifts
Extremely high fluid temperature shown
Check engine or transmission lamp depending on manufacturer

c: Transmission connector loose or corroded, wire open
P0713.d: The transmission fluid temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor whose resistance falls as the fluid warms; the module feeds it with 5 V through a resistor. A low signal therefore means very hot or a short to ground, a high signal very cold or an open circuit. P0713 means the signal is too high – the sensor reads extremely cold, or the circuit is open or shorted to positive. GM's 2025 modules flag above 284 kΩ for 5 of 6 s after two trips; the 2007 Allison 1000 −45 °C or below for 2.5 s; Saab's AF40 below −43 °C; Ford above 4.6 V for 5–12 s without MIL. Many require prior running time or a warm engine so a genuine −40 °C cold start does not count (Allison: coolant above 20 °C; Saab: over 10 minutes of driving). The transmission then stays in its cold strategy: open converter clutch, late upshifts.
s: Fluid temperature shown around −40 °C
Converter clutch stays open, late upshifts
Higher fuel consumption
Check engine or transmission lamp depending on manufacturer

c: Loose contact in transmission connector (oil, corrosion, spread pins)
Internal harness chafing from movement or vibration
P0714.d: The transmission fluid temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor whose resistance falls as the fluid warms; the module feeds it with 5 V through a resistor. A low signal therefore means very hot or a short to ground, a high signal very cold or an open circuit. P0714 means the signal drops out or jumps briefly – not long enough for P0712 or P0713. Ford's 2012 6R80 transmission names P0714 among its fluid temperature checks for open, short and in-range faults. Ram 6.7 bulletins of 2013 changed P0711–P0714 from a one-trip to a two-trip MIL to avoid needless warnings. GM files such jumps under P0711 instead. No source publishes thresholds for P0714 itself. A loose contact in the transmission connector or a chafing internal harness is the usual cause.

Jumping fluid temperature display
Check engine or transmission lamp depending on manufacturer

P0715.d: The input or turbine shaft speed sensor – a Hall sensor with square-wave output or an inductive sensor with sine output – reports the speed behind the torque converter. With output and engine speed it gives the actual gear ratio, converter slip and shift timing. P0715 is the general circuit code. Ford uses it for 'no signal' too: the vehicle is moving under power (engine above converter stall speed, output speed plausible) but the sensor reports under 200 rpm for 5–30 s; Ford's DPS6 dual-clutch sets it for a hardware-detected fault of input shaft sensor 1. Subaru-based systems flag an open or shorted circuit, Saab's Aisin box no input signal while the output sensor works, substituting output speed. GM does not use P0715. Limp mode, harsh shifts and a disabled converter clutch follow.

Limp mode with fixed gear, harsh shifts
Torque converter clutch does not apply
Input speed shows 0 or implausible in the scan tool

P0716.d: The input or turbine shaft speed sensor – a Hall sensor with square-wave output or an inductive sensor with sine output – reports the speed behind the torque converter. With output and engine speed it gives the actual gear ratio, converter slip and shift timing. P0716 means a signal is present but implausible: too high, or dropping suddenly without recovering. GM's 2025 modules count drops of more than 650 rpm between 25 ms samples and fail after more than three; the 6T70 in the Saab 9-4X flags a 1350 rpm drop for 1 s; the 2007 Allison 1000 also detects noise and swapped sensor wires; all after one trip. Ford's 6R80 flags turbine speed above 7700 rpm. The 6T70 then runs only reverse and fifth gear, with maximum line pressure and no converter clutch.

P0717.d: The input or turbine shaft speed sensor – a Hall sensor with square-wave output or an inductive sensor with sine output – reports the speed behind the torque converter. With output and engine speed it gives the actual gear ratio, converter slip and shift timing. P0717 means there is practically no input speed signal although the vehicle is driving under power. P0718.d: The input or turbine shaft speed sensor – a Hall sensor with square-wave output or an inductive sensor with sine output – reports the speed behind the torque converter. With output and engine speed it gives the actual gear ratio, converter slip and shift timing. P0718 means the signal is present but jumps or drops out briefly. Ford's petrol modules from 2012 to 2023 count 200 turbine speed spikes above 400 rpm with at most 1.5 s between them in a forward gear. P0719.d: Brake switch B is the brake signal to the transmission module or a second brake switch channel, used to release the converter clutch, adapt shift strategy on grades and cancel cruise control. Low and high describe the signal voltage, and what that means depends on polarity: GM's converter clutch brake switch is closed at rest (12 V), while Saab's Trionic 8 sees 12 V when braking. Detection is always a plausibility check against driving: the brake reads applied during accelerations or never applied during decelerations. P0719 means the signal stays low. For GM that reads as brake applied: 2006 transmission modules flag it after eight accelerations without the brake releasing, without MIL. Saab's Trionic 8 flags the brake light signal not changing during four decelerations from 40 to 3 km/h and disables cruise control. The opposite is P0724.

Unusual shifting, converter clutch behaviour changed

P071A.d: A transmission mode switch selects an alternative shift schedule such as sport, winter or tow/haul; J2012 does not define which button is A or B. No manufacturer document available to us uses P071A–P071F: GM monitors its analog drive mode switch under its own codes (low below 21–29 % of 5 V, high from 94 %, 200 of 250 samples, two trips), which shows how such buttons are read as coded voltages. P071A is the general circuit fault of mode switch A: its state is invalid or implausible. The transmission then usually stays on its normal schedule. Low and high are P071B/P071C, switch B has P071D–P071F; the range sensor (PRNDL) is P0705 ff.

P0720.d: The output shaft speed sensor (Hall or inductive) reports the speed of the transmission output; it gives the gear ratio together with input speed and on many vehicles also the road speed for speedometer and cruise control. P0720 is the general circuit code. Ford also uses it for 'no signal': while engine and turbine speed show the vehicle moving, the sensor reports under 100–200 rpm for 5–30 s; ZF's 6HP26 in Ford vehicles flags an open or short after 0.6 s. Subaru-based systems (Saab 9-2X) flag an impossible 255 km/h or 0 km/h while driving and light the MIL after two trips, substituting the other sensor. GM does not use P0720 but P0722. Speedometer and cruise control may fail, often with a vehicle speed code as well.

P0721.d: The output shaft speed sensor (Hall or inductive) reports the speed of the transmission output; it gives the gear ratio together with input speed and on many vehicles also the road speed for speedometer and cruise control. P0721 means the output speed is present but implausible: too high (Ford 6R80 above 7450 rpm), not matching wheel or input speed in the engaged gear (ZF 6HP26 more than 200 or 250 rpm apart, Ford's F21 more than 15 % for 10 s), or jumping (Allison 1000: 500 rpm within 0.15 s). Wrong tyre sizes or a faulty wheel speed sensor can also falsify the comparison.

P0725.d: The transmission module needs engine speed for converter slip, shift quality and to check the turbine speed. Today it almost always arrives over CAN from the engine module with a validity flag; only GM's 2007 Allison 1000 tables show a separate engine speed sensor read by the transmission module. P0725 is the general fault of this input; with CAN it means the engine module marks its speed value as invalid. Saab's Aisin transmissions and a 2006 GM table set it after about 4 s, the GM table with immediate MIL. A Saab bulletin notes that behind P0725 there is always a crankshaft or camshaft sensor code in the engine module (P0016, P0335–P0339) – so read the engine module first. Limp mode follows; a completely missing CAN message is U0100.

P0726.d: The transmission module needs engine speed for converter slip, shift quality and to check the turbine speed. Today it almost always arrives over CAN from the engine module with a validity flag; only GM's 2007 Allison 1000 tables show a separate engine speed sensor read by the transmission module. P0726 means the engine speed value is present but implausible. The Allison 1000, which reads its own sensor, flags a jump of 600 rpm within 0.15 s or noise of ±650 rpm, with the engine above 600 rpm and a gear engaged, after two trips. P0727.d: The transmission module needs engine speed for converter slip, shift quality and to check the turbine speed. Today it almost always arrives over CAN from the engine module with a validity flag; only GM's 2007 Allison 1000 tables show a separate engine speed sensor read by the transmission module. P0729.d: The transmission module divides input (turbine) speed by output speed and compares the result with the ratio of the commanded gear; a deviation means slip – a clutch or brake not holding, too little pressure – or a wrong gear. Thresholds: Ford more than 30 rpm off for 1.8 s three times (diesel 2023: over 20 % for 12 s), GM's 2006 tables and the Allison 1000 converter slip of 200–230 rpm for 2.25 s after one trip, Saab's Aisin boxes over 20 % twelve times without MIL. P0729 concerns sixth gear. Saab's Aisin six-speed also checks whether the actual ratio matches fourth or fifth – the sixth gear clutch is not holding and the box drops into another gear. Ford stores it only if the fault does not fit a particular solenoid (otherwise P0751 ff). On GM manual transmissions (LT4) it checks the gear position sensor instead.

P072A.d: Ford's DPS6 dry dual-clutch transmission moves its gears with two electrically driven shift drums whose position is read by Hall sensors: drum A shifts 1st, 3rd and 5th, drum B reverse, 2nd, 4th and 6th. Ford's 2012 summary lists 'stuck in gear' codes for each drum: the module commands the drum out of a gear, but the gear stays engaged. It gives no thresholds or MIL rating. P072A means the transmission stays in neutral although a gear is commanded – no drive. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the DPS6 reports drum position faults under its own codes. On dual-clutch or automated manuals a drum or fork would fail to engage a gear, on planetary automatics clutch pressure would be missing. The opposite is P073D.

P0730.d: P0730 reports a wrong transmission ratio without assigning it to a gear. Two uses are documented. Older Aisin-type automatics (a 2006 GM table, Saab's 9-5 of 2002) set it when fourth or fifth gear shows the ratio of third – a shift solenoid (Saab: S3) is not switching; GM lights the MIL at once, Saab enters limp mode. GM's continuously variable transmissions of 2023 and 2025 use it when the pulleys do not reach the commanded variator ratio – the belt or chain slips or clamping pressure is too low – after one trip. Ford and newer GM step automatics use gear-specific or clutch valve codes instead. Check fluid level and condition first.

Slip is engine speed minus turbine speed. P075F.d: P075F is not a circuit fault but a condition: a working fluid level sensor reports a level above the target band – the counterpart of P070F. In the Allison patent the transmission module reports 'too high, drain a quart or more', measuring only with the vehicle at rest, warm fluid and low input speed. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. Overfilling makes rotating parts churn the fluid, which foams, pressure control becomes unsteady, fluid escapes at the vent and temperature rises; an FCA bulletin traces poor shifting after repairs to overfilling. Automatic transmission fluid level depends strongly on temperature – topping up cold often overfills.

On Saab's Aisin 5-speed E is valve S1. P0773 is the electrical code for solenoid E. GM's 2006 Allison tables flag a driver hardware fault for more than 0.1 s, cross-checked by pressure switch E, after one trip; Saab's Aisin 5-speed checks the current of valve S1 with fluid above 20 °C and shows 'check gearbox'; Hyundai/Genesis 8-speeds use it for clutch valve E and replace valve and electronic module. Ford does not use P0773.

Limp mode in a fixed gear
Harsh shifts

P077A.d: Some transmissions use an output shaft speed sensor that also reports direction of rotation: in a GM patent two offset Hall elements send one pulse per tooth whose width encodes forward or reverse. The direction is needed to detect rolling back on a hill (a Hyundai patent raises idle speed then), for hill hold, stop-start and the forward/reverse change. P077A means the sensor still delivers speed pulses but no usable direction information – the pulse width stays outside the direction windows or one Hall element has failed. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; GM checks direction coherence under P0721. Hill hold, auto hold or stop-start may then be disabled and the forward/reverse change runs in a substitute mode.

Rolling back on a hill not caught

P077B.d: Some transmissions use an output shaft speed sensor that also reports direction of rotation: in a GM patent two offset Hall elements send one pulse per tooth whose width encodes forward or reverse. The direction is needed to detect rolling back on a hill (a Hyundai patent raises idle speed then), for hill hold, stop-start and the forward/reverse change. P077B means the sensor reports a direction that does not fit – for example reverse while a forward gear is engaged and the input and intermediate shaft sensors confirm forward motion. GM's transmission modules list P077B as a blocking condition for other checks, but run the actual check under their own codes: direction contradicts the gear for 2.5 s above 500 rpm, after one trip. Speed and direction are then unreliable: hill hold and the park and reverse logic fall back to substitute modes.

P077C.d: GM's transmission modules from 2019 to 2025 (9- and 10-speeds) also read the active output speed sensor's line voltage as an analog value. P077C means this voltage is below 0.25 V – a short to ground of under about 0.5 Ω between signal and module ground – for more than 0.05 s with the system above 10 V; GM rates it after one trip. GM then blocks the no-signal and ratio checks so that P0722 is not set instead of the actual short. Without output speed the transmission enters limp mode and road speed may be missing. On GM's 10-speed input and output sensors share a supply.

P077D.d: GM's transmission modules from 2019 to 2025 (9- and 10-speeds) also read the active output speed sensor's line voltage as an analog value. P077D is the mirror of P077C: the voltage is above 4.75 V – a short to the module supply of under about 0.5 Ω – for more than 0.05 s, after one trip. GM then blocks the no-signal and ratio checks; a GM hybrid also blocks its idle diagnosis. Without usable output speed the transmission enters limp mode, and speedometer or cruise control may fail.

P077E.d: P077E is a plausibility check between several fluid temperature readings – for example sensors A and B, sump and valve body, or the module's internal temperature. If they differ by more than allowed after a settling time, such as a long stop, the code sets, without being able to blame a single sensor. No manufacturer document available to us uses it: GM checks each sensor alone (P0711, with the module temperature on the 6T70), and Ford has no multi-sensor check. A substitute value then limits converter clutch and shift adaption.

P077F.d: P077F checks the ratio in a second reverse gear: input speed divided by output speed lies outside the tolerance band around the target ratio – a slipping clutch, a wrong gear or a sensor fault. Only transmissions with two reverse ratios need it, such as Mercedes' 7G-Tronic (−3.42 and −2.23, with the second reverse kept in limp mode) and its 5G-Tronic predecessor; GM's 9- and 10-speeds, Ford's 10R and ZF's 8HP have one. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the check works like the other ratio codes such as P0736.

P0780.d: Shift codes are a functional check of the gear change itself: the module compares the commanded shift with the speed trace and flags a shift that takes too long, is too short or abrupt, does not happen, flares or ties up. Ford does not use P0780–P0784 (its shift completion check feeds the solenoid codes), nor do GM's 2018–2025 tables. P0780 is the collective code when the faulty shift is not assigned to a gear. GM's 2006 Aisin-type five-speed counts five shifts that are too long, too short or tied up with fluid above 60 °C and lights the MIL at once; GM's Honda-built unit flags a 3–4 shift that stays in the lower ratio after two trips; Saab's 2010 Aisin six-speed counts ten faulty shifts without MIL, limits torque and keeps second and reverse. Nissan fixed P0780 on the 2021 Rogue CVT with new software.

P0791.d: The intermediate shaft speed sensor measures a shaft between input and output – a countershaft on Toyota's U760 six-speed, the intermediate shaft behind the overdrive set on Ford's 5R110W. Together with turbine and output speed it lets the module check each gear stage and control clutch slip. Ford uses P0791 as its only intermediate shaft code, for 'no or too little signal': while the vehicle drives under power (turbine at least 1500 rpm, output at least 650 rpm or 15 mph), the sensor reports below 250 rpm for 5 s – in the 2012 and 2020–23 summaries, with MIL. A Toyota bulletin for the U760 (Highlander, Venza, Camry 2009–10) replaces the countershaft sensor for P0791/P0793. GM's 10-speed has two such sensors but uses its own codes. Limp mode and harsh shifts follow.

P0792.d: The intermediate shaft speed sensor measures a shaft between input and output – a countershaft on Toyota's U760 six-speed, the intermediate shaft behind the overdrive set on Ford's 5R110W. Together with turbine and output speed it lets the module check each gear stage and control clutch slip. P0792 means a signal is present but implausible: intermediate shaft speed does not match turbine or output speed for the detected gear stage, exceeds a maximum or jumps unrealistically. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code – Ford uses only P0791, Toyota's bulletin P0791/P0793, GM its own codes; the logic follows GM's range checks for input and output sensors (P0716/P0721). Ratio codes, by contrast, point to clutch slip rather than a sensor fault.

P07B2.d: With electronic gear selection the park position sensor/switch reports the park request or position. On GM's shift-by-wire selectors (2017 LaCrosse, XT4/XT5, Bolt EV, later SUVs and pickups) it is the P button, read by two redundant analog sensors A and B with separate 'released' and 'pressed' voltage zones. P07B2 means the circuit of sensor A is open: the module sees a missing or undefined signal. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; GM covers an open analog circuit under its low and high codes (P07B3/P07B4), which CARB allows when an open cannot be told apart from an out-of-range value. Park may then not be selectable by button.
